stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.question: Why do scores differ even within one method?
stages.miniPlan: Three students, their group, and their score.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a row to highlight the same dot; distinguish individual scores from group means.
stages.reference:
Imagine we are comparing test scores across three different teaching methods (Group A, B, and C).

If you look at the raw data in the visual panel, you'll notice that not everyone in Group A scored exactly the same. There is a natural spread, or noise, within every group. This is everyday biological, psychological, or measurement variation.

stages.title: The Research Question
stages.question: Is the gap large compared with ordinary variation?
stages.miniPlan: Same mean gap with small versus large within-group spread.
stages.interactionPlan: Adjust signal or noise separately with a fixed seed; keep the other quantity constant.
stages.reference:
Our question isn't about individuals; it's about the group averages (the group-mean markers).

Are the gaps between these group means large enough to confidently say the teaching methods have different effects? Or are the means just slightly off from each other by pure chance, drowning in the natural noise of the students?

Teaching Interaction: Shape the Data

stages.title: The Rules of the Game
stages.question: Which assumptions support this comparison?
stages.miniPlan: Assumption → visual symptom → appropriate response.
stages.interactionPlan: Switch between unequal spread, outlier, and repeated-student examples; state that design cannot be diagnosed from a plot alone.
stages.reference:
Before we build an ANOVA model, we must check our assumptions. If the data breaks the rules, standard ANOVA might mislead us.

Normality

Technically, ANOVA assumes the residuals (the error or distance of each point from its group mean) are normally distributed. In practice, researchers often check if the data within each group resembles a bell curve.

Homogeneity of Variance

The spread (variance) of scores should be roughly equal across all groups. ANOVA is robust to minor violations, provided sample sizes are equal.

Independence

Data points must not influence each other. If the same student is tested multiple times, you must use a Repeated-Measures ANOVA instead.

stages.title: Variance Decomposition
stages.question: Where does total variation come from?
stages.miniPlan: One observation's distance to its group mean and the grand mean.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal within-group and between-group squared distances in sequence; show their sum with correct weighting.
stages.reference:
• Between-Group Variance (Signal) The systematic variance associated with the independent variable. Measured by how far each group mean (group mean) deviates from the Grand Mean (dashed line).
  • Within-Group Variance (Noise) The unsystematic variance or error. Measured by how much individual dots deviate from their own group mean.

stages.title: The F-Statistic
stages.question: Why divide one mean square by another?
stages.miniPlan: A two-row MS-between / MS-within comparison.
stages.interactionPlan: Link each term of F to its visual component; compare a null-like and separated-groups scenario.
stages.reference:
ANOVA summarizes this decomposition into a single ratio, the F-statistic. It compares the size of the treatment effect to the size of the error.

$$F = \frac{\text{Between-Group Variance}}{\text{Within-Group Variance}}$$

stages.title: Degrees of Freedom
stages.question: Why are only some values free?
stages.miniPlan: Two editable numbers, a fixed total of 30, and computed third number.
stages.interactionPlan: Correct 8 + 15 + 7; transfer the constraint to k−1 and N−k using group counts.
stages.reference: Degrees of freedom count independent pieces of information after constraints are imposed. Three values with a fixed mean of 10 must sum to 30. If the first two are 8 and 15, the third is forced to be 7. For k groups and N observations, between-group df = k − 1 and within-group df = N − k. Dividing sums of squares by their appropriate df produces mean squares on a comparable variance scale.

stages.title: A Worked Example
stages.question: How do the numbers produce F?
stages.miniPlan: SS → df → MS → F arithmetic receipt.
stages.interactionPlan: Step through the displayed dataset calculation; synchronize the worked values with the current preset.
stages.reference:
Let’s bring this together using the data currently on display. We divide our sums of squared deviations (Sum of Squares, SS) by our degrees of freedom to get the Mean Squares (MS), which are variance quantities used in F = MS_between / MS_within. Under the null hypothesis and standard ANOVA assumptions, both estimate the same error variance.

From The Displayed Scores

Group means: A = 80, B = 68, C = 56. Grand mean = 68. Each group has n = 12, so N = 36.

Between-Group Signal

SSbetween = 12[(80 - 68)2 + (68 - 68)2 + (56 - 68)2] = 3456

Within-Group Noise

SSwithin = 132 + 132 + 132 = 396

Applying Degrees of Freedom

dfbetween = 2; dfwithin = 33.
MSbetween = 3456 / 2 = 1728.
MSwithin = 396 / 33 = 12.
F = 1728 / 12 = 144.

Scroll down to see these quantities organized into the universal language of statisticians: the ANOVA table.

stages.title: Reading the ANOVA Table
stages.question: How do I read an ANOVA table?
stages.miniPlan: Column glossary with SS, df, MS, F, and p.
stages.interactionPlan: Focus or tap a table cell to highlight its geometric meaning; keep explanations available without hover.
stages.reference: An ANOVA table reports a source of variation, its sum of squares, its degrees of freedom, and its mean square. The between-group F statistic divides MS between by MS within. Under the null and the ordinary independent normal equal-variance model, use numerator df = k − 1 and denominator df = N − k to obtain an upper-tail probability. A rejection concerns the family of means collectively; planned contrasts or adjusted follow-up comparisons address particular differences.

stages.title: How Big Is The Effect?
stages.question: Does a small p-value mean a large effect?
stages.miniPlan: Same effect size under two sample sizes.
stages.interactionPlan: Link eta-squared to the variance partition; separate association, uncertainty, and causal interpretation.
stages.reference:
A small p-value indicates that the observed result would be unusual under the null hypothesis, assuming the model assumptions hold. It is not the probability that the null is true or a measure of practical importance, so report an effect size and confidence intervals too.

Eta-Squared ($\eta^2$)

Eta-squared shows the proportion of the total variation in scores that is associated with differences between teaching-method groups, without establishing causation. We calculate it using the Sum of Squares from the table:

$\eta^2 = \frac{SS_{between}}{SS_{total}} = \frac{3456}{3852} = 0.90$

About 90% of the variation is associated with the group differences; this does not establish causation.

Notice the new column added to the ANOVA table in the visual panel. Depending on your software, this might be reported as Eta Squared, Partial Eta Squared, or $R^2$.

stages.title: Post-Hoc Testing
stages.question: Which groups differ?
stages.miniPlan: Three pairwise differences with intervals.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal adjusted pairwise comparisons together; show the multiplicity family and avoid an automatic unadjusted t-test sequence.
stages.reference:
A significant ANOVA is an omnibus test—it tells you a difference exists, but not where. Is A different from B? Is B different from C?

The Multiple Comparisons Problem

If you run three separate t-tests, your 5% chance of a false positive (Type I error) compounds. The more tests you run, the higher the Family-Wise Error Rate.

To follow up safely, we use Post-Hoc tests like Tukey's HSD. Under its assumptions, Tukey's controls the family-wise error rate at the chosen alpha level across the full set of pairwise comparisons. Look at the visual panel for the breakdown.

stages.title: Enter Two-Way ANOVA
stages.question: Why add a second factor?
stages.miniPlan: A 3 × 2 design grid.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a method–sleep cell and reveal its observations; preserve the distinction between factors and outcomes.
stages.reference:
So far, we've used a One-Way ANOVA to ask a single question: Does the teaching method matter? But reality is complex.

Let's extend our example. We take our original three teaching methods (A, B, and C) and introduce a second factor: the student's Sleep Level (High vs. Low).

Two-Way ANOVA now asks three questions at once: Does teaching method matter? Does sleep matter? And crucially, does the effect of one depend on the other? We are no longer comparing only 3 group means, but 6 distinct cells (3 methods × 2 sleep levels).

This allows us to explore how both variables simultaneously influence test scores.

stages.title: Cells & Marginal Means
stages.question: What is a marginal mean?
stages.miniPlan: Cell means, row means, column means, and weighting.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace a selected average from its cells; flag that equal averaging here assumes the balanced teaching design.
stages.reference:
To understand a two-way design, it helps to see how the data is organized. Look at this numeric structure for our extended teaching example:

Two-Way Data Structure

Sleep \ Method A B C Sleep Mean
High Sleep 82 74 66 74
Low Sleep 62 66 70 66
Method Mean 72 70 68 Grand: 70
  • Cell Means (The middle grid) A cell mean is the average score for one exact combination—like the students who received Method A AND High Sleep (82). Our design has 6 distinct cells.
  • Marginal Means (The outer edges) A marginal mean averages across one factor while ignoring the other. The marginal mean for Method A (72) combines both sleep levels. "Main effects" look only at these outer marginal means.

stages.title: The Interaction Effect
stages.question: What does an interaction mean?
stages.miniPlan: Difference of differences with a concrete numeric example.
stages.interactionPlan: Move from parallel to nonparallel lines; crossing is optional, and observed patterns alone do not establish significance.
stages.reference:
If the gap between methods stays consistent regardless of sleep, the lines in our plot will be roughly parallel. That suggests no interaction.

But if the lines are not parallel, it suggests an interaction. Crossing lines are not technically required for an interaction, but this example uses a strong crossing pattern to make the concept visually obvious: the effect of Method completely flips depending on Sleep.

How to Read the Interaction Plot

  1. Step 1: Check for parallel lines. If lines are roughly parallel, there is likely no interaction. If they cross or clearly change relative position, an interaction is present.
  2. Step 2: Look at overall height. If one line tends to sit higher on average, that suggests a main effect of Sleep.
  3. Step 3: Look at how the ranking changes. Notice which method is best under High Sleep, and then notice how that changes under Low Sleep. Here, the best method completely reverses!

stages.title: Building the ANOVA Table
stages.question: How is two-way variation partitioned?
stages.miniPlan: Method / sleep / interaction / residual contribution ledger.
stages.interactionPlan: Add one component at a time; retain clear balanced-design assumptions behind the decomposition.
stages.reference:
How do we get from our six cells to the statistical output? We partition the total variation into four distinct buckets:

Method (Main Effect)

Variation among the three Method marginal means (

72 vs 70 vs 68

). It asks if one teaching method is better on average. 2

Sleep (Main Effect)

Variation between the two Sleep marginal means (

74 vs 66

). It asks if well-rested students do better on average. 3

Method × Sleep (Interaction)

The leftover structured variance when the gaps between methods change across sleep levels. For High Sleep, A beats C by

+16

points. But for Low Sleep, C beats A by

+8 Error (Within-Cell Noise)

The natural random noise of individual students

within

each of the six specific cells.

To turn these buckets into our final results, each source gets its own Sum of Squares (SS). We divide each SS by its degrees of freedom (df) to get a Mean Square (MS). Finally, we compare each effect's MS to the Error MS to produce an F-ratio.

Why Averages Can Hide The Truth

Notice that our Method marginal means are quite close (72, 70, 68). Because the crossover pattern partly cancels out when averaged across sleep levels, the main effect of Method looks modest. But the interaction is large because the best method changes completely depending on sleep! This is why interactions should be considered before summarizing main effects.

stages.title: Reading the Two-Way Table
stages.question: What should I read first in the output?
stages.miniPlan: Interaction, then conditional comparisons, then qualified main effects.
stages.interactionPlan: Select output rows to highlight relevant lines and cells; remove claims that crossing alone confirms a population interaction.
stages.reference: Begin with the study design, model specification, and interaction estimates. A meaningful interaction means the effect of one factor depends on the other factor; inspect cell means and relevant contrasts rather than summarizing everything by one main effect. Report magnitudes and intervals alongside tests. In unbalanced designs, state the weighting and sums-of-squares convention because main-effect tests may answer different questions. A non-significant interaction test does not prove that the interaction is zero.

stages.title: Caveats & Recap
stages.question: When should I choose a different analysis?
stages.miniPlan: Design/variance condition → suitable method family.
stages.interactionPlan: Run a short scenario choice; distinguish invalid reference inference from an uncomputable F statistic.
stages.reference:
ANOVA is a beautiful, mathematically elegant tool for partitioning variance. But it is only a model of reality.

Assumptions are Key

ANOVA is robust, but severe violations of normality or independence will produce a completely meaningless F-statistic. Always check your residuals.

Look at the Data

Never rely solely on the p-value, tables, or bar charts. Plot the raw data (like our dot plot), check the boxplots, and ensure extreme outliers aren't driving the omnibus result.

Choose the ANOVA variant from the design:

use standard one-way ANOVA for similar variances, Welch ANOVA for unequal variances, Kruskal–Wallis or a robust alternative for strong non-normality or ordinal outcomes, and repeated-measures or mixed models for repeated observations. After a significant omnibus test, use planned contrasts or multiplicity-corrected post-hoc comparisons. Report group intervals and a named effect size such as eta-squared or omega-squared.

In one sentence: ANOVA asks whether the observed between-group variation would be unusual under an equal-means null model, assuming the chosen model and design conditions hold.

stages.title: The Prediction Problem
stages.question: Why can fitted predictions differ from reality?
stages.miniPlan: True function, noisy observation, fitted prediction.
stages.interactionPlan: Use a known simulated population and label which quantities are hidden in real data.
stages.reference:
Every dataset contains two things: the true signal we want to learn, and random static we should ignore.

A model's goal is to capture the underlying function f(x) while ignoring the irreducible error ε.

For our concrete example, let's predict a person's Income based on their Years of Education.

The dots are our raw historical data. The horizontal axis is Years of Education, and the vertical axis is Income. We need to draw a reliable line through them.

stages.title: High Bias (Underfitting)
stages.question: What does a consistently rigid model miss?
stages.miniPlan: Several underfit curves on repeated samples.
stages.interactionPlan: Resample with a fixed population and show their mean prediction as well as individual fits.
stages.reference:
The model is too stubborn. It assumes the relationship is completely straight and simple, ignoring reality.

Bias is the error introduced by choosing a model that lacks the complexity to represent the true data distribution.

A high bias model makes the exact same systematic mistake over and over again, regardless of how much data you feed it.

Quick Check: Does a high-bias model memorize the noise?

No. It does the opposite. It ignores the noise entirely, but unfortunately, it also ignores the genuine shape of the data.

The rigid red line forces a straight path through curved data. It is completely missing the underlying wave.

stages.title: High Variance (Overfitting)
stages.question: What makes a flexible fit unstable?
stages.miniPlan: The same x with predictions from several training samples.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare repeated fits; separate variability across datasets from residual noise within one dataset.
stages.reference:
The model is too easily distracted. It memorizes every single typo and random bounce in our training data.

Variance is the amount by which our model's curve would change if we estimated it using a different set of training data.

Like a student who memorizes a practice exam but fails the real test, an overfitted model cannot generalize to unseen future data.

The erratic blue line twists wildly to touch almost every single dot. It has learned the noise alongside the signal.

stages.title: The Error Decomposition
stages.question: Where does the squared-error decomposition apply?
stages.miniPlan: Noise + squared bias + variance at a fixed input.
stages.interactionPlan: Accumulate terms from repeated simulated samples; label empirical estimates and squared-error conditions.
stages.reference: At a fixed input x, assume Y = f(x) + ε with zero-mean noise independent of the training sample. Under squared loss, expected prediction error equals squared bias of the fitted prediction plus its variance across training samples plus the noise variance. Expectations refer to repeated training samples and a new outcome, not the residuals of one fitted dataset. Greater flexibility can change bias and variance, but neither the decomposition nor a neat U-shaped validation curve is a universal law for every learning problem or loss.

stages.title: Interactive: The Trade-Off
stages.question: Must error always follow a neat U-shape?
stages.miniPlan: Actual simulated error versus a schematic tradeoff curve.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub complexity and inspect repeated-sample results; avoid treating the illustrated sweet spot as a universal law.
stages.reference:
Let's look at how error changes step-by-step as we add complexity. As flexibility increases (moving right), Bias drops but Variance eventually spikes.

The purple model dynamically fits the data above, updating your position on the U-Curve below. Hitting the absolute bottom of the black Total Error curve is the Golden Rule.

stages.title: The Testing Problem
stages.question: Why is training error insufficient?
stages.miniPlan: Same model on seen versus unseen examples.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal an untouched development holdout and ask which score supports selection.
stages.reference:
A model that aces the practice quiz might still fail the final exam.

Training error often underestimates test error and is not a reliable estimate of future performance.

If we use all our finite data to train the model, we are flying blind. We must safely evaluate models on data they haven't seen yet.

The Solution: Resampling Methods. Resampling is how we practically estimate where the sweet spot lies using finite data. We strategically recycle our data by making repeated splits, rotating held-out folds, or redrawing samples.

stages.title: 1. The Validation Set
stages.question: Why can one validation split be noisy?
stages.miniPlan: Split IDs and validation MSE.
stages.interactionPlan: Redraw an explicit development split; rename Test labels to Validation and keep final test separate.
stages.reference:
Think of this as a practice exam used to choose a study strategy. A separate final exam remains hidden until that strategy is locked.

The dataset is randomly partitioned into two mutually exclusive sets: a "training set" to build the model, and a "validation set" to test it.

It is simple but noisy. If the validation pile happens to contain unusually hard cases, the score changes substantially. The estimate depends on one random split.

The Process:
1. Shuffle eligible independent observations.
2. Split development data into training and validation piles.
3. Fit candidate models on training data.
4. Choose among them using validation data.
5. Keep the separate final test set untouched.

The Trade-off:

We use a 50/50 development split below so it is easy to see. An 80/20 training/validation split is common, but the right choice depends on sample size and structure. A small validation set produces a noisy selection score; the final test set is separate. 👀

stages.title: 2. k-Fold Cross-Validation
stages.question: What does K-fold validation average?
stages.miniPlan: Per-fold fit, held-out prediction, score, and mean.
stages.interactionPlan: Step the folds with distinct fitted models; explain dependence among scores and limits on uncertainty claims.
stages.reference:
Instead of risking one lucky or unlucky test, we take turns. We divide the class into groups. Every single group gets exactly one chance to be the test group while everyone else studies.

The data is divided into k equal chunks (folds). We train k separate models, holding out a different chunk for validation each time, then average the k validation errors.

By averaging multiple different tests together, we dilute the "luck of the draw" from any single random split. It gives us a much fairer, more stable picture of how the model will actually perform in the real world.

The Process:
1. Chop the data into 5 equal chunks (folds).
2. Train a new model on 4 chunks. Test it on the 1 chunk left out.
3. Rotate. Pick a new chunk to be the test.
4. Repeat until every chunk has been the test exactly once.
5. Average all 5 test scores together.

Step through the folds. The orange test block slides down automatically. We build 5 entirely different models and log their scores. By averaging them all, we smooth out the jumps and find the truth.

stages.title: 3. Leave-One-Out (LOOCV)
stages.question: What changes in leave-one-out?
stages.miniPlan: One held-out row and almost-overlapping training sets.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a row, inspect its held-out error, and discuss computation and estimator-dependent variance without absolute claims.
stages.reference: Leave-one-out cross-validation fits n models, each withholding one of n observations, and averages the n held-out losses. Nearly all observations are available to every fit, but the fitted models overlap heavily. Its bias and variability depend on the learning procedure and the population; it is not uniformly better or worse than K-fold validation. Computational cost can be high, although some linear-model calculations have efficient shortcuts. The live fold selector illustrates five development folds; this paragraph explains the distinct leave-one-out procedure.

stages.title: 4. The Bootstrap
stages.question: What does sampling with replacement mean?
stages.miniPlan: Original IDs and a resample with repeated IDs.
stages.interactionPlan: Draw one bootstrap sample, then many; link duplicate counts to the estimator distribution and interval method.
stages.reference:
Imagine tasting a giant pot of soup. You take a spoonful and score it a 7.0. Is that score reliable, or was that just a lucky scoop? To find out, you stir the soup and taste it multiple times, getting slightly different scores: 6.8, 7.2, 6.9, 7.1. Bootstrap checks how much these scores vary or "wiggle."

Bootstrap is about generating many possible answers from the exact same data to check for stability. We repeatedly sample our original data with replacement, and recalculate our target number on each new sample.

If our taste scores stay tightly packed together (e.g., 6.8–7.2), our answer is highly stable. If they spread out wildly (e.g., 5.0–9.0), our result is unreliable. This gives us our margin of error.

The Process:

  1. Start with your original dataset (say it’s got 100 points).
  2. To make one ‘bootstrap sample,’ randomly pick one data point from your original set.
  3. Write it down, but don’t remove it. Put it back, so all points stay equally available.
  4. Repeat this random picking (with putting back) until you have a new sample the same size as the original. So if you started with 100 points, you pick 100 times.
  5. Now, calculate the average (or whatever metric you’re checking) from that new sample.
  6. Repeat this entire process hundreds or thousands of times. Each time, you get a slightly different average.
  7. Finally, look at all those averages. Their spread tells you how stable (or not) your original estimate is.
One-Sentence Takeaway:

stages.title: Limitations in Practice
stages.question: Which resampling method answers my question?
stages.miniPlan: Model selection / uncertainty / groups / time decision table.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a method for a scenario; include block or cluster resampling where independence fails.
stages.reference: A validation split is simple but its estimate can depend strongly on the allocation of a small dataset. K-fold cross-validation spreads held-out evaluation across the development observations. Leave-one-out uses the largest possible training fraction in each fold but can be computationally demanding or variable. Bootstrap resampling draws with replacement and supports many uncertainty procedures under suitable assumptions. These methods do not automatically handle temporal, spatial, or grouped dependence: the resampling unit must reflect the data-generating and deployment process.

stages.title: Summary & Synthesis
stages.question: Can I distinguish bias, variance, and uncertainty?
stages.miniPlan: Three short scenarios with different sources of error.
stages.interactionPlan: Require an explanation before revealing the method; retain a comparison table for later reference.
stages.reference:
A successful model must navigate the error puzzle. It requires enough complexity to avoid Bias, but enough restraint to avoid Variance. We rely on computational resampling to estimate how our model will generalize to the real world.

Memory Checklist

  • Bias: The model is too rigid (Underfitting).
  • Variance: The model is too jumpy (Overfitting).
  • Cross-Validation: Used to estimate future Test Error.
  • Bootstrap: Used to estimate Uncertainty and Std Errors.
Method Best Use Case Key Trait
Validation Set Quick, rough checks High Variability
k-Fold CV Model selection & Test Error Balanced
LOOCV Very small datasets Low Bias

stages.title: The Raw Counts
stages.question: Why use counts instead of averages?
stages.miniPlan: Four people allocated to four mutually exclusive cells.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a person and highlight their table cell; distinguish observed counts from percentages.
stages.reference:
The Chi-Square test evaluates categorical data—data placed into distinct bins or groups without an inherent numeric value.

Imagine we survey 50 students to see if there is a relationship between two categorical variables: Club Choice (Art vs. Sports) and Favorite Snack (Apples vs. Chips).

Rule of thumb: frequencies

(counts), not averages. Every individual belongs to exactly one cell in our table.

stages.title: Hypotheses & Marginals
stages.question: What does independence predict?
stages.miniPlan: Marginal totals and a common conditional proportion.
stages.interactionPlan: Lock margins and compare tables with different association patterns.
stages.reference:
Are club choice and favorite snack related, or are they completely independent? We formalize this question using hypotheses.

Null Hypothesis:

Club choice and favorite snack are

independent Alternative Hypothesis:

Club choice and favorite snack are

not independent

To test this, we must first look at the margins. The row totals and column totals tell us the overall preferences of the group, ignoring the split between the variables.

stages.title: Expected Counts
stages.question: Why multiply row and column totals?
stages.miniPlan: 30 Art students × 25/50 apple share = 15.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight each denominator and margin as the expected cell fills; reveal the other cells only after a prediction.
stages.reference:
If the Null Hypothesis is perfectly true, the counts inside the table should be directly proportional to the totals on the margins. This gives us our Expected Counts—the baseline of what we would expect if there were no relationship at all between club choice and snack preference.

To find the expected count for any cell in our table, we use this simple formula:

Expected Count = (Row Total × Column Total) ÷ Grand Total

In standard algebraic shorthand, it is written as:

E = (Row Total × Column Total) / Grand Total Step-by-Step Calculation: Art & Apple

Let's calculate the expected value for the first cell (Art students who prefer Apples):

E = (30 × 25) / 50 = 750 / 50 = 15

Why does this work?

Out of 50 total surveyed students, 25 like apples. That is exactly half (50%) of all students. If snack preference and club choice are completely unrelated (independent), then apples should be spread proportionally across both clubs.

Since 50% of the entire sample likes apples, we expect 50% of each club to like apples. Art has 30 students, and half of 30 is 15.

"If everything were random, about half of the Art students should like apples."

Interactive: Build an Expected Count

Select a cell to see how expected frequencies are generated under the assumption of independence:

Calculating the Remaining Cells

We apply the exact same formula to the other three cells:

  • Art & Chips: E = (30 × 25) / 50 = 15
  • Sports & Apple: E = (20 × 25) / 50 = 10
  • Sports & Chips: E = (20 × 25) / 50 = 10

The total number of apples is 25. If independent, we split these apples across the rows based on the size of each club:

  • Art has 30 out of 50 students (60% of the sample). Therefore, Art gets 60% of the expected apples: 60% of 25 = 15.
  • Sports has 20 out of 50 students (40% of the sample). Therefore, Sports gets 40% of the expected apples: 40% of 25 = 10.

The same logic applies to the chips category, which also has a column total of 25.

Expected count means:

how much this row deserves × how much this column deserves.

Warning:

Expected counts are not guesses from our opinion. They are calculated from the table totals under the assumption that the variables are independent.

stages.title: Residuals & Contributions
stages.question: Why square and divide by expected count?
stages.miniPlan: Observed → residual → square → contribution.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a cell and link its signed residual with its nonnegative contribution; sum unrounded values.
stages.reference:
The core intuition of Chi-Square is to compare what we Observed (O) with what we Expected (E). We square the residuals and divide by the expected count to scale the difference.

χ² = Σ [ (O - E)² / E ] Worked Example: Art & Apple contribution

Let's calculate the individual score contribution for Art students who prefer Apples:

Residual (O - E) = 20 - 15 = 5

Divide by expected: 25 ÷ 15 = 1.67

This cell contributes exactly 1.67 points to the overall Chi-Square statistic. Bigger contributions mean that cell is more responsible for the overall relationship.

Interactive Matrix:

We do this for every cell and add them all together to get our final test statistic. (Note: visual contributions are shown rounded to two decimals, but the true sum is roughly 8.33).

Check Your Progress: Residuals

Question: If observed = 20 and expected = 15, what does residual = +5 mean?

stages.title: The Reference Distribution
stages.question: How unusual is the statistic under independence?
stages.miniPlan: Statistic, df, alpha, and right-tail area.
stages.interactionPlan: Move a hypothetical statistic along the reference curve; replace the claim that chance has been ruled out.
stages.reference:
To evaluate our test statistic of 8.33, we map it onto a Chi-Square distribution. The curve's exact shape is determined by the Degrees of Freedom (df).

df = (Rows - 1) × (Cols - 1) = 1

If our statistic lands past the critical boundary (here, 3.84 for α = 0.05), the deviation is too large to be attributed to random chance.

stages.title: Reading the Output
stages.question: What can I conclude from the output?
stages.miniPlan: Evidence / association size / direction / causation, each separate.
stages.interactionPlan: Link the report to residual signs and effect size; mark descriptive size conventions as context dependent.
stages.reference: For the separate worked table with observed counts [20, 10; 5, 15], expected counts are [15, 15; 10, 10], N = 50, χ² = 8.333, df = 1, and the approximate upper-tail p-value is 0.00389. Before closing the book on this relationship, we must acknowledge the strict assumptions required for a valid Chi-Square test.

Required Conditions (Assumptions)

Before trusting any Chi-Square test, you must ensure your study meets these three non-negotiable assumptions:

Beginner meaning: You must use actual counts of people or items falling into categories, not averages or scores.

❌ Bad:

using average happiness ratings or continuous test scores.

✓ Good:

counting how many students chose apples or chips.

Beginner meaning: Each person should only appear once in the table. They cannot belong to multiple cells.

❌ Bad:

the same student is counted under both Art and Sports.

✓ Good:

each student belongs to one club category and one snack category.

Expected Counts are Large Enough

Beginner meaning: The expected numbers computed under independence should not be too tiny.

❌ Bad:

many expected cells are 1 or 2 (which can make the approximation unreliable).

✓ Good:

all expected counts in this example are at least 5 (our cells are 15, 15, 10, and 10).

Tiny expected counts can make the Chi-Square approximation unreliable. Yates' continuity correction applies specifically to 2×2 tables and does not guarantee a reliable approximation for very sparse data. Fisher's Exact Test is mainly used for small or sparse 2×2 tables; larger sparse tables may need other exact or Monte Carlo alternatives.

Interactive: Test Your Interpretation

Complete the sentences below to craft the final conclusion in plain English:

"There is evidence of a relationship between .

Art students are more likely than expected to prefer .

Sports students are more likely than expected to prefer ."

📖 The Whole Story in Plain English

Let's connect all the dots we've covered on this page into one simple, logical narrative:

  1. We counted students by club and snack: We started by putting students into categories based on two characteristics: their club (Art/Sports) and snack preference (Apples/Chips).
  2. We assumed independence: We asked: "What would this table look like if club and snack preferences had absolutely nothing to do with each other?"
  3. That gave us expected counts: Answering that question mathematically gave us our expected baseline counts (15, 15, 10, 10).
  4. We compared observed counts to expected counts: We looked at how far our actual observed numbers (20, 10, 5, 15) fell from that independent baseline.
  5. The differences were large enough: We squared and scaled these discrepancies, giving us a final test statistic of χ² = 8.33.
  6. The p-value was small, so we rejected independence: A discrepancy at least this large would be unusual under independence (p = 0.0039), assuming the test conditions hold. The data provide evidence against independence; Cramér’s V and residuals describe magnitude and contributing cells.
  7. The residuals showed the pattern: Looking closely at our cells, we saw the exact direction of this pattern—Art students lean apples, Sports students lean chips.

We have strong statistical evidence that club choice and snack preference are connected. However, Chi-Square demonstrates association, not causation. We cannot declare that joining the Art club causes students to eat apples.

Every problem starts with data. We have measurements for fruit — Weight (x-axis) and Color Intensity (y-axis).

Each fruit is already labeled: an Apple or an Orange. The goal of our tree is to learn rules to sort them into cleaner groups.

The Whole Idea of Classification Trees

A Classification Tree is a supervised machine-learning model that learns a sequence of simple yes/no flowchart-like questions to sort data into categories.

Raw Labeled Data → Root Node → Scan Best Question → Split Data → Repeat Recursively → Leaf Prediction → Evaluation

Tiny Tree Dictionary

• Feature:

A measurable property or input variable used to make predictions (e.g., Weight, Color Intensity).

• Label:

The target outcome or true answer we want the model to predict (e.g., Apple, Orange).

• Class:

One of the specific categorical outcomes (e.g., Apples vs. Oranges).

• Root Node:

The very first top-level block containing 100% of the training data.

• Split:

A division of a parent node into two child nodes based on a feature question.

• Child Node:

The subgroups created after splitting a parent node.

• Leaf Node:

A final terminal node that does not split further. It makes the final prediction.

• Impurity:

A measure of how mixed or diverse the class labels are within a particular node.

• Gini Impurity:

A mathematical metric used to calculate impurity (0.0 means perfectly pure; 0.5 is the maximum for a balanced binary node).

• Weighted Impurity:

The combined impurity of child nodes, weighted by the proportion of samples that went into each child.

• Impurity Decrease:

The difference between parent Gini and weighted child Gini. The tree maximizes this "gain".

• Decision Boundary:

The geometric line(s) dividing different class zones on the coordinate map.

• Tree Depth:

The length of the longest path from the root node down to any leaf node.

• Pruning:

Cutting back branches to simplify the model and improve generalizability on unseen data.

• Overfitting:

Memorizing noise in the training set, causing failure on unseen test data.

• Underfitting:

Creating a model that is too simple (e.g. too shallow) to learn the real underlying patterns.

Training Data Preview

This is a classification task because we want to predict a specific category or discrete group, rather than a continuous number.

To split effectively, the tree needs a way to measure how mixed a box is. We use a math rule called Gini Impurity.

A Gini score of 0.0 means the box is perfectly pure. For this binary example, 0.5 is the maximum at a 50/50 mix; multiclass maxima differ.

Gini Impurity Formula

Gini = 1 - Σ pᵢ² For two classes (Apple & Orange): Gini = 1 - [ P(Apple)² + P(Orange)² ]

Live Root Node Calculation

Gini Impurity vs. Entropy

While Gini is highly popular in CART (Classification and Regression Trees), another metric called Entropy is also widely used:

Both metrics measure the same core property: disorder. A node with equal proportions of classes has a Gini score of 0.50 and an Entropy score of 1.0. Both reach 0.0 when a node is perfectly pure. In practice, Gini and entropy often choose very similar splits, but not always. This guide uses Gini because it is simple, common, and easy to compute.

How does the tree find the best split? It tries testing candidate split points between observed values across the map.

The Candidate Search Strategy

How does a decision tree find the best threshold? It doesn't guess random decimals. Instead, it uses a deterministic mathematical process:

  1. Sort values: For a given feature (like Weight), it sorts all observed training values in ascending order.
  2. Compute Midpoints: It calculates the halfway points (midpoints) between every adjacent pair of unique values.
  3. Evaluate Splits: It treats each midpoint as a candidate threshold (e.g., Weight < 5.40), splits the data, and evaluates the resulting weighted Gini impurity.

The tree isn't done. It now treats each of the two new boxes as a separate problem, and asks again: "Can I perform another split to make these even cleaner?"

It repeats this process recursively, carving the map into smaller and smaller axis-aligned rectangles until a box becomes pure, gets too small, or reaches the depth limit.

Tree Stopping Rules

To prevent the tree from growing infinitely, we define stopping constraints (hyperparameters in ML frameworks):

  • Node Purity: Stop if all items in a node belong to a single class (Gini = 0).
  • Max Depth (`max_depth`): Stop if the path length from the root matches our limit.
  • Min Samples Split (`min_samples_split`): Stop if a node contains too few samples to allow another split.
  • Min Samples Leaf (`min_samples_leaf`): Prevent splits that leave a child with too few samples.
  • Min Impurity Decrease (`min_impurity_decrease`): Stop if Gini gain is below a small threshold.

stages.reference:
Classification Trees are incredibly intuitive, but they are not always the best tool for every job. Understanding their trade-offs is crucial for a data scientist.

Strengths vs. Weaknesses

When they shine:

  • Explainability: Outputs simple rules that any non-expert can read and audit.
  • No Scaling Required: Features are evaluated independently, so feature magnitude does not matter.
  • Handles Mixed Types Conceptually: Trees can split numerical and categorical predictors, but raw categorical support depends on the software. Some libraries require encoded categories; others implement native categorical splits.

When they struggle:

  • High Variance: Extremely sensitive to tiny training set alterations, which can yield completely different splits.
  • Axis-Aligned Boundaries: Since splits are purely horizontal or vertical, diagonal patterns require jagged, inefficient steps.
  • Overfitting: Easily memorize noise if depth is unchecked.
  • Class Imbalance: If one class is much more common, the tree may favor that class unless class weights, resampling, or better evaluation metrics are used.

Model Comparison Roadmap

Model Boundary Type Interpretability Best Used For...
Decision Tree Axis-Aligned Boxes High (Flowchart) Rules-based audits, mixed categorical/numerical data.
Logistic Regression Smooth Linear Medium (Weights) Linear associations with log-odds; estimated probabilities may need calibration.
K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Irregular / Local Low (Instance-based) Complex local shapes, feature manifolds.
Random Forest Complex / Smooth Low (Ensemble) High-accuracy, non-linear tasks (reduces variance).

The Upgrade Path: To overcome the instability and high variance of a single Classification Tree, we combine hundreds of trees into an ensemble. Models like Random Forests (voting trees) and Gradient Boosted Trees (sequential error correction) represent the state-of-the-art for tabular data!

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: How do alpha, beta, power, and effect size connect?
stages.miniPlan: A true-null/false-null decision table.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare null and specified alternative distributions; power is prospective for an alternative, not observed truth probability.
stages.reference:
A p-value is a tail probability calculated under H₀ and every model assumption; the null is conditioned on, not assigned a probability. A compatible confidence interval often inverts a family of tests. Sample size affects precision, so tiny effects can be statistically clear and important effects can remain uncertain. Power is planned against a specific meaningful alternative and is not the probability that an observed finding is true. Type I error means rejecting a true null hypothesis; α controls its probability under the test assumptions. Type II error means failing to reject a false null; its probability β depends on the particular alternative. Power = 1 − β is the chance of detecting that alternative. All else equal, lowering α generally lowers power, while larger sample sizes or larger effect sizes generally raise it. Family-wise and false-discovery-rate procedures answer different multiplicity goals. Neither repairs optional stopping, outcome switching or selective reporting after results are known.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

In statistics, we use a sample to make guesses about an entire population. To test if a correlation is "real", we set up formal hypotheses.

Null Hypothesis (H₀): ρ = 0

There is no linear correlation between the variables in the population. Any observed relationship is just random chance.

Alternative Hypothesis (H₁): ρ ≠ 0

There is a significant linear relationship between the two variables.

We use the Greek letter rho (ρ) for the population, and r for our sample.

stages.question: Why multiply deviations from the means?

How does the math actually figure out if they move together? It looks at the means.

r = Σ((X - X̄)(Y - Ȳ)) √[Σ(X - X̄)² × Σ(Y - Ȳ)²]

Translation: The sum of how they vary together, divided by the total of how they vary individually.

We draw a vertical line for the average of X, and a horizontal line for the average of Y. This creates four quadrants.

If points mostly fall in the Top-Right (both above average) and Bottom-Left (both below average), they are moving together. The formula multiplies their distances from the mean. Positive × Positive = Positive. Negative × Negative = Positive!

  • Linearity: The relationship must be relatively straight.

Imagine a scenario where cramming too much causes sleep deprivation, hurting test performance. Scores rise initially, then fall.

The math yields an r near 0, suggesting "no relationship." But visually, there is a strong curvilinear relationship. Always inspect the scatterplot first.

Pearson’s r uses covariance—products of deviations from the two means—scaled by the standard deviations. Extreme deviations can strongly change these quantities; a distant point can have high leverage, pulling the apparent linear relationship and the r value toward itself.
