We found a statistically significant relationship. But how far can we stretch our interpretation?

Interpretation:

"There was a significant positive correlation between hours studied and test score, r = --, --. Students who studied more tended to score higher."

However, we cannot say that studying caused the score to increase.

Correlation does not equal causation. Two variables might move together because of a third, confounding variable (e.g., Ice cream sales and sunburns both rise together, but the sun causes both).

stages.title: Limitations & Summary
stages.question: Which correlation should I use?
stages.miniPlan: Pearson / Spearman / neither, with conditions.
stages.interactionPlan: Classify linear, monotonic curved, and U-shaped examples; give corrective feedback rather than a blanket switch rule.
stages.reference:
To recap, correlation is an observational tool, not an experimental proof.

  • r measures linear tightness (from -1 to +1).
  • Check the plot: r is blind to curves and highly sensitive to outliers.
  • Significance vs. Size: A small p-value means the observed result would be unusual under H₀: ρ = 0, assuming the test assumptions hold. Report r, its confidence interval, sample size, and practical relevance.
  • Pearson versus Spearman: Pearson measures linear association; Spearman measures monotonic association through ranks. Spearman is not simply an outlier-proof Pearson, and neither fixes confounding, dependence, or a non-monotonic relationship.
  • Pearson vs. Spearman: Use Pearson for continuous data. Switch to Spearman if your data is ranked/ordinal or has a monotonic non-linear relationship.
  • No Causal Claims: It is only evidence of an association.

When you encounter a correlation, always ask: What does the scatterplot look like, and could a hidden variable be driving the pattern?

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: How can a good score be misleading?
stages.miniPlan: A feature available before versus after the outcome.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal the timing of each feature and identify an unavailable-at-prediction clue.
stages.reference: A model can appear excellent because information crossed the boundary between development and evaluation. Leakage estimates performance for a procedure that cannot exist in deployment.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What information is allowed to cross a split?
stages.miniPlan: Fit on train; transform held-out rows with frozen parameters.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace a scaler statistic across a pipeline and expose an intentionally leaked version.
stages.reference: Treat the pipeline—not only the final algorithm—as the model. Anything that learns a mean, category frequency, component, selected feature, threshold, or synthetic observation must learn it inside each training fold.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: What does leakage change in a concrete example?
stages.miniPlan: Safe versus leaked workflow with identical split IDs.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare an explicitly computed toy example or labeled schematic; explain why score inflation is not a fixed amount.
stages.reference: Suppose missing ages are filled with the mean of all 1,000 rows and then five-fold CV is run. Every validation fold has influenced its own imputed values. The honest workflow fits five separate imputers, each on that fold’s 800 training rows, and applies it to the 200 held-out rows.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: What kinds of leakage exist?
stages.miniPlan: Features, duplicate rows, groups, time, and repeated selection.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect one case per type; replace the repeated generic paragraph with specific causal paths.
stages.reference:
Leakage can enter through features, rows, groups, time or repeated comparison. A post-outcome billing code is feature leakage; duplicate images across folds are row leakage; tomorrow’s rolling average is time leakage; repeatedly checking the same test score creates selection leakage. Nested cross-validation separates inner model selection from outer evaluation. Target encoding, oversampling, outlier rules, feature selection, PCA and threshold selection are all estimators. Each must be re-learned within every training fold. The decisive audit question is whether a value, rule or analyst decision could have known anything about the held-out outcome.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: Can I repair this pipeline?
stages.miniPlan: Current ordering of split, imputation, scaling, selection, fit, score.
stages.interactionPlan: Select/move steps using buttons as well as drag; show exactly which fit call crossed the boundary.
stages.reference: Classify each pipeline as safe or leaking. Feedback identifies exactly where information crosses the boundary.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What can pipelines fail to prevent?
stages.miniPlan: Bad timestamps, target proxies, wrong groups, and changing availability.
stages.interactionPlan: Show an operationally impossible feature that remains invalid despite correct software ordering.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

The split must match the unit of independence and deployment timing. Features must exist at the moment a prediction is made.

When the method fails

Random CV fails for time order, repeated patients, households, organisations, duplicated rows, and target-derived features. Oversampling before CV creates near-duplicates across folds.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: How should nested selection work?
stages.miniPlan: Outer evaluation around an inner tuning loop.
stages.interactionPlan: Step one outer fold and reveal refitted inner transforms; preserve group/time constraints.
stages.reference:
1. Define prediction time and independent unit
  2. Reserve the final test set
  3. Choose stratified, grouped, time-series, or nested resampling
  4. Fit every learned transform inside training folds
  5. Lock and evaluate once

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: How do I document a defensible pipeline?
stages.miniPlan: Feature availability, split unit, fitted steps, and sealed test.
stages.interactionPlan: Produce a compact provenance checklist from concrete choices.
stages.reference:
What to report: Document split units, dates or groups, pipeline order, cross-validation variant, test isolation and every target-aware transformation.

Common misuse: Preprocessing the full dataset before splitting because “it is not the model.”

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I spot a new leakage path?
stages.miniPlan: One unfamiliar grouped/time-dependent scenario.
stages.interactionPlan: Ask which information crossed the boundary and how to repair it; give specific feedback for the chosen misconception.
stages.reference:
Answer and explanation

Scale all rows, then cross-validate. Scaling all rows lets each validation fold influence its own transformation.

Where should oversampling happen?

Answer and explanation

Inside each training fold. Oversampling must not create synthetic or duplicated information across held-out boundaries.

Repeated visits from each patient require…

Answer and explanation

Grouped CV by patient. All visits from one patient belong in the same fold.

Answer and explanation

Time-ordered validation. Every validation observation must occur after the observations used to fit it.

Answer and explanation

Using information unavailable at prediction time that reveals the outcome. Availability at the real prediction moment is the key test.

stages.title: Define the finish line
stages.question: What exactly should the system output?
stages.miniPlan: Classify / locate / segment, with one input image.
stages.interactionPlan: Keep the image stable while outputs change; explain that example scores are illustrative.
stages.reference:
Frame the question

Deep learning starts with a decision, not a network. You first describe the real task in a way that can be demonstrated with examples and measured with evidence.

A vague goal such as “recognise animals” leaves too many questions unanswered. Should the model find every animal, draw a box around it, or choose one label? Clear boundaries determine the data you need, the output layer you build, and the mistakes you measure.

  1. 1

    Write down one realistic input and the exact output you want back.

  2. 2

    Name the task: classification, regression, detection, segmentation, sequence prediction, or generation.

  3. 3

    Choose success measures that reflect the real cost of mistakes—not simply the easiest score to calculate.

Picture it: Imagine writing an exam rubric before teaching the course. The rubric decides what counts as a correct answer.

For our animal example, one image goes in and three probabilities come out. The largest probability becomes the predicted class.

Example output

0.89 0.08 0.03

stages.title: Collect reality, not shortcuts
stages.question: What shortcut might the model learn?
stages.miniPlan: Animal label versus background, with counterexamples.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a suspicious cue and reveal a counterexample; connect data collection choices to failure modes.
stages.reference:
Build the evidence

A dataset is the model’s entire experience of the world. It will use any regular pattern that helps, whether that pattern expresses the true idea or an accidental shortcut.

If every dog is photographed on grass and every cat is photographed on a sofa, “background” becomes an easier clue than “animal.” The model can score well in the lab and fail immediately in a real home, park, shelter, or veterinary clinic.

  1. 1

    Collect variation in lighting, background, angle, distance, appearance, position, and image quality.

  2. 2

    Inspect examples by class and source; look for rare classes, duplicate files, broken records, and inconsistent labels.

  3. 3

    Ask what unrelated clue could reveal the answer. Then deliberately collect counterexamples that break that shortcut.

Picture it: A child shown only red apples may decide that “apple” means “red.” Variation teaches which features stay true when the scenery changes.

More examples help only when they add useful coverage. Ten thousand copies of the same narrow situation are still narrow data.

stages.title: Split before you tune
stages.question: Which examples may influence which choices?
stages.miniPlan: Training weights / validation choices / sealed final test.
stages.interactionPlan: Move a duplicate or related-source group into an intentionally wrong split, then repair it with keyboard controls.
stages.reference:
Protect the experiment

To know whether a model can handle new cases, some examples must remain outside the learning process. Each split has one job and should not quietly take on another.

When the model—or the people tuning it—repeatedly sees the final test answers, the score stops measuring generalisation. Duplicate images, the same patient in two splits, or future data leaking into the past can create confidence without real ability.

  1. 1

    Use training data to update weights and validation data to compare choices, tune settings, and decide when to stop.

  2. 2

    Seal the test set until the architecture and meaningful choices are fixed, then use it once for the final estimate.

  3. 3

    Keep related people, videos, devices, or time periods together, and learn preprocessing statistics from training data only.

Picture it: Training is the textbook, validation is the practice exam, and testing is the sealed final. Copying a question between them breaks the exam.

A 70/15/15 split is only an example. The important idea is separation; the right percentages depend on dataset size and structure.

stages.title: Turn examples into tensors
stages.question: What is a tensor's shape?
stages.miniPlan: One image channel, token ID, embedding row, or audio window.
stages.interactionPlan: Follow one input through the chosen representation; avoid implying token IDs have numeric semantic distances.
stages.reference:
Translate the world

A network cannot receive “a dog,” “a sentence,” or “a melody” directly. It receives a tensor: an organised block of numbers whose shape preserves useful structure.

The representation determines what relationships are easy to learn. Images need nearby pixels to stay nearby, text needs token order, and audio needs precise changes through time. Preprocessing is therefore part of the model’s language, not mere housekeeping.

  1. 1

    Images become rows and columns of pixel intensities, usually with red, green, and blue channels.

  2. 2

    A tokeniser breaks text into reusable pieces—sometimes a whole word, punctuation mark, or word fragment. Each piece receives an integer ID from a fixed vocabulary.

  3. 3

    An embedding table replaces each token ID with a learned vector. Audio is sampled into amplitude numbers; a spectrogram then summarises which frequencies are strong in each short time window.

Picture it: Think of representation as translation. The language changes from pictures or words to numbers, but the useful grammar—space, order, or time—must survive.

The same resize, tokeniser, vocabulary, sample rate, and normalisation must be used during training and real use. Changing them changes what the numbers mean.

Image · position becomes tensor shape

  1. 1

    Resize or crop the image to a known height and width.

  2. 2

    Turn each pixel channel into a number, often scaled to a small common range.

  3. 3

    Keep the row, column, and colour-channel axes so nearby pixels remain neighbours.

Picture it: A 224 × 224 × 3 tensor is a numbered colour grid: height, width, and three colour channels.

stages.title: Inside one neuron
stages.question: What does one neuron do?
stages.miniPlan: x·w terms, bias, sum, activation.
stages.interactionPlan: Change one weight and trace a computed result; synchronize the left receipt and right neuron.
stages.reference:
Meet the smallest learner

One artificial neuron is a small decision-maker. It combines several signals into one new signal that later neurons can use.

The neuron matters because the whole network is built from this repeatable operation. The complexity comes from learning many useful combinations and stacking them, not from one magical component.

  1. 1

    Multiply every input by a weight. A large positive weight strengthens a clue; a negative weight can argue against it.

  2. 2

    Add a bias, which shifts how much total evidence is needed before the neuron responds.

  3. 3

    Apply an activation such as ReLU. This non-linearity lets layers combine into curved, flexible decision boundaries.

Picture it: Picture a sound-mixing desk. Each input has a volume slider, the bias sets the baseline, and the activation decides what signal leaves the desk.

stages.title: Depth builds features
stages.question: Why might depth help?
stages.miniPlan: Local pattern → composition → task-useful feature.
stages.interactionPlan: Step through a labeled illustrative hierarchy; explain that every network need not learn literal ears or eyes.
stages.reference:
Stack useful transformations

A deep network turns the same example into a sequence of increasingly useful descriptions. Each layer receives the previous layer’s features and composes them into larger ideas.

Raw pixels are a poor language for “dog.” Edges are more useful; groups of edges can describe fur or curves; those patterns can form ears, eyes, and snouts. Hierarchy lets the model reuse simple discoveries to build complex ones.

  1. 1

    Early layers respond to local changes such as edges, colour transitions, or short sound patterns.

  2. 2

    Middle layers combine repeated local clues into textures, shapes, or meaningful phrase fragments.

  3. 3

    Later layers gather evidence across a wider area and make features useful for the final task.

Picture it: It is like looking through a stack of tracing sheets. Each sheet redraws the scene using the patterns that matter at its level.

The feature names are a helpful simplification, not rules written by a programmer. Training discovers the filters that reduce the loss.

stages.title: How learning happens
stages.question: How does the correction cycle work?
stages.miniPlan: Forward/loss/backprop/update with one numeric parameter.
stages.interactionPlan: Keep marks persistent across phases; gradients appear before weights change; provide pause and rewind.
stages.reference:
The correction cycle

Learning is a repeated correction loop. Forward pass → loss → backpropagation computes gradients → optimiser updates weights. The network makes predictions, measures error, computes how the loss changes with each weight, and uses those gradients to adjust the weights.

A loss number alone says only “this was wrong.” Backpropagation turns that complaint into useful directions for millions of parameters, so an optimiser can use the loss gradients to update the weights.

  1. 1

    Forward propagation moves a batch through the layers and produces predictions.

  2. 2

    A loss function compares predictions with the correct answers; backpropagation calculates gradients from output to input.

  3. 3

    An optimiser uses those gradients to update the weights. The learning rate controls how large each step is.

Picture it: Imagine descending a foggy hill. The gradient tells you which way slopes downward; the learning rate decides whether you take careful steps or dangerous leaps.

One update teaches very little. Useful behaviour emerges from many batches of examples providing many small, partly noisy corrections.

stages.title: Learn patterns, not the answer sheet
stages.question: How do we reduce overfitting?
stages.miniPlan: Method / what changes / when used / tradeoff.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare dropout training/evaluation, augmentation, weight decay, and early stopping as distinct interventions.
stages.reference:
Train with discipline

Training must continue long enough to discover stable patterns, but not so blindly that the model memorises quirks of the training set.

Training loss almost always rewards more training. Validation data asks the more important question: are these improvements useful on examples that did not update the weights?

  1. 1

    Train on small batches; one pass through every training example is an epoch. Switch to evaluation mode before validation.

  2. 2

    Plot training and validation curves together. High values for both suggest underfitting; a widening gap suggests overfitting.

  3. 3

    Use augmentation, weight decay, dropout, a simpler model, or early stopping—and save the best validation checkpoint.

Picture it: One coach watches practice; another watches an unseen match. If practice keeps improving while match performance worsens, the player is learning the drill rather than the game.

Hyperparameters such as learning rate, batch size, depth, and dropout are chosen with validation evidence. They are not learned like ordinary weights.

Move through training epoch 12

underfit useful fit overfit

stages.title: Choose an architecture
stages.question: Why choose CNN, RNN, or attention?
stages.miniPlan: Locality / sequential state / pairwise context comparison.
stages.interactionPlan: Give each architecture a readable subscene and one traceable input; avoid fitting all mechanisms into miniature labels.
stages.reference:
Match shape to problem

An architecture is a set of useful assumptions about how information is organised. The right design makes important patterns easier and cheaper to learn.

Images contain many local patterns, not one universal feature. Sequences need memory or direct links across time. Architecture decides how information is shared, how far context can travel, and what the model can compute efficiently.

  1. 1

    A CNN layer learns many filters. Every filter scans every image, producing its own feature map. Training changes the filter values; testing reuses the learned filters without inventing new ones.

  2. 2

    An RNN reads one item at a time and updates a hidden state—a fixed-length vector that compresses what it has seen. That state can produce scores for the next word or another sequence output.

  3. 3

    A Transformer creates a query, key, and value for every token. Query–key matches become attention weights, which gather useful values into context. Training rewards links that help reduce prediction error.

Picture it: Choose a tool shaped like the material: a movable stencil for space, a notebook passed through time, or a web of spotlights for attention.

Choose with evidence, not fashion. CNNs remain natural for spatial data. RNNs can suit compact streaming systems. Transformers usually handle long context and parallel training better, but standard attention can require much more memory as a sequence grows.

CNN · a bank of reusable spatial detectors

  1. 1

    A layer learns many filters—not only one. Early filters may respond to different edges, colours, or textures.

  2. 2

    Every learned filter scans every training image and every test image. One filter produces one feature map showing where its pattern responded.

  3. 3

    Training adjusts all filter values. At test time those values are frozen and reused; the model does not design a special filter for each new picture.

  4. 4

    Later layers combine the stack of feature maps into more complex evidence such as curves, parts, or whole objects.

Picture it: Picture a case of many reusable stencils. Every stencil is swept across every picture, producing its own map of matches.

When to choose it: Choose a CNN when locality and spatial reuse matter—images, video frames, grids, or compact vision systems. CNN ideas are also often combined with attention.

stages.title: Start from a pretrained model
stages.question: What is reused during transfer learning?
stages.miniPlan: Frozen backbone, new head, then selected unfrozen layers.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle trainable regions with clear parameter labels; show the exact adaptation sequence and domain-mismatch caveat.
stages.reference:
Reuse useful experience

Transfer learning starts from a model that has already learned general patterns from a large dataset, then adapts that knowledge to your narrower task.

Training a large network from random weights can require enormous amounts of labelled data and computation. Useful early features—edges, textures, shapes, language patterns—often transfer between related tasks.

  1. 1

    Replace the old output head with one that matches the new classes or target.

  2. 2

    First freeze the pretrained backbone and train only the new head; this tests the existing features cheaply.

  3. 3

    If needed, unfreeze some layers and fine-tune gently with a smaller learning rate so useful knowledge is not destroyed.

Picture it: A trained carpenter does not relearn how to measure and cut wood for every new table. They reuse general craft and learn the new design.

Transfer works best when the earlier data and new task share useful structure. A model can also transfer unwanted biases, so evaluation still matters.

stages.title: Make an honest judgement
stages.question: What would make an evaluation honest and useful?
stages.miniPlan: Per-class counts, calibration, subgroup slices, chosen threshold.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect errors after a locked choice; label subsequent model revisions as needing fresh evaluation.
stages.reference:
Earn confidence

Evaluation asks not only “how often is it right?” but “where, for whom, and with what confidence does it fail?” The final test set estimates performance on actually unseen data.

A model can reach 95% accuracy by always predicting the common class in an imbalanced dataset. In medicine, fraud, or safety, one missed positive can matter far more than one false alarm.

  1. 1

    Evaluate the selected checkpoint once on the untouched test set and report class-level precision, recall, F1, and support.

  2. 2

    Read the confusion matrix and inspect individual errors for bad labels, rare conditions, occlusion, or shortcut patterns.

  3. 3

    Check calibration, uncertainty, and subgroup performance. Choose decision thresholds on validation data using real-world costs.

Picture it: Accuracy is the final grade; the confusion matrix is the marked paper showing which questions were misunderstood.

Lower thresholds usually find more true positives but create more false alarms. Higher thresholds usually do the opposite.

find more balance fewer alarms

stages.title: Ship the whole pipeline
stages.question: What does deployment actually package?
stages.miniPlan: Input contract → transforms → model → decision → monitoring.
stages.interactionPlan: Break one contract deliberately and repair it; show drift monitoring without implying drift alone proves failure.
stages.reference:
Move beyond the notebook

A deployed model is not only a weights file. It is a complete, repeatable route from raw input to a decision that behaves the same way outside the training notebook.

A brilliant model can produce nonsense if the live system resizes differently, swaps class order, forgets normalisation, or leaves dropout active. Failures can occur at the interfaces around the network.

  1. 1

    Save the architecture, weights, class order, dimensions, normalisation, tokeniser, threshold, software versions, and configuration.

  2. 2

    Validate the input, apply the same preprocessing, switch to evaluation mode, disable gradients, predict, and decode the result.

  3. 3

    Test the complete pipeline in its target environment for latency, memory, privacy, energy use, throughput, and failure handling.

Picture it: Treat deployment like sealing a recipe with its ingredients, measurements, oven settings, and serving rule—not saving only the cake tin.

The same pipeline may run on a phone, API, browser, hospital system, edge device, or cloud GPU. The constraints can change which model is best.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: What causal comparison do we want?
stages.miniPlan: Population, treatment, comparator, outcome, time.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a concrete estimand before choosing a statistical test.
stages.reference: Causal conclusions depend more on assignment, measurement and follow-up than on a sophisticated final test. Design defines what comparison the data can identify.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What does random assignment accomplish?
stages.miniPlan: Confounder balance in expectation versus one realized allocation.
stages.interactionPlan: Randomize repeatedly and show finite-sample imbalance; separate assignment from random sampling.
stages.reference: Random assignment balances confounders in expectation. Blocking improves balance on known prognostic variables; clustering changes the independent unit; blinding protects measurement and behaviour.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: Why are twenty schools not six hundred independent assignments?
stages.miniPlan: School clusters with student members.
stages.interactionPlan: Select an assignment unit and highlight all its students; keep the independent unit explicit.
stages.reference: Twenty schools—not 600 students—are randomised to a teaching programme. Student outcomes remain clustered within schools. Treating 600 rows as independent exaggerates precision; analysis and power must account for 20 randomisation units and intraclass correlation.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: How do blocking, blinding, and intention-to-treat differ?
stages.miniPlan: Design choice / threat addressed / what it does not fix.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace one participant from assignment through analysis; retain noncompliance and interference caveats.
stages.reference:
An estimand specifies population, treatment strategies, comparator, outcome, time and summary contrast. Allocation concealment protects enrolment; blinding protects behaviour and measurement. Blocking randomises within prognostic strata. Cluster randomisation assigns groups and reduces effective sample size through intraclass correlation, so power and analysis must use the randomisation unit. Intention-to-treat preserves the randomised contrast; per-protocol analysis answers a different, more selection-sensitive question. Noncompliance, attrition and interference should be anticipated in the protocol. Power planning must include meaningful effect, variance, allocation, clustering, multiplicity and attrition.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: How does clustering affect effective information?
stages.miniPlan: Design effect 1+(m−1)ICC and n/design effect.
stages.interactionPlan: Adjust n, cluster size, and ICC; label approximation assumptions and replace the ad hoc power formula before presenting it as calculated power.
stages.reference: For equal cluster sizes m and intraclass correlation ρ, the approximation DE = 1 + (m − 1)ρ describes inflation in variance relative to simple independent sampling under its assumptions. Effective n = n/DE is a rough information comparison. It is not a complete power calculation: power also depends on the number of clusters, allocation, effect and outcome variance, analysis model, unequal sizes, attrition, and multiplicity. The live example reports design effect and approximate effective sample size only.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What can break a randomized comparison?
stages.miniPlan: Attrition, spillover, noncompliance, and outcome switching.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a failure and show the broken comparison; do not suggest randomization cures every later bias.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

Assignment is implemented as planned, outcomes are measured consistently, interference is limited or modelled, and attrition does not destroy exchangeability.

When the method fails

Noncompliance, differential attrition, spillovers, outcome switching, hidden multiplicity and analysing below the randomisation unit can bias results or uncertainty.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: What should be planned before recruitment?
stages.miniPlan: Estimand, unit, allocation, power, outcomes, analysis, missingness.
stages.interactionPlan: Build the protocol in causal order; include plausible attrition and number of clusters.
stages.reference:
1. Define population, intervention, comparator, outcome and estimand
  2. Choose the randomisation unit
  3. Block or stratify when justified
  4. Plan sample size with clustering and attrition
  5. Pre-specify primary analysis and multiplicity
  6. Track adherence and missingness
  7. Report intention-to-treat and justified secondary analyses

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What belongs in a transparent report?
stages.miniPlan: Allocation, exclusions, adherence, effect/interval, harms, deviations.
stages.interactionPlan: Fill a short report and identify a missing design fact.
stages.reference:
What to report: Report protocol, randomisation and concealment, units, exclusions, attrition, adherence, effect with confidence interval, harms, multiplicity and deviations.

Common misuse: Randomising classrooms but analysing pupils as though all observations were independent.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I identify the unit and analysis implication?
stages.miniPlan: A new clinic/classroom randomization scenario.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose the independent unit and explain why row count is insufficient; retain static feedback.
stages.reference:
Schools assigned to treatment means the randomisation unit is…

Answer and explanation

School. Assignment occurred at the school level.

Clustering usually makes naive standard errors…

Answer and explanation

Too small. Within-cluster similarity reduces effective independent information.

Answer and explanation

The population-level causal contrast of interest. It defines precisely what effect the study aims to estimate.

Answer and explanation

Improve balance and precision on known factors. Randomisation still occurs within planned blocks.

Twenty outcomes tested without a plan create…

Answer and explanation

Multiplicity risk. More tests create more chances for a small p-value.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: Why add another learner to the current model?
stages.miniPlan: Current prediction, error, proposed correction.
stages.interactionPlan: Show a weak learner contributing a small improvement rather than replacing the ensemble.
stages.reference: Instead of averaging independent trees, boosting builds a sequence in which each new weak learner targets the current model’s loss gradient.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What is learned at the next round?
stages.miniPlan: Negative loss gradient; squared-error residual as a special case.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight targets for a new learner under squared loss, then explain why other losses differ.
stages.reference: Learning rate controls how much each tree contributes; tree count controls how many correction steps occur. Small learning rates often need more trees, so these settings must be tuned together.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How do three rounds build a prediction?
stages.miniPlan: Initial prediction + learning-rate-scaled corrections.
stages.interactionPlan: Step the additive calculation with actual values and a consistent selected row.
stages.reference: Start with the training mean, for example F₀ = 10. If three fitted learners return 4, −1, and 2 for the same row, a learning rate of 0.2 gives F₃ = 10 + 0.2(4 − 1 + 2) = 11. Each learner was fitted to the loss gradient created by the preceding model, so changing the learning rate generally requires refitting the entire sequence. The live experiment uses actual residual trees and measured training and validation MSE; no universal best learning rate or stopping round is assumed.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: Why do learning rate and round count interact?
stages.miniPlan: Few large steps versus many small contributions.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare trajectories with fixed training data; explain that their product alone is not a complete equivalence.
stages.reference:
Boosting creates an additive predictor by fitting each learner to a negative loss gradient. For squared error this resembles residual fitting, but other losses create different pseudo-residuals. Learning rate scales contributions, tree depth limits interactions, and row or feature subsampling regularises. These settings interact, so learning rate and round count must be tuned together. Training loss normally keeps falling and cannot select stopping. Validation-based early stopping is a hyperparameter choice. Class weighting changes the objective and can damage calibration. Gain importance and attribution methods explain the fitted model, not a causal mechanism.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: The Uncharted Planet
stages.question: What does grouping without an answer key mean?
stages.miniPlan: Two reasonable partitions of the same objects.
stages.interactionPlan: Select the feature representation first; avoid claiming there is one natural grouping waiting to be discovered.
stages.reference:
Imagine landing on a distant planet with no map or guidebook. Your goal isn't to reach a destination; it's simply to see what is there. This is the essence of Unsupervised Learning.

Unlike supervised learning, where we try to predict a specific answer, here we only have features. We are discovering the natural structure of the data.

The Toy Box Analogy:

Think of a child given a massive box of mixed toys and told to "find the patterns." Without instructions, they group them naturally by similarity.

To the right, we have a raw dataset. Just points in space waiting to be understood.

Takeaway: Unsupervised learning is about revealing structure that is already hiding in the data.

stages.title: Measuring "Close"
stages.question: How do we define close?
stages.miniPlan: One distance calculation with x/y contributions.
stages.interactionPlan: Link a distance-matrix cell to two points; compare Euclidean and an appropriate alternative.
stages.reference:
Before we can group anything, we must define what "similar" means. The most common way is to measure the physical distance between data points.

We use the Euclidean distance (the straight-line distance) to find out who is closest to whom. It is common, but not the only option; Manhattan, cosine, or domain-specific distances can make more sense for different data.

d(A, B) = √[ (x₂ - x₁)² + (y₂ - y₁)² ]

By measuring the distance between every single pair of points, we build a "distance matrix"—a lookup table for similarity.

Takeaway: Clustering depends on your distance choice, because "close" is a design decision.

stages.title: The First Merge
stages.question: Why merge this pair first?
stages.miniPlan: Sorted candidate distances with a tie policy.
stages.interactionPlan: Predict the closest pair, then merge while preserving member identities.
stages.reference:
Hierarchical clustering (specifically the Agglomerative or "bottom-up" kind) starts with a simple rule:

  1. Every point starts as its own separate cluster.
  2. Find the two clusters that are closest together.
  3. Merge them.

Watch as the algorithm scans all points, finds the single closest pair, and binds them into a new, single cluster.

Takeaway: Agglomerative clustering grows structure from the bottom up, one merge at a time.

stages.title: Defining Group Distance (Linkage)
stages.question: How far apart are groups?
stages.miniPlan: Single / complete / average / Ward definitions.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight contributing pairs and recompute the selected linkage; label Ward's increase-in-variance meaning.
stages.reference:
Linkage and distance are not interchangeable. Ward linkage is tied to Euclidean geometry and increases in within-cluster variance. Single linkage can chain; complete linkage favours compact groups; average linkage is a compromise. Dendrogram heights do not represent the same quantity for every method.

Merging two individual points is easy. But how do you measure the distance between a single point and a group? Or between two groups?

This is called Linkage. The linkage method you choose changes the shape of the clusters.

Takeaway: Linkage is the rulebook for deciding which groups are "closest" once clusters start to grow.

stages.title: The Process in Motion
stages.question: How is the merge history built?
stages.miniPlan: Before/after group membership for one merge.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub cached merge snapshots in both directions; synchronize point clusters, matrix, and dendrogram.
stages.reference:
Now, the algorithm repeats the rule over and over. It constantly recalculates distances using the linkage method, finding the next closest pair of clusters, and merging them.

Slowly, tiny groups fuse into medium groups, which fuse into large groups. It only stops when everything becomes one giant family. Use the merge scrubber in the visual to step through the history one merge at a time.

Takeaway: The algorithm keeps rebuilding the distance picture after every merge, so the path matters.

stages.title: The Family Tree (Dendrogram)
stages.question: What does dendrogram height represent?
stages.miniPlan: One merge annotated with the selected criterion.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight a branch and its original members; never imply all linkage heights mean the same distance.
stages.reference:
Instead of just looking at circles on a map, we can record the exact history of these merges in a tree structure called a Dendrogram.

As the points align at the bottom, watch the tree grow upwards. The vertical height of each branch is critical: it tells us exactly how far apart the two groups were when they merged.

Rule of thumb:

A fusion low on the tree means the items were very similar. A fusion high up means they were quite different.

Takeaway: A dendrogram preserves the full merge history, and branch height tells you how costly each merge was.

stages.title: Cutting the Tree
stages.question: How does a horizontal cut produce K groups?
stages.miniPlan: Cut height → intersected branches → memberships.
stages.interactionPlan: Drag or numerically set the cut; keep leaf identity and colors stable across nearby cuts.
stages.reference:
What if you don't know how many clusters you need? That is the superpower of hierarchical clustering: you don't have to guess upfront.

By drawing a horizontal line across the dendrogram, you "cut" the branches. The number of vertical lines you intersect is your number of clusters (K).

How do you choose the cut? A good first strategy is to look for a big jump in merge height and cut just below it, because that often means the algorithm has started forcing together groups that were meaningfully different. If you want a more quantitative check, you can also compare several cuts with a metric such as silhouette score.

Takeaway: Choose cuts where the tree shows a natural separation, not just where a slider gives a convenient K.

stages.title: The Detective's Challenge
stages.question: How sensitive is the tree to preprocessing?
stages.miniPlan: Same data under raw scale, standardized scale, and one outlier.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare alternative trees with stable leaf IDs; make each metric change explicit.
stages.reference:
Clustering is subjective detective work. Because there is no "true" answer (no target variable Y), the results rely entirely on your choices.

The "Socks and Computers" Problem

If variables use different units or their raw scales should not control distance, scale them using training data only. When variables share meaningful units and variance differences matter, standardisation may be undesirable.

Furthermore, an outlier can distort the tree, pulling a group away from its true members just to accommodate the stranger.

Takeaway: Scaling and outliers can change the tree dramatically, so preprocessing matters.

stages.miniPlan: Output, K choice, geometry, scale, and computational tradeoffs.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a method for a scenario and justify the tradeoff; include stability and domain validation.
stages.reference:
Hierarchical clustering gives us a rich, explorable structure rather than a single flat answer. Let's compare it to the other famous method, K-Means:

Feature Hierarchical K-Means
Setup Pick K after Pick K first
Output Tree (Dendrogram) Flat groups
Speed Usually slower because it builds the full merge tree and repeatedly compares clusters Faster

Final Advice: Never take one clustering result as absolute truth. Try different linkages and cut heights. If the same patterns emerge every time, you've found something truly interesting.

Takeaway: Hierarchical clustering is valuable when you want an explorable merge history, not just one fixed partition.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.question: What is stored by KNN?
stages.miniPlan: One labeled row and its two coordinates.
stages.interactionPlan: Select an observation and explain that training largely stores usable examples rather than a boundary formula.
stages.reference:
Every machine learning model starts with data. Here we have measurements of fruits — each one scored on Sweetness and Color Intensity.

Each fruit is already labeled: it's either an Apple or an Orange. Because we have labels, this is supervised learning.

💡 Supervised learning means the model learns from examples where the answer is already known. Here, each fruit already has a known label: Apple or Orange. Later, KNN uses these known examples as its "memory" to classify any new, unknown fruit.

The Whole Idea of KNN

KNN stands for K-Nearest Neighbors. The concept is incredibly straightforward:

To classify a new unknown item, look at the K closest known examples (neighbors) in your dataset. Then, simply copy the label that appears most often among those neighbors!

Example: If we want to identify a mystery fruit, and its 3 closest neighbors are 🍎, 🍎, and 🍊, then Apple gets 2 votes and Orange gets 1 vote. KNN predicts Apple.

New unknown fruit → Find closest old fruits → Count their labels → Predict majority label

Tiny ML Dictionary

Before moving forward, let's establish a few basic terms:

• Feature:

A measurement used to make a prediction (e.g.,

Sweetness Color Intensity • Label:

The correct answer already known for our examples (e.g.,

Apple Orange • Class:

The category we are trying to predict (e.g.,

Apple class Orange class • Query Point:

The new, unknown item we want to classify. In our visual plots, the query point is represented by a star

★

"We know the query point's features, but we do not know its label yet. KNN tries to guess the label based on its neighbors."

Training Dataset

💡 KNN needs labeled examples to learn from. It doesn't build a formula — it simply remembers all the data and compares new points to what it already knows.

stages.title: Choosing Good Features
stages.question: What makes a feature useful for distance?
stages.miniPlan: Relevant signal versus a seeded irrelevant feature.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare neighbor identity after adding noise; do not choose features from final test outcomes.
stages.reference:
Not every measurement helps separate classes. We pick features where the groups actually differ — like Sweetness and Color Intensity.

Bad features (random IDs, row numbers) add noise without signal. KNN is especially sensitive to irrelevant features because they pollute the distance calculation.

Why Feature Selection Matters

A good feature helps separate the classes clearly. A bad feature adds confusion and distorts the distance between points.

Useful Examples:

  • Sweetness helps because apples and oranges have different natural sweetness profiles.
  • Color Intensity helps separate reddish apples from yellowish-orange citrus fruits.

Not Useful Examples:

  • Row number is just the order in the table; it contains zero predictive power.
  • Day picked is unrelated to fruit sweetness or species and would only add noise.

Feature Quality

✅ Sweetness — The two fruit groups show different sweetness patterns
✅ Color Intensity — Apples score higher on red
❌ Row number — meaningless for prediction
❌ Day picked — no predictive power

💡 Notice how the two classes form somewhat distinct clusters on the plot — a good sign. KNN relies entirely on spatial proximity.

stages.title: Train / Test Split
stages.question: Why separate development and final evaluation?
stages.miniPlan: Immutable train/validation/test membership.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal the split and keep held-out labels out of the neighbor pool.
stages.reference:
We hold out a small test set (2 apples + 2 oranges) that the model will not see during training. The remaining points are used as the "memory" KNN will search through.

Testing on training data is one of the most common mistakes — it gives inflated confidence. A model that memorizes isn't smart; it's just a parrot.

Training vs. Testing Sets

• Training Set:

The collection of examples KNN is allowed to remember and search through. This is the model's "memory".

• Test Set:

Hidden examples set aside from the beginning, used ONLY at the very end to check if the model can accurately classify new, unseen data.

⚠️ Critical Warning (Data Leakage): Do not use the test set to choose K or tune features. If the model is exposed to the test set during its construction, your evaluation results are no longer honest. This is called data leakage!

stages.title: Feature Scaling
stages.question: Why do units affect neighbors?
stages.miniPlan: Each feature's contribution to distance.
stages.interactionPlan: Switch a training-fitted scaler on the same data; never refit scaling on a queried/test row.
stages.reference:
This is the most common mistake with KNN. If Sweetness ranges 0–10 but Color ranges 0–100, the Color feature would completely dominate distance calculations.

We use Min-Max Scaling to squish every feature into the 0–1 range, giving each feature equal voice.

Scaling is usually necessary when features use different units or magnitudes. If features already share meaningful units and scale, automatic rescaling may not be desirable. The distance metric and scaling choice together define what “near” means.

Scaled Value = (Value − Min) ÷ (Max − Min) Example: Sweetness = 7, Min = 2, Max = 9 Scaled Value = (7 − 2) ÷ (9 − 2) = 5 ÷ 7 ≈ 0.71

Important: Scale Using Training Data Only

To prevent data leakage, we calculate the Minimum and Maximum values using only the training set. We then use this exact same scale factor for training, test, and any future query points.

Training Data finds Min/Max ➔ same Min/Max scales training, test, and new query points

If we used the test set to calculate the scale range, information from the test set would leak into the training process, leading to over-optimistic performance estimates.

🧠 Concept Check

Why do we scale features before using KNN?

💡 Watch the points shift on the plot — they're being rescaled to [0, 1] on each axis. The order of points along each axis stays the same, but the scale changes. This makes distance fairer because Sweetness and Color now use comparable ranges.

stages.title: Measuring Distance
stages.question: How is distance calculated?
stages.miniPlan: Delta x, delta y, squared terms, total.
stages.interactionPlan: Select two points and trace the calculation; offer numeric query coordinates alongside direct manipulation.
stages.reference:
KNN's entire logic boils down to one question: "Who lives closest to me?" To answer that, we need a way to measure distance between points.

The most common choice is Euclidean distance — the straight-line distance between two points.

Euclidean distance assumes each scaled direction should contribute through straight-line geometry. Manhattan, mixed-data, or domain-specific distances may be more appropriate. Scaling cannot rescue irrelevant features or the curse of dimensionality.

d(a, b) = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²] This is just the Pythagorean theorem — the same formula you learned in geometry class.

What Does Distance Mean Here?

In machine learning, distance represents dissimilarity between items:

  • Short distance means high similarity. The items have very similar features.
  • Long distance means high difference. The items are very dissimilar.

Step-by-Step Distance Calculation:

Let's calculate the distance between our mystery fruit and a training fruit manually:

Query point (Mystery Fruit ★):

Sweetness = 0.45, Color = 0.55

Training point (Known Fruit):

Sweetness = 0.50, Color = 0.65

Euclidean Distance Formula:

d = √[(0.50 − 0.45)² + (0.65 − 0.55)²]

d ≈ 0.1118

Note: While Euclidean distance is the straight-line default, other metrics exist (e.g., Manhattan distance, which calculates distance along grid paths like city streets). This page uses Euclidean distance.

stages.title: Choosing K
stages.question: Why does K change the behavior?
stages.miniPlan: Small-K versus large-K neighbor sets.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub K on fixed data; show a query's changing vote and validation performance.
stages.reference:
K is one of the most important hyperparameters in KNN — the number of neighbors to consult before making a prediction.

Small K (e.g. K=1): Very sensitive to noise. One outlier can flip the prediction.
Large K (e.g. K=15): Too smooth. Local patterns get drowned out by distant voters.

We do not just guess K blindly. Later, in Stage 12, we compare several K values using cross-validation and look for a sensible choice.

Who Chooses K?

K is a hyperparameter. In machine learning, a hyperparameter is a setting selected using validation data or cross-validation, rather than a coefficient fitted directly during training.

The Trade-Off:

  • Too Small K (e.g., K=1): Extremely sensitive to outliers and noise. The model may overfit (memorize noise as pattern).
  • Too Large K (e.g., K=15): Overly smooth and generic. Local patterns are drowned out by far-away votes. The model may underfit (miss the actual pattern).

How a Machine Learning Task is Configured:

Component Who Decides? Meaning
Features Human / Designer Measurements selected to describe items (e.g., Sweetness)
Scaling Method Human choice How feature ranges are made comparable (e.g., Min-Max)
Distance Metric Human choice Mathematical formula to measure closeness (e.g., Euclidean)
K value Human choice Number of neighboring votes allowed to participate
Training labels Existing Data The ground-truth answers for old examples
Prediction KNN vote rule Majority vote among the K closest neighbors

stages.question: How do neighbors vote?

stages.title: Decision Boundary
stages.question: Where do predictions change?
stages.miniPlan: Two nearby query points with different winning votes.
stages.interactionPlan: Move a query through a persistent decision surface; recompute surface only when data or K changes.
stages.reference:
What if we classified every possible point on the plot? The result is a colorful map showing which regions belong to which class.

Unlike linear models, KNN boundaries are non-linear — they bend and curve around the data naturally. The boundary is just wherever the majority vote flips from one class to the other.

What is a Decision Boundary?

A Decision Boundary is the invisible dividing line or contour across the feature space where the model switches from predicting one class to another. Any point that falls on one side is predicted as Apple; any point on the other is Orange.

• Non-parametric:

KNN has no underlying assumptions or mathematical weights to fit (unlike linear equations). The boundary adapts organically to the data density.

• Bias-Variance Tradeoff:

Adjusting K alters this boundary:

K = 1 (High Variance / Low Bias):

Extremely flexible, wiggly, and complex boundary. It fits every outlier precisely, memorizing noise and likely overfitting.

Medium K (Balanced Tradeoff):

Smooth, reasonable boundary shapes that filter out minor noise while preserving genuine group clusters.

Large K (Low Variance / High Bias):

Highly smooth, almost straight boundaries. It ignores localized trends completely, risking underfitting.

Boundary Properties

The decision boundary emerges organically from the data — no formula is fitted. This is what makes KNN a non-parametric model.

💡 Small K = wiggly, complex boundaries. Large K = smoother boundaries. This is the classic bias-variance tradeoff.

K is one of the most important tuning knobs. Watch how the decision boundary changes as K increases.

Start with Five-Fold Cross-Validation

Five-fold cross-validation is the usual practical starting point. Ten-fold cross-validation is also common. In either case, the training data is divided into folds, and each candidate K is scored several times using different train/validation folds.

⚠️ This toy dataset is very small, so this lesson demonstrates leave-one-out cross-validation (LOOCV) instead. That is a small-data teaching choice, not the usual default. With a larger dataset, five-fold or ten-fold CV would typically be more practical.

Cross-Validation Compares K; It Does Not Choose K for You

Cross-validation is a loop: try several candidate values of K, calculate an average validation score for each one, then choose the K with the strongest average score. The procedure produces the comparison; the modelling workflow makes the selection.

Illustrative five-fold example:

Candidate KAverage CV accuracyWhat we do
K = 175%Compare
K = 388%Compare
K = 592%Best average score
K = 790%Compare

In this example, we carry K = 5 forward because it has the highest average CV score. The live chart below uses LOOCV because this toy training set is tiny.

Recommended Workflow Order

  1. Split once: Separate the full dataset into training and test sets. Keep the test set hidden.
  2. Cross-validate on training only: Run five-fold CV for several candidate Ks. In this demonstration, use LOOCV because the training set is very small.
  3. Choose K: Compare the average CV scores and select the best-performing candidate.
  4. Retrain: Fit KNN on all of the training data using the selected K.
  5. Test once: Evaluate that locked model once on the untouched test set.

Elbow / Knee: A Secondary Heuristic

An elbow or knee is where the CV curve begins to flatten as K increases. It can help you read the curve, but it is a heuristic, not a rule. In most cases, start with the K that has the best average cross-validation score. Use the elbow only as a secondary aid when nearby K values perform similarly, then document the tie-breaker you used.

Example: If K = 5 has the highest average CV score and the curve also starts flattening after K = 5, the knee supports the choice. It does not replace the score comparison or select K automatically.

⚠️ Do not choose K from a single split, from the curve's shape alone, or by repeatedly checking the final test set.

stages.title: Strengths and Weaknesses
stages.question: When does KNN become unreliable or expensive?
stages.miniPlan: Density, dimensionality, scaling, missingness, and query cost.
stages.interactionPlan: Add an irrelevant dimension or reduce local density in a labeled toy example.
stages.reference:
Before using K-Nearest Neighbors in practice, it is vital to know when it shines and where it struggles.

💪 Strengths

  • Simple to understand: Intuitive to explain to stakeholders.
  • No Parameter-Learning Phase: KNN does not fit weights or coefficients. It stores the training examples and uses them during prediction.
  • Highly Flexible: Can easily construct complex, non-linear decision boundaries.
  • Naturally Multi-class: Works seamlessly for predicting 3 or more classes.

⚠️ Weaknesses & Limitations

  • Sensitive to Scale: Scaling is usually necessary when features use different units or magnitudes; otherwise larger-scale features dominate distance.
  • The Curse of Dimensionality: When there are too many features, distance often becomes less useful because many points start to seem similarly far apart. This makes it harder for KNN to find truly meaningful neighbors.
  • Slow at Scale: Must calculate distance to every single stored point for every new query. High memory and computing costs.
  • Class Imbalance: If you have 95% Apples and 5% Oranges, votes will naturally skew heavily to Apple.

The Whole Story in Plain English

Here is the complete machine learning workflow we walked through today:

  1. Labeled Examples: Start with known data (fruits with known categories).
  2. Feature Selection: Select high-quality, relevant properties (sweetness, color).
  3. Train/Test Split: Set aside a final held-out test set to keep final evaluation fair.
  4. Feature Scaling: Fit an appropriate scaling transformation using the training data when feature units or magnitudes would otherwise dominate the distance calculation. Standardisation, min-max scaling, robust scaling and domain-specific transformations are all possible choices; apply the fitted transformation unchanged to validation and test data.
  5. Mystery Input: Introduce an unknown query point (★) on the plot.
  6. Distance Measuring: Run Euclidean distance against all stored training examples.
  7. Hyperparameter K: Choose K (the count of voting neighbors) using validation or cross-validation.
  8. Locate Neighbors: Gather the K nearest samples.
  9. Tally Votes: Perform a democratic, equal-weight majority vote.
  10. Predict: Assign the winning class to the unknown query point.
  11. Independent Testing: Run the held-out test points to check the model's accuracy.
  12. Evaluate Quality: Read the confusion matrix, recall, precision, and F1 metrics.
  13. Tune K: Use cross-validation inside the training memory to find the best K.
  14. Analyze Trade-offs: Know KNN's limits, such as scale sensitivity and the curse of dimensionality.

stages.title: The Raw Data
stages.question: What do the labeled clouds represent?
stages.miniPlan: One observation, two features, and a class.
stages.interactionPlan: Link table and point before introducing ellipses or a separating direction.
stages.reference:
Every machine learning model starts with data. Here we have measurements of fruits — each one scored on Sweetness and Color.

Each fruit is already labeled: it's either an Apple or an Orange. Because we have labels, this is supervised learning.

The Whole Idea of LDA

Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA) is a supervised classification method. It uses labeled examples to learn a straight-line rule that separates classes.

Simple Idea: LDA looks for a direction (projection axis) where:
• Different class centers are as far apart as possible.
• Points inside each class are as tightly bunched (low spread) as possible.

LDA General Pipeline:

Labeled Data → Class Centers → Class Spread → Optimal Direction → Boundary → Prediction

"LDA is like looking at a messy 2D cloud of points from the best angle so the two groups look as separated as possible."

Tiny LDA Dictionary

Feature:

A measurement used to make a prediction (e.g., Sweetness or Color).

Label:

The known category of an example (e.g., Apple or Orange).

Class:

The target group we want to predict (Apple class or Orange class).

Mean (μ):

The average position or center of a class point cloud.

Variance:

How much a single feature fluctuates.

Covariance:

How two features move in relation to each other.

Scatter (S):

A mathematical measure of data spread or messiness.

Projection:

Squashing 2D coordinates down onto a single 1D axis.

Discriminant Score (δ):

A numerical score LDA computes for each class; the highest score wins!

Training Dataset

LDA needs labeled examples to learn the pattern that separates classes. Without labels, it cannot learn.

stages.question: Why group observations by class?
stages.miniPlan: Labeled rows sorted into class-specific columns.
stages.interactionPlan: Brush one class and reveal its sample size without changing point positions.
stages.reference:
LDA first separates the training data by label. All apples together, all oranges together. Now it can study each group independently.

Why group by class? This step is critical because LDA calculates a separate center (mean) and spread (scatter) for each individual class.

Understanding the hulls:

A convex hull is just a visual outline drawn around the training points in a class. It is not the LDA model itself! It only helps us see where each class cloud lives in our feature space.

stages.title: Compute Class Means
stages.question: What is a class mean?
stages.miniPlan: Coordinate-wise average of three points.
stages.interactionPlan: Draw deviations into a class center; show the center can sit where no observation exists.
stages.reference:
The mean is the center of each class — its average position in feature space. LDA uses these to understand where each group lives.

Mean = Class Center

The class mean is the average location of all points in that class. It is like the center of gravity of the class cloud.

Example: If most apples have high Sweetness and high Color Score, the apple mean center (μ_apple) will appear right in the middle of the apple cluster.

μ_apple = average position of all apple training points

μ_orange = average position of all orange training points

The markers on the plot show each class center. The gap between them is what LDA will try to exploit.

stages.title: Within-Class Scatter
stages.question: What does within-class scatter describe?
stages.miniPlan: Two variances and one covariance.
stages.interactionPlan: Link covariance-matrix entries to ellipse spread and tilt with a short symbol dictionary.
stages.reference:
Not all apples are identical. SW measures how much the points in each class wiggle around their own mean.

The covariance ellipses on the plot show the spread shape. Diagonal entries = how much each feature varies. Off-diagonal = how features vary together.

What does within-class scatter mean?

Within-class scatter tells us how messy or spread out each class is inside itself.
• If all apples are clustered tightly together, apple scatter is small.
• If apples are spread out all over the plot, apple scatter is large.

What is covariance?
Covariance tells us whether Sweetness and Color move together:
• Positive covariance: Sweetness goes up, and Color Score also tends to go up.
• Negative covariance: One goes up, while the other goes down.
• Near Zero: They do not move together in any pattern.

Understanding the Scatter Matrix:
• Diagonal entries: How much each feature varies by itself (variance).
• Off-diagonal entries: How much the two features move together (covariance).

stages.title: The Shared Covariance Assumption
stages.question: Why share one covariance estimate?
stages.miniPlan: Separate class covariances versus pooled covariance.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare shared and separate shapes; explain the stability-versus-flexibility tradeoff.
stages.reference:
Here's LDA's key assumption: all classes share the same covariance shape. The groups can have different centers, but their spread is assumed to be roughly the same.

So LDA pools the individual covariance matrices into one shared estimate. Watch the ellipses morph into a single shape.

Why does LDA pool covariance?

LDA assumes that the classes have similar spread shapes. Instead of keeping separate shapes for Apple and Orange, it combines them into one shared covariance estimate.

Simple meaning: Different centers, same general spread shape.

stages.title: Between-Class Scatter
stages.question: What counts as between-class separation?
stages.miniPlan: Class means versus the overall mean.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight mean differences independently from within-class spread.
stages.reference:
SB measures how far apart the class centers are. The further apart, the easier it is for LDA to separate them.

LDA's goal is to maximize the ratio of between-class scatter to within-class scatter:

Between-class scatter = gap between class centers

Let's contrast the two scatter metrics:
• Within-class scatter asks: "How messy and spread out is each class inside itself?"
• Between-class scatter asks: "How far apart are the class centers (means)?"

LDA's Ultimate Goal: We want the gap between classes to be BIG, and the messiness inside each class to be SMALL!

J(w) = wᵀ S_B w / wᵀ S_W w In simple terms, J(w) is maximized when: 1. Projected class means are far apart. 2. Projected class spreads are small.

stages.title: The Optimal Direction
stages.question: Why project along this direction?
stages.miniPlan: Separation divided by projected within-class spread.
stages.interactionPlan: Rotate a candidate projection, then reveal the fitted LDA direction; distinguish this from PCA.
stages.reference:
In this 2-class example, LDA gives one main discriminant direction w — the angle where classes appear most separated.

What is projection and why do we do it?

Projection means dropping every 2D point (Sweetness, Color) down onto a single 1D line or direction.

This turns a 2D pair of numbers into a single 1D score:

Fruit (Sweetness, Color) → [Project] → One LDA Score

Why project? If the projected Apple scores sit neatly on one side of the line and the projected Orange scores sit on the other side, LDA has found an excellent direction for separation!

w ∝ S_W⁻¹ (μ₁ − μ₂) This isn't just the straight line between means. It also tilts to avoid the direction of maximum within-class spread.

stages.title: The Decision Boundary
stages.question: Why is the boundary linear?
stages.miniPlan: Shared quadratic terms that cancel in a score difference.
stages.interactionPlan: Link mean, covariance, and prior changes to the boundary; keep algebra in expandable steps.
stages.reference:
Because LDA is linear, the boundary between classes is a straight line (in 2D). Everything on one side is classified as Apple, the other as Orange.

Discriminant Scores: Highest Score Wins

LDA calculates a separate scoring function for each class, called the Discriminant Score (δ):

δ_apple(x) = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Apple

δ_orange(x) = Score indicating how much point x looks like an Orange

For any point, LDA compares the two scores: whichever score is higher is the predicted class!

Example Fruit Prediction: (Simple illustrative example, not a live value from the current dataset) 2.31 -1.44

Since 2.31 is higher than -1.44, LDA predicts

Apple

What are priors (π_k)?

The prior probability (π_k) represents the class probability before observing its features. Priors may be estimated from training prevalence or specified externally.
• If apples and oranges are equally common, priors are equal (50% each).
• If we estimate priors from 90% apples in training, the apple score gets a prior boost, shifting the boundary slightly to favor Apple predictions.

δ_k(x) = xᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ_k − ½ μ_kᵀ Σ⁻¹ μ_k + log(π_k) Predict class k with the highest δ_k(x)

stages.title: Assumptions & Limitations
stages.question: When is the shared-shape assumption costly?
stages.miniPlan: Similar shapes / unequal shapes / small samples.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare fixed LDA and QDA scenarios on identical splits; discuss singularity and regularization.
stages.reference:
To use LDA effectively, you need to understand when it thrives and when it falls short.

LDA Works Best When:

  • Linearity: A straight-line boundary is a reasonable way to separate classes.
  • Normality: Each class looks like a symmetrical oval cloud (multivariate normal distribution).
  • Equal Spread: All classes share roughly the same spread/covariance shape.
  • Independence: Data samples are collected independently.
  • Data Volume: There are many more rows than features.
  • No Outliers: Extreme values are absent (outliers pull means away easily).

LDA Struggles When:

  • The true dividing boundary is highly curved.
  • Classes have very different shapes or spreads (e.g., one is a tight circle, the other is a giant flat ellipse).
  • There are severe outliers that skew centers.
  • You have too many features and not enough rows (overfitting).
  • Features are redundant or highly correlated (collinearity).

Alternative Methods

If LDA doesn't fit, consider these standard alternatives:

QDA (Quadratic Discriminant Analysis):

Excellent if class spreads are highly unequal.

Logistic Regression:

Also estimates class probabilities, but avoids LDA’s Gaussian class-conditional and shared-covariance assumptions.

KNN or Decision Trees:

Great for highly complex, non-linear boundaries.

stages.reference:
Imagine you run an ice-cream shop. Every day you note the temperature, whether it was sunny, and whether someone bought ice cream.

The plot shows each day as a dot: temperature on the x-axis, outcome (bought or didn't) on the y-axis.

Legend

● Bought (y = 1)   ● Didn't buy (y = 0)

What is probability? 🤔

Probability means "how likely something is to happen." It is always written as a number between 0 and 1:

  • 0 means impossible (0% chance).
  • 0.5 means 50-50 (50% chance).
  • 1 means certain (100% chance).

In this guide, probability means: "How likely is someone to buy ice cream?"

Bought = 1 and Didn't buy = 0 are just category labels. They do not mean someone bought one ice cream or zero ice creams. They simply mark the two possible outcomes for the model.

Notice how higher temperatures tend to cluster near y = 1? That's the signal our model will learn to capture.

📌 This is a small toy dataset with 20 rows designed for teaching. Real datasets have hundreds or thousands of rows.

stages.title: Why Lines Break
stages.question: Why is an ordinary line awkward for probability?
stages.miniPlan: A linear prediction below zero or above one.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare the raw linear score and a probability output using the same observations.
stages.reference:
Your first instinct might be to draw a straight line through the data — that's linear regression.

But watch what happens: the line predicts values above 1 and below 0. Those aren't valid probabilities!

ŷ = b₀ + b₁ · Temperature Can give 1.5 or −0.3 … not a probability!

Why Bounds Matter 🚧

A probability cannot be below 0 or above 1:

  • Below 0 would mean “less than impossible.”
  • Above 1 would mean “more than certain.”

So a prediction like 1.5 means 150%, which makes no real-world sense. We need a curve that stays strictly between 0 and 1.

We need a function that squishes any number into the 0–1 range. Enter the sigmoid.

stages.title: From a Raw Score to a Probability
stages.question: What does the sigmoid do?
stages.miniPlan: z → exp(−z) → probability, with a small value table.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub z and move a marker along the sigmoid; keep this distinct from changing a fitted coefficient.
stages.reference:
First, logistic regression starts the same way linear regression does. For each data point, one linear equation combines that point's features with the model's learned weights and produces one raw number, called z.

z = b₀ + b₁x₁ + b₂x₂ + ··· one data point → one raw score z

z is not a z-score or a standard score. It is not learned separately for each point. It is simply the model's raw opinion before that opinion becomes a probability. z can be any number from negative infinity to positive infinity. If z = 0, the model is exactly at 50/50.

Only after that do we apply the sigmoid function to turn z into a probability between 0 and 1.

p = 1 / (1 + e⁻ᶻ) Large positive z → probability near 1 Large negative z → probability near 0 z = 0 → probability exactly 0.5

See the Sigmoid Respond

Raw score z = 0.0 0.500Probability

Where Does z Come From? 🤔

In a real machine learning model: no, you do not choose z manually. The model runs its linear equation on each data point's features and learned weights.

Features + Weights → raw score z

raw score z → Sigmoid → Probability

“The z slider is only a teaching demo. In real logistic regression, the model calculates a separate raw score z for each row, then the sigmoid turns it into a probability.”

stages.title: Weighted Clues
stages.question: How do weighted clues form z?
stages.miniPlan: Intercept plus each feature's signed contribution.
stages.interactionPlan: Change one input or coefficient at a time; synchronize the contribution receipt and score-to-probability diagram.

How do we construct the score z? Think of our features (Temperature, Sunny, Weekend) as clues. Each weight describes the change in log-odds for a one-unit increase in that feature, holding the other modeled predictors fixed:

• A positive weight pushes the score toward "Buy" (y = 1).
• A negative weight pushes the score toward "Don't Buy" (y = 0).
• The final raw score z is the total combined push from all clues. The Sigmoid then turns this raw score into a clean final probability.

These sliders are a sandbox. You are manually changing the weights only to see how the mathematical curve reacts. In real training, the model learns these weights automatically by reducing log loss.

Stage 04 (Sandbox):

You adjust weights manually to see the shapes of the decision curve.

Stage 05 (Machine Learning):

The model adjusts weights automatically using gradient descent.

z = b₀ + b₁·standardized Temp + b₂·Sunny + b₃·Weekend

b₀ = bias (baseline push) · b₁, b₂, b₃ = individual clue pushes

Standardized temperature means we convert raw temperature values into a scaled version with a mean of 0 and standard deviation of 1. Scaling mainly helps optimisation run smoothly and makes regularisation penalties more comparable across features. Large raw values do not inherently overpower the final fitted model: coefficients account for feature units.
