stages.title: Learning from Mistakes
stages.question: What does learning minimize?
stages.miniPlan: One prediction's log loss and gradient direction.
stages.interactionPlan: Step an actual parameter update and plot loss; distinguish gradients from the optimizer's action.
stages.reference:
The model starts with initial weights, makes predictions, measures how wrong it was using log loss, then nudges the weights to improve. This is gradient descent.

Training does not directly choose z. Training learns better weights. Once the weights improve, the model calculates better z values for each row of data automatically:

Training updates weights → weights calculate z → sigmoid turns z into probability → threshold turns probability into Yes/No L = −[ y·log(p) + (1−y)·log(1−p) ] The model is punished more when it's very confident but very wrong.

How Log Loss Thinks 🧠

Log loss measures the penalty of wrong answers. If the actual answer is 1 (Bought):

Real Answer Predicted Prob Meaning Loss Penalty
1 (Bought) 0.95 Confident & correct Small Loss (0.05)
1 (Bought) 0.55 Unsure but leaning right Medium Loss (0.60)
1 (Bought) 0.05 Confident & wrong! Huge Loss (3.00)

* Note: These loss values are examples for one single prediction. The training loss shown below is the average loss across all training rows.

Gradient descent is like adjusting a recipe little by little. If the model is wrong, it changes the weights in the direction that reduces loss. The learning rate controls how big each adjustment step is. Gradient descent is one teaching-friendly optimiser, not the definition of logistic regression: Newton, quasi-Newton, coordinate-descent and other solvers are also common. Feature scaling often improves numerical optimisation and is especially relevant with regularisation; fit scaling inside training folds.

⚠️ Warning on Learning Rate:
• Too small: Learning is very slow, requiring thousands of steps.
• Too large: The model may jump right over the best values and fail to settle.

stages.question: Why does a probability need a decision threshold?
stages.miniPlan: Probability / threshold / resulting action.
stages.interactionPlan: Move the threshold and immediately update labels on development data; preserve continuous probabilities.
stages.reference:
The sigmoid gives a probability. But we need a decision: Yes or No. We pick a threshold.

If p ≥ threshold → predict Yes (1)
If p < threshold → predict No (0)

The model only gives probabilities. The threshold is a decision rule chosen by humans. We choose it based on what kind of mistake is worse or more costly for our specific situation:

Threshold vs. Probability 🔍

The threshold does not change the probability itself. It only changes how we convert that probability into a final Yes/No decision.

Example:

If the model predicts a probability of

0.62 0.50 Yes 0.70 No

The probability stayed exactly 0.62. Only the decision rule changed.

Lowering the Threshold (e.g., 0.30):

Predicts "Yes" more easily. You catch more real buyers (high recall), but you also create more false alarms (false positives).

Raising the Threshold (e.g., 0.70):

Predicts "Yes" only when highly confident. You reduce false alarms (high precision), but you might miss many real buyers (false negatives).

Select this threshold on validation data, never the final test set. Use error costs, prevalence, capacity, and the real objective. Lock the threshold with all preprocessing and calibration choices, then report final test performance once. Probability calibration and classification accuracy answer different questions.

🧠 Concept Check Quiz 3

Who chooses the decision threshold?

💡 A medical test might use 0.3 (catch more sick people), while a spam filter might use 0.7 (avoid false alarms).

stages.title: Select the Decision Rule on Validation Data
stages.question: Which mistakes does this threshold create?
stages.miniPlan: Confusion-cell definitions with their actual denominators.
stages.interactionPlan: Select TP/FP/FN/TN to brush corresponding validation cases; update counts and costs together.
stages.reference:
Use the validation set to explore threshold-dependent trade-offs. The final test set remains hidden while the threshold, metrics and model choices are still changing.

Every validation prediction falls into one of four boxes:

• TP (True Positive): Predicted Bought, and they really bought. Correct prediction!
• TN (True Negative): Predicted Didn't buy, and they did not buy. Correct prediction!
• FP (False Positive): Predicted Bought, but they did not buy. (False alarm!).
• FN (False Negative): Predicted Didn't buy, but they actually bought. (Missed buyer!).

Validation Confusion Matrix

● Dim dots = training set     ● Vivid dots = validation set

⚠️ Threshold Dependencies: Changing the decision threshold changes the validation TP, TN, FP, and FN counts. Use these development results to select and lock the rule; do not repeatedly inspect the test set.

Validation Metrics

Overall Accuracy

-- Formula: (TP + TN) / (TP + TN + FP + FN)

Meaning: How often was the model correct overall? Best used when mistakes are equally costly.

Precision (Reliability of Yes Predictions)

Meaning: When the model predicts Bought, how often is it right? Critical when false alarms (FP) are expensive.

Recall (Sensitivity / Detection Rate)

Meaning: Out of all real positive buyers, how many did the model catch? Critical when missing a real positive (FN) is costly.

F1-Score

-- Formula: 2 × (Precision × Recall) / (Precision + Recall)

Meaning: F1 is a balance score between precision and recall. It is not a normal average; it gives a low score if either precision or recall is weak. Perfect when you want to look at general model balance.

Final untouched test evaluation

Hidden until the model and validation-selected threshold are locked. Reveal this result once, after development is complete.

Locked threshold: —

Confusion matrix: TP — · TN — · FP — · FN —

Final test metrics: accuracy — · precision — · recall — · F1 —

stages.title: The Validation ROC Curve
stages.question: What does the ROC curve summarize?
stages.miniPlan: TPR and FPR denominator mini diagrams.
stages.interactionPlan: Sweep a validation threshold and move its ROC operating point; keep AUC separate from accuracy and calibration.
stages.reference:
The validation ROC curve shows: at every possible threshold, how does recall trade off against false-alarm rate? It is a development visual and never reads the final test set.

Think of a smoke alarm: too sensitive and it goes off when you cook toast; too lenient and it misses an actual fire.

Accuracy vs. ROC / AUC:

• Accuracy shows model performance at a single chosen threshold (like 0.50).

• ROC shows performance trade-offs across all possible thresholds.

• AUC (Area Under Curve) is not the same as accuracy. AUC summarizes how well the model separates/ranks positive cases from negative cases across all thresholds.

Key ROC Metrics Explained

An ROC curve plots two key metrics against each other at all possible thresholds from 0.0 to 1.0:

True Positive Rate (TPR / Recall): Meaning:

Out of all real buyers, what percentage did we catch? (Higher is better!)

False Positive Rate (FPR / False Alarm Rate): Meaning:

Out of all non-buyers, what percentage did we wrongly predict as buyers? (Lower is better!)

The ROC curve checks many possible thresholds, not just 0.5. Each point on the curve comes from a specific threshold value. Moving the threshold changes TPR and FPR.

• AUC = 1.0: Perfect separation on this dataset.
• AUC = 0.5: Random guessing. The model has no predictive strength.
Note: AUC does not mean the model is perfect forever. It only summarizes separation performance on the data being evaluated.

📌 Note: Because this teaching example has a very small validation set, the ROC curve looks coarse and jumpy. With a larger validation sample, the curve would usually be smoother.

stages.title: What the Numbers Mean
stages.question: What is an odds ratio?
stages.miniPlan: Probability ↔ odds ↔ log-odds with one coefficient example.
stages.interactionPlan: Change a feature by one unit while holding others fixed; avoid interpreting coefficient size as causal importance.
stages.reference:
We often want to know how the model estimates each feature (temperature, sunny day, weekend status) is associated with higher or lower predicted odds, while holding other features constant. Logistic regression gives us weights that can be converted into Odds Ratios.

Probability vs. Odds 🎲

Probability and Odds are related but express likelihood differently:

• Probability (p) asks: "Out of all outcomes, how likely is Yes?" (Varies between 0 and 1).
• Odds asks: "How much does the chance of Yes beat No?" (Varies from 0 to infinity). Formula: Odds = p / (1 - p)

Probability (p) Odds Formula Odds Value Meaning
0.50 (50%) 0.50 / 0.50 1 to 1 (1.0) Yes and No are equally likely
0.75 (75%) 0.75 / 0.25 3 to 1 (3.0) Yes is three times as likely as No
0.80 (80%) 0.80 / 0.20 4 to 1 (4.0) Yes is four times as likely as No

Taking the exponent of a weight (eweight) gives us the Odds Ratio (OR). This ratio tells us how the odds of buying are multiplied for each unit increase in that feature.

⚠️ Beginner Warning:
Odds are not the same as probability. An odds ratio of 2 does not mean the probability doubles! It means the odds ratio doubles (e.g. from 1:1 odds to 2:1 odds).

⚠️ Coefficient ≠ proof of cause:
A positive coefficient means the feature is associated with higher predicted probability in this model. It does not prove that modifying the feature directly causes buying behavior.

Our Weights & Odds Ratios

Positive Weight (OR > 1): Feature is associated with pushing probability and odds up.
Negative Weight (OR < 1): Feature is associated with pushing probability and odds down.
Near Zero Weight (OR ≈ 1): Feature has little to no association with predicted odds.

stages.title: The Full Picture
stages.question: What is locked before the final test?
stages.miniPlan: Training, validation choices, locked model, final evaluation.
stages.interactionPlan: Preserve the existing one-time reveal; demonstrate that threshold changes cannot silently tune the sealed test.
stages.reference:
You've walked through the entire logistic regression pipeline! Let's review the whole story in plain English:

The Story of Logistic Regression 📖

  1. We collect historical raw data: temperature, sunny weather, weekends, and whether someone bought ice cream.
  2. A straight linear regression line is not suitable because it predicts impossible values (below 0 and above 1) for probabilities.
  3. Instead, logistic regression builds an intermediate score called z by adding up weighted features (clues).
  4. The mathematical sigmoid function gracefully "squishes" this score z into a valid probability between 0% and 100%.
  5. A decision threshold translates probabilities into labels. Select it on validation data from error costs, prevalence and objectives; 0.50 is only a convention.
  6. During training, the model starts with baseline weights and iteratively adjusts them using gradient descent to minimize average log loss.
  7. A validation confusion matrix is used to compare threshold choices without touching the final test set.
  8. Performance is summarized using descriptive metrics: Accuracy (overall correctness), Precision (purity of Yes calls), Recall (capture rate of actual positives), and F1-score (their balanced harmony).
  9. The validation ROC curve and AUC summarize ranking trade-offs across thresholds during development.
  10. After the model and threshold are locked, the test set is revealed once for the final performance estimate.
  11. By analyzing coefficients and odds ratios, we can interpret how the model estimates each feature is associated with higher or lower odds of a purchase.

Concept Checklist

✓ Collected and plotted raw data
✓ Saw why linear regression can't predict probabilities
✓ Met the sigmoid that squishes scores into 0–1
✓ Built the score z from weighted features
✓ Trained with gradient descent to minimize log loss
✓ Chose a threshold to turn probabilities into decisions
✓ Evaluated with confusion matrix and metrics
✓ Explored the ROC curve for threshold trade-offs
✓ Interpreted coefficients and odds ratios

stages.reference: Imputation predicts or substitutes missing values; encoding represents categories numerically. Both are learned transformations and belong inside the pipeline.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: Why can mean filling distort an analysis?
stages.miniPlan: Observed values, filled value, and changed variability.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace a high-income missingness example; preserve the uncertainty about unseen values.
stages.reference: Income is missing more often for high earners. Mean imputation pulls their values toward the centre and understates variation. A missingness indicator may help prediction, but it does not make the missing-at-random assumption true for inference.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: How do MCAR, MAR, MNAR, and encoding differ?
stages.miniPlan: Mechanism assumptions separately from representation choices.
stages.interactionPlan: Use one miniature for mechanisms and one for one-hot/ordinal/target encoding; do not overload a single chart.
stages.reference:
MCAR, MAR and MNAR are assumptions about the missingness process, not labels that a plot can prove. Complete-case analysis is valid for limited targets under restrictive conditions. Single imputation treats filled values as known and usually understates inferential uncertainty; multiple imputation combines within- and between-imputation variation. Encoding defines geometry: one-hot separates unordered levels, ordinal encoding asserts order, and target encoding borrows outcome information. Target and frequency encoders need fold-safe fitting and an unseen-level policy. Raw columns and a data dictionary should be retained so every transformation remains auditable.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

When the method fails

Single imputation understates inferential uncertainty; ordinal codes create fake distances; target encoding leaks without cross-fitting; unseen categories can break deployment.

stages.title: The Overfitting Trap
stages.question: Why can extra flexibility hurt new predictions?
stages.miniPlan: Training and validation errors on the same candidate models.
stages.interactionPlan: Add a seeded noise feature; avoid claiming more features always cause overfitting.
stages.reference:
Building a predictive model is tricky. It is tempting to include every available piece of data. We often assume that more clues guarantee better answers.

However, adding too many variables introduces massive noise. This noise obscures the true relationship. The model ends up memorizing random accidents in the training data rather than learning the actual signal.

The Illusion of Accuracy: A highly complex model performs flawlessly on its "homework" (the training data). But it collapses in the real world on unseen data. This failure is called overfitting.

stages.title: The n-p Puzzle
stages.question: What happens when coefficients are not identifiable?
stages.miniPlan: n, p, rank, and two equally fitting coefficient vectors.
stages.interactionPlan: Show nonunique coefficients separately from generalization; introduce regularization as an additional constraint.
stages.reference:
To build a reliable model, we must balance two things. First is the number of samples ($n$). Second is the number of variables or clues ($p$).

Think of this in three simple steps:

  1. Step 1: You need enough examples to prove a real pattern exists.
  2. Step 2: Every new variable adds a whole new dimension for the model to search.
  3. Step 3: When $p>n$, ordinary least squares has no unique coefficient solution unless constraints are imposed. Ridge, Lasso, or other regularisation can still support useful prediction, although instability and overfitting are serious concerns.

At this point, the design matrix is rank deficient. Without additional constraints, many coefficient vectors may fit the training data equally well. This makes coefficient interpretation unstable and creates a high risk of overfitting. Useful prediction may still be possible with appropriate regularisation, feature structure and honest validation.

Keep the ideas separate: non-unique coefficients concern identifiability; interpolation means matching the observed training outcomes; overfitting is poor generalisation caused by learning sample-specific patterns; predictive performance must be measured on unseen data. Ridge, Lasso and Elastic Net impose different constraints that can produce estimable predictors, but they are not automatic cures.

stages.title: Picking the Best Team
stages.question: Why not search every subset?
stages.miniPlan: Candidate counts for small p, then 2^p.
stages.interactionPlan: Step forward/backward selection on a tiny example; describe computational growth without saying all sizes are impossible.
stages.reference:
One way to fix this is Subset Selection. This means literally picking a specific group of variables and throwing the rest out.

Forward Start empty. Add the single best predictor. Then add the next one that helps the most. Keep going.

Backward Start with all variables. Find the weakest predictor and bench them. Repeat until only the best are left.

Hybrid Add the best predictors one by one. But constantly re-evaluate. If an old predictor becomes redundant, remove it.

Why don't we just test every single combination of variables?

stages.title: The Scorecards
stages.question: What does each scorecard penalize?
stages.miniPlan: Criterion / objective / direction / assumptions / parameter count.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare identical fitted candidates; standardize AIC/BIC/Cp conventions and distinguish ranking-equivalent rescalings.
stages.reference:
As we add variables, the raw training error always goes down. The model looks better, even if it is just memorizing noise. To find the truly best model, we need scorecards.

These scorecards punish us for adding unnecessary complexity.

$C_p$, AIC, BIC Like a golf score: Lower is better. They measure Total Error + Complexity Penalty. Adj. $R^2$ Higher is better. Adjusts the traditional $R^2$ relative to total variation and complexity. $C_p = \frac{1}{n}(RSS + 2p\hat{\sigma}^2)$

$AIC = \frac{2p}{n} - \frac{2}{n}\ln(L)$

$\text{Adj. } R^2 = 1 - \frac{RSS/(n-p-1)}{TSS/(n-1)}$

Plain English Breakdown

Most scorecards use the same basic logic: Total Score = Error + Penalty.

  • $C_p$, AIC, and BIC: These measure how much your model's guesses miss the actual marks ($RSS$ or $-2\ln(L)$) and add a mathematical tax for every variable ($p$) you use. You want these to be low.
  • BIC's extra strictness: BIC multiplies the penalty by $\ln(n)$, meaning for most datasets, it applies a much harsher penalty than AIC, strongly forcing you to choose simpler models.
  • Adjusted $R^2$: Unlike the others, higher is better here. It measures the percentage of variation your model explains, but mathematically penalizes you if you add useless variables to artificially inflate the score.

stages.title: The Shrinking Trick
stages.question: What does shrinkage trade away?
stages.miniPlan: Prediction error plus coefficient penalty.
stages.interactionPlan: Change lambda on a fixed standardized training matrix; keep the intercept treatment explicit.
stages.reference:
Subset selection is an "all-or-nothing" approach. A variable is either in or out. But what if we just made a weak variable's influence smaller?

This is called Regularization. Imagine a soundboard where each slider controls a variable. Regularization turns down the volume on loud, messy variables. It shrinks their coefficients ($\beta$) toward zero using a tuning dial called $\lambda$ (Lambda).

Crucial Step: Variables should be centered first, and usually standardized when their scales differ, to create a level playing field. Otherwise, a variable measured in huge numbers (like dollars) would face unfair shrinkage compared to a variable measured in small numbers (like years).

stages.title: Ridge Regression (L2)
stages.question: Why does Ridge usually keep all predictors?
stages.miniPlan: Two correlated coefficients and the L2 penalty.
stages.interactionPlan: Animate actual solution paths; replace the absolute never-zero claim and explain units.
stages.reference: Ridge minimizes squared-error fit plus a squared coefficient penalty. In this notebook the objective is mean squared error divided by two plus λ times the sum of squared non-intercept coefficients divided by two. The intercept is unpenalized. Larger λ discourages large weights and can stabilize an ill-conditioned design. Ridge generally does not create sparse solutions, although a coefficient can equal zero in special cases. Penalty strength depends on feature units, so scaling is part of the modeling choice and must be learned inside training folds.

stages.title: Lasso Regression (L1)
stages.question: Why can Lasso produce zeros?
stages.miniPlan: L1 constraint geometry and a coefficient path.
stages.interactionPlan: Follow a coefficient to zero; show instability under correlated features and an Elastic Net comparison in deeper reading.
stages.reference:
Lasso regression is the "Strict Parent." It looks at the variables and says, "Some of you are helping. Some of you are just standing here. Leave."

Minimize: $RSS + \lambda \sum |\beta_j|$

Plain English Breakdown
  • $\sum |\beta_j|$: Instead of squaring the coefficients, Lasso takes their absolute value.
  • What to notice: Because it uses absolute values, the geometry changes. Lasso can force coefficients to drop to exactly zero.

Watch this: Slide the $\lambda$ dial and observe coefficients reach zero. In real samples we do not know which variables are truly useless. With highly correlated predictors, Lasso may select one, discard another, and swap that choice after a small sample change.

Sparse does not mean causal or uniquely important. Lasso supports prediction and variable selection, but selection stability must be checked across resamples. Elastic Net combines L1 and L2 penalties and can behave more stably when predictors share signal.

stages.title: Finding the Sweet Spot
stages.question: How do we choose lambda honestly?
stages.miniPlan: Fold-safe transforms and a validation-error curve.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare candidates using the same folds; expose the one-SE choice only with an explicit uncertainty calculation.
stages.reference:
How do we know the right amount of shrinkage? We use K-Fold Cross-Validation to find the optimal $\lambda$ dial setting.

Choose CV from the data structure. Use stratified folds for imbalanced classes, grouped folds for repeated subjects or organisations, time-series CV for ordered observations, repeated CV for stability, and nested CV when model selection and unbiased evaluation must both occur. Imputation, scaling, encoding, feature selection, PCA, outlier rules, oversampling and threshold tuning all belong inside the training folds.

First, we divide our training data into chunks called "folds".

Train Train Train Train Validate

We train the model on four folds. We then validate it on the one held-out fold (highlighted above). We repeat this process, rotating which fold is held out, until every fold has been tested. Finally, we average the errors.

Why average them? Averaging prevents a "lucky split." It stops us from accidentally choosing a model that just happened to get easy data during validation.

stages.title: The "Super-Variable" Secret
stages.question: How do PCR and PLS differ?
stages.miniPlan: Whether y participates in choosing the new directions.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare a high-variance irrelevant direction with a predictive direction; fit all transforms inside training folds.
stages.reference:
If we have 100 highly correlated variables, they provide redundant information. Dimension Reduction allows us to "squish" them into a few super-variables called Principal Components.

PCR

Compress first, predict later. It squishes variables together without looking at what you are trying to predict.

PLS

Compress while paying attention. It squishes variables together by finding directions that best explain the target you want to predict.

Think of PCR as combining 100 photos of a dog into a single "Super-Photo" of the whole dog. PLS knows you are trying to predict happiness, so it squishes the photos specifically to highlight the wagging tail.

stages.question: Which tradeoff matters for this task?
stages.miniPlan: Prediction, compact explanation, correlated inputs, and causal questions.
stages.interactionPlan: Return conditional options with reasons; stop equating feature selection with causal explanation.
stages.reference:
Select your goals to see which tool fits best (you can select multiple):

Best match: Lasso & Best Subset Selection You prioritize explaining 'why' and keeping models simple.

Lasso & Best Subset Selection

Best for Interpretability & Simplicity. These methods drop variables entirely, leaving a clean, short list of the most important drivers. Essential in healthcare or finance where explaining the "why" matters.

Ridge & PCR

Best for Pure Prediction & Correlated Data. When you have many overlapping clues and prediction accuracy matters more than a simple explanation, keeping all variables with smaller, stable weights helps minimize error on new data.

stages.title: Common Mistakes
stages.question: How does repeated evaluation bias our choices?
stages.miniPlan: Training, repeated validation decisions, sealed test.
stages.interactionPlan: Demonstrate selection optimism and nested evaluation; avoid universal claims about every training score.
stages.reference: Model selection uses information even when a human, rather than a fitting algorithm, makes the decision. Repeatedly choosing settings after inspecting the same held-out scores can overfit that evaluation set. Separate parameter fitting, development selection, and final evaluation. Use cross-validation or an appropriate group/time validation design for development; an outer evaluation loop can estimate the performance of the whole selection procedure. Report uncertainty and the number and type of choices considered.

stages.title: Final Synthesis
stages.question: Can I justify the selected model?
stages.miniPlan: Chosen method, validation basis, preprocessing, limits.
stages.interactionPlan: Produce a short model card from explicit choices; check that no final-test result influenced the selection.
stages.reference:
We do not want a model that is too simple (underfitting). We do not want a model that is too dramatic (overfitting).

By using Cross-Validation, we compare and validate models fairly. By applying Regularization or Subset Selection, we penalize messiness and force the model to focus only on what matters.

The ultimate goal is Generalization. We want to build a model that stays trustworthy and useful when reality shows up and starts ruining everyone's assumptions.

stages.title: The Least Squares Method
stages.question: How does least squares select the weights?
stages.miniPlan: A tiny design matrix and residual sum.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal fitted coefficients with one action; retain rank-deficiency and nonunique-solution caveats in deeper detail.
stages.reference:
Instead of guessing, the computer uses matrix algebra to instantly derive the absolute lowest possible Sum of Squared Errors directly from the dataset.

By minimizing the squared outcome residuals at the observed input combinations, it finds the least-squares fit under the model.

Why Square the Errors?

. It stops positive (+4) and negative (-4) misses from canceling out to zero.

. It heavily punishes huge misses (a miss of 10 costs 100 points), forcing the model to compromise evenly across all variables.

stages.title: The Superpower: Holding Constant
stages.question: What does holding constant mean?
stages.miniPlan: Two hypothetical rows differing only in study hours.
stages.interactionPlan: Slide along a fixed-sleep/practice slice; distinguish conditional association from a causal intervention.
stages.reference:
This is the most critical concept in multiple regression. What does a Study Boost (β1) actually mean when we have an optimal fit?

It means: If a student studies one extra hour, their score increases by exactly that boost amount—assuming their sleep and practice papers stay exactly the same.

This logic applies to each predictor's coefficient: β1 is the estimated association with Study while Sleep and Practice are held fixed, β2 is the estimated association with Sleep while Study and Practice are held fixed, and β3 is the estimated association with Practice while Study and Sleep are held fixed. These are not automatically causal effects.

The model does not literally freeze variables in real life—rather, it does this mathematically to estimate each variable's conditional association holding other modeled predictors fixed.

Notice the highlighted slice on the plane. We've locked "Sleep" at 6 hours (and Practice at its average). As we move purely along the Study axis, the score rises in a perfect straight line determined solely by β1.

0 β1(Study)

stages.title: Building the Prediction
stages.question: How is a prediction assembled?
stages.miniPlan: Intercept plus three signed contributions.
stages.interactionPlan: Build a waterfall with a consistent scale and numeric receipt; preserve negative contributions.
stages.reference:
Now we transition away from the 3D plane. In multiple regression, the prediction is built from a base intercept plus separate contributions from each predictor.

Each predictor adds or subtracts its own specific amount. The final score is simply the sum of all these individual parts. Because of how the model fits the data, each of these contributions is added while the other predictors are treated as fixed.

Predicting a specific student

  • Study 4.0 hrs
  • Sleep 7.5 hrs
  • Practice 2 pps
  • • Base Score = Starting point
  • • Study Boost = β1 × Study hours
  • • Sleep Boost = β2 × Sleep hours
  • • Practice Boost = β3 × Practice papers

Final Score = Sum of all parts

stages.title: The Spurious Trap
stages.question: Why can an apparent relationship disappear?
stages.miniPlan: Simple versus adjusted coefficient, with a confounder sketch.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare fits on the same data; explain why adjustment alone does not establish causality.
stages.reference:
If multiple variables just stack, why not run a simple regression for each variable separately? Because of Spurious Correlations.

Imagine we want to predict Shark Attacks. If we run a simple model using Ice Cream Sales, the correlation is huge! It looks like ice cream causes shark attacks.

But the true driver is a lurking variable: High Temperature. Hot days cause both ice cream sales and beach visits (which lead to shark attacks).

The Power of "Holding Constant"

Multiple regression estimates a variable's

conditional association holding other modeled predictors fixed

, which can reveal when a variable only looked important because it moved together with another predictor. If we put both Ice Cream and Temperature into the model, the model essentially compares days with the

same temperature

. Holding temperature constant, ice cream sales have almost zero conditional association with shark attacks in this example.

If a coefficient shrinks close to zero after the other predictors are included, that suggests it has little

conditional

association with the predicted outcome (y) after accounting for the others. This does

not

prove the variable has no real-world effect at all, only that its estimated conditional association is small within this specific model.

Note: A larger coefficient doesn't always mean a "more important" predictor, as they depend on the unit of measurement.

stages.title: The Adjusted R² Penalty
stages.question: Why can training R-squared reward useless variables?
stages.miniPlan: Training R², adjusted R², and validation error.
stages.interactionPlan: Add a seeded noise predictor; recompute all three without implying adjusted R² always rejects it.
stages.reference:
How do we know if our team of variables is actually good? R² tells us what percentage of the variance we explained.

For least-squares models with an intercept fitted to the same training observations, adding predictors makes training R² stay the same or increase. Even "Student's Shoe Size" may increase it, without improving predictions on new data.

Adj R² = 1 - [ (1 - R²)(n - 1) / (n - p - 1) ]

Adjusted R² corrects for this by penalizing model complexity. In the formula, n is the number of observations and p is the number of predictors.

Every new predictor (p) uses up flexibility and increases the penalty. Adjusted R² can rise or fall, even for an irrelevant variable in a particular sample. It is a descriptive aid, not an automatic feature-retention rule: consider validation performance, the modeling goal, and subject knowledge.

stages.title: Reading the Model Output
stages.question: How do I read a regression summary?
stages.miniPlan: Estimate / SE / interval / test statistic / units.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a coefficient row and link its interval and prediction effect; replace universal t≈2 shortcuts with conditions.
stages.reference:
When a data analyst fits a multiple linear regression, they don't look at a 3D plot—they look at a summary table to evaluate the results.

  • Estimate: The coefficient (β). How much the prediction changes for a one-unit increase in this predictor, holding all other predictors constant.
  • Std. Error: The uncertainty around the estimate. A smaller standard error means we are more confident in the coefficient.
  • t value: The estimate divided by its standard error. A larger absolute value (typically > 2) indicates strong statistical evidence that the true effect is not zero.

Note: Each coefficient should be read as "the change in predicted y for a one-unit increase in this predictor, holding the others constant." Because predictors can be measured in entirely different units, coefficients cannot be compared as pure "importance scores" unless the predictors are on comparable scales.

Diagnostics belong with the output.

Inspect residual-versus-fitted, Q–Q, scale-location, leverage and influence plots. Use VIFs and coefficient intervals to diagnose multicollinearity; document categorical reference levels and interactions. Report confidence intervals for mean responses and wider prediction intervals for new observations. These coefficients are adjusted associations, not causal effects without a causal design. Multiple linear regression is a powerful detective. It models additive effects, isolates individual drivers, and finds the mathematically optimal fit by minimizing squared errors.

stages.title: The whole idea: learn patterns from examples
stages.question: What does learning from examples mean?
stages.miniPlan: Conventional rule versus learned parameters.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace a labeled student example to a prediction; keep the running example consistent with the visuals.
stages.reference:
A neural network is a model made of small calculation units called neurons. Each neuron receives numbers, gives some of them more importance than others, combines them, and passes a new number forward.

Imagine teaching a child to recognize cats. You do not write every possible cat rule. You show many examples labeled cat or not cat. The child gradually notices patterns. A neural network does something similar with numbers.

Plain-English translation: examples go in, a prediction comes out, mistakes are measured, and the internal settings are adjusted so the next prediction is less wrong.

Normal programming versus machine learning

Normal programming: a human writes the rules, the computer applies them, and an answer comes out. Machine learning: a human supplies examples and correct outcomes, then the model learns useful rules from those examples. Neural networks are valuable when the rules are too numerous or complicated to write by hand.

You only need basic comfort with multiplication, averages, and percentages. Every specialist word is defined before it is used.

stages.title: Data becomes features and labels
stages.question: How do rows become inputs and targets?
stages.miniPlan: Raw row, encoded feature vector, separate label.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a student and follow every value; explain dimensions and units before introducing tensors.
stages.reference:
Data is the collection of examples the model learns from. In our toy problem, each row describes one student.

Study hoursSleep hoursAttendancePassed?
8790%Yes
2440%No
5670%Yes

Features

The clues the model receives: study hours, sleep hours, and attendance.

Label

The correct answer it must learn to predict: passed or failed.

Supervised learning means the training examples already contain the correct answers. Features are the clues; the label is the answer key.

stages.title: Clean, encode, scale, then split
stages.question: When should preprocessing be learned?
stages.miniPlan: Split first → fit transforms on train → apply unchanged.
stages.interactionPlan: Correct the heading; contrast a safe pipeline with one that uses held-out statistics.
stages.reference:
Real data is rarely ready to train on. Missing values, duplicates, impossible values, inconsistent labels, and suspicious outliers must be investigated before the model sees them.

1. Clean

Fix or remove records that are missing, duplicated, impossible, or inconsistent.

2. Encode

Turn words and categories into numbers because the network performs mathematics.

3. Scale

Put numerical features on comparable ranges so a large unit does not look important merely because its number is bigger.

4. Split

Keep separate training, validation, and test sets so memorization cannot impersonate learning.

Training set ≈ 70% → teaches the model Validation set ≈ 15% → tunes choices during development Test set ≈ 15% → final, untouched exam

Keep the final exam separate: the test examples must not be used to teach or tune the model. Otherwise the final score no longer shows how well the model handles actually unseen data.

stages.title: A network is layers of tiny calculators
stages.question: What does a layer compute?
stages.miniPlan: Input vector → neuron calculations → output vector.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal one layer at a time without moving all nodes or shrinking annotations.
stages.reference:
The input layer receives study, sleep, and attendance. Each hidden neuron receives its own weighted mixture of those inputs. Across training, different mixtures become sensitive to different combinations—perhaps high study with low sleep, or strong attendance with moderate study. These are emergent feature detectors: useful sensitivities discovered from data, not roles assigned to neurons by a person.

Student pass/fail architecture: 3 → 8 → 4 → 1 3 inputs → hidden patterns → 1 pass-score neuron What you choose

Design decisions before training

  • How many hidden layers
  • How many neurons per layer
  • Hidden and output activations
  • Optimizer and learning rate

Parameters discovered from examples

  • Every connection weight
  • Every neuron bias
  • Useful internal sensitivities
  • Representations that reduce loss

Why not something simpler? A linear model may be enough when one straight boundary captures the pattern. Hidden layers are justified only when interactions and reusable intermediate patterns improve performance on new data.

The visual begins with the skeleton you designed, then animates the connection strengths that training learns. A larger network is not automatically better: more depth and width need more data, computation, and protection against overfitting.

stages.title: One feature has a different weight into every hidden neuron
stages.question: Why does each connection have its own weight?
stages.miniPlan: One input feeding two neurons through different weights.
stages.interactionPlan: Select an edge and trace its contribution; changing one weight must not change unrelated edges.
stages.reference:
There is not one universal “sleep weight.” Sleep connects to every neuron in the next layer, and each connection learns a separate value. One neuron may respond strongly to sleep, another weakly, and another negatively because it combines sleep with different evidence.

Choose an input to reveal its four independently learned connections.

hidden neuron j score = study × wstudy,j + sleep × wsleep,j + attendance × wattendance,j + biasj w

What: weights control sensitivity and biases shift activation. How: training changes all of them to reduce loss. Why: separate weights let neurons specialize in different combinations. Why not assign roles? Human labels would constrain the model before the data reveals which combinations are useful.

Interpretability note: you can inspect every weight, but raw numbers rarely translate into one clean human rule. A neuron usually participates in a distributed pattern with many other neurons.

stages.title: Non-linearity lets stacked layers learn bends
stages.question: Why are nonlinear activations necessary?
stages.miniPlan: Two linear layers collapsed into one versus a nonlinear bend.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle activation on a tiny deterministic network; state that extra linear layers alone remain linear.
stages.reference:
First ask why an activation is needed. If every layer performs only a linear weighted sum, stacking ten layers still collapses into one linear transformation. The network gains more arithmetic, but not a more flexible decision boundary.

inputs → weighted sum + bias → raw score → activation function → output signal Boundary experiment

ReLU is a learned-pattern gate. A positive raw score passes as evidence that one learned pattern is present; zero means that neuron does not pass evidence for that pattern. It is misleading to say the network simply “throws away negative information”: other neurons—with different weights and biases—can represent opposing or complementary evidence.

Hidden layers: ReLU

ReLU(2.5) = 2.5 passes positive evidence; ReLU(-3) = 0 gates that detector off.

Binary output: sigmoid

One raw output becomes a score from 0 to 1, such as a pass score of 0.82.

Multiclass output: softmax

Several class scores are converted together into probabilities that total 100%.

Regression output: linear

The output remains a direct number because a probability constraint would be inappropriate.

Design decision: humans choose activations before training. Training learns the weights and biases that determine which patterns produce positive or non-positive raw scores.

stages.title: Forward propagation makes one pass-score prediction
stages.question: What happens in one forward pass?
stages.miniPlan: Multiply → sum → bias → activation receipt.
stages.interactionPlan: Step a single student's actual values through the network; preserve the same selected row throughout.
stages.reference:
Forward propagation means information moves from the three inputs, through every hidden layer, to the single output neuron used by this binary task.

study + sleep + attendance → hidden-layer calculations and ReLU activations → one raw output score → sigmoid → pass score between 0 and 1

For one student, the output neuron might produce 0.82. We read that as an 82% model score for “pass.” The corresponding fail score is 1 − 0.82 = 0.18.

The output neuron does not yet make the final Pass/Fail decision. Stage 14 will apply a separate decision threshold, such as 0.50, to turn this continuous score into a class label.

stages.title: Loss measures how wrong the prediction was
stages.question: What does loss measure?
stages.miniPlan: Prediction, label, selected loss, numeric contribution.
stages.interactionPlan: Change the prediction and show the loss curve; explain the difference between a probability, decision, and loss.
stages.reference:
A loss function converts prediction error into a number. Smaller loss is better. Larger loss tells the training process that the current weights need more correction.

Regression

When predicting a number, mean squared error is common. It squares mistakes, so large errors receive extra punishment.

Classification

When predicting a class, cross-entropy loss is common. It strongly penalizes a model that is confidently wrong.

Loss is the teacher's marking pen. It does not merely say “wrong.” It gives the optimizer a numerical signal showing how much improvement is needed.

stages.title: Backpropagation computes gradients—only gradients
stages.question: What does backpropagation compute?
stages.miniPlan: Local derivative × upstream derivative.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace gradients backward while keeping weights fixed; make this distinction explicit in the controls.
stages.reference:
A gradient is a collection of slopes: for each weight, it answers “if this weight increased a tiny amount, how would the loss change?” The sign gives a direction and the magnitude describes local sensitivity.

forward pass → prediction prediction + truth → loss backpropagation → gradient for every weight and bias weights are still unchanged

Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss backward through the network. It calculates how local changes connect to the final error. It does not choose a learning rate and it never updates a parameter.

Plain distinction: backprop computes gradients only. The optimizer later uses those gradients to update weights.

stages.title: The optimizer takes iterative, local steps
stages.question: What does the optimizer change?
stages.miniPlan: Current weight − learning rate × gradient.
stages.interactionPlan: Apply one update; compare step sizes and overshoot in the model behavior without decorative numeric overshoot.
stages.reference:
Gradient descent applies the update. It combines the local gradient with a learning rate: next weight = current weight − learning rate × gradient. Because the gradient describes only the slope near the current point, optimization must repeat rather than jump directly to the answer.

Small steps need many updates. Medium steps descend efficiently. Large steps can overshoot and bounce away. Drag the current point on the curve to inspect a different local slope.

What: a gradient is local slope. Why: it tells the optimizer which nearby direction lowers loss. How: multiply it by the learning rate and update. Why not one giant step? the landscape bends, and the local slope does not reveal the whole terrain.

Why local does not guarantee global

A low point reached from the current start may be a local minimum, while a lower global minimum exists elsewhere. Initialization, optimizer behavior, noise from batches, and the shape of the loss surface all affect the path.

stages.title: One update has a strict causal order
stages.question: Why must operations happen in this order?
stages.miniPlan: Forward → loss → gradients → update.
stages.interactionPlan: Require the learner to choose the next operation; snapshot all values for reversible inspection.
stages.reference:
The model usually learns from a small batch. Each update follows the same sequence; confusing these steps hides what actually causes learning.

. take data 2. forward pass makes predictions 3. loss measures error 4. backpropagation computes gradients 5. optimizer applies parameter updates 6. updated weights change the next prediction 7. repeat Batchexamples per updateIterationone update stepEpochone full pass through training data 1,000 examples ÷ batch size 100 = 10 iterations per epoch ↻

The forward pass supplies a prediction; loss supplies an objective; backprop supplies gradients; the optimizer supplies the update. Repetition turns many local corrections into learned behavior.

stages.title: Choose the model before validation gets worse
stages.question: Why monitor validation during training?
stages.miniPlan: Train and validation curves with checkpoint markers.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub real or honestly labeled illustrative epochs; select the best validation checkpoint and preserve test isolation.
stages.reference:
Training loss can keep falling while validation loss eventually rises. That is the causal signature of overfitting: the model is improving on examples it trains on while becoming less useful on unseen data. Keep the checkpoint near the lowest validation loss, not the final training step.

Local is not global: an optimizer follows nearby slopes and may settle in one valley even if a lower valley exists elsewhere. Validation asks a different question: whichever valley training reaches, does that model generalize?

Why can dependence be bad? A neuron might learn a brittle shortcut such as “attendance decides everything.” If later neurons rely heavily on that one pathway, the network may fail when the shortcut does not hold for new students.

Decrease the rate and more hidden neurons stay active on the right. Increase it and more paths switch off, which can reduce shortcut dependence but may underfit; at 100%, this simplified visual switches off every hidden neuron.

During training

Different hidden neurons are temporarily switched off on different updates.

Validation and real use

Dropout is switched off, the full network is used, and the framework handles the required scaling.

Decrease dropout

More paths stay active, but the model may overfit by leaning on shortcuts.

Increase dropout

More paths switch off in the visual, spreading reliance until excessive dropout starts to underfit.

Keep this model: save the checkpoint at the validation minimum. Dropout is one possible regularizer, not an automatic requirement; its value depends on the architecture, data, and observed overfitting.

stages.title: Humans choose the architecture and hyperparameters
stages.question: Which settings do humans choose?
stages.miniPlan: Parameter versus hyperparameter table.
stages.interactionPlan: Change layer width, activation, or learning rate in separate experiments; show computation and capacity tradeoffs.
stages.reference:
Parameters are learned by the model: every weight and bias. Hyperparameters are design decisions made before or around training.

Binary classification

Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: one neuron with sigmoid.

Multi-class classification

Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: one score per class with softmax.

Regression

Hidden layers: ReLU. Output: usually one linear numerical value.

Feature engineering

Structured problems may improve when raw fields are turned into more useful clues, such as date of birth → age.

There is no universal “best” architecture. A design must match the task, data quantity, noise, complexity, and cost of mistakes.

stages.title: The test set evaluates both scores and decisions
stages.question: What is evaluated on the final test set?
stages.miniPlan: Scores, chosen decision threshold, and confusion counts.
stages.interactionPlan: Lock the threshold before reveal; offer a distinct validation workspace for experimentation.
stages.reference:
After training and tuning are finished, the model is evaluated once on the untouched test set. For our binary task, sigmoid first produces a pass score. A separate classification decision threshold then converts that score into Pass or Fail.

model pass score = 0.72 decision threshold = 0.50 0.72 ≥ 0.50 prediction = Pass

This threshold is not the school’s exam passing mark. It is the model’s cutoff for turning a score between 0 and 1 into a predicted class.

Decision controlClassification decision threshold: 0.50

Lowering the threshold predicts Pass more easily: recall usually rises, but false positives may increase. Raising it is stricter: false positives may fall, but more actual passes can be missed.

.75Precision0.75Recall0.75F1-score

Actually passedActually failed
Predicted passTrue positive: 3False positive: 1
Predicted failFalse negative: 1True negative: 3

Accuracy alone can mislead. Precision asks whether predicted passes were usually correct. Recall asks how many actual passes the model successfully found.

stages.title: Error analysis starts with individual students
stages.question: What can an individual error teach us?
stages.miniPlan: One wrong student's inputs, score, action, true outcome.
stages.interactionPlan: Brush error groups and inspect cases; avoid selecting future model changes by repeated final-test checking.
stages.reference:
Overall scores hide which people are affected. Move the threshold, inspect the highlighted false positives and false negatives, and connect each case to the metric that represents its cost.

Case-level threshold explorer Classification threshold: 0.50

Noor, score 0.68, actually failed: at the starting 0.50 threshold this is a false positive. If wrongly predicting success is costly, prioritize precision.

Sam, score 0.43, actually passed: at the starting 0.50 threshold this is a false negative. If missing a student who would pass is costly, prioritize recall.

Ana, score 0.57, actually passed: at the starting threshold this is a borderline true positive that flips when the threshold rises past 0.57. F1 is useful when both false positives and false negatives matter and one balanced summary is needed.

Threshold changes only the decision rule; it does not repair weak features, biased labels, or poor calibration. Inspect concrete errors, diagnose the cause, change the appropriate part, then evaluate again by relevant groups.

stages.title: Saving, deployment, and monitoring finish the lifecycle
stages.question: What must be saved with the weights?
stages.miniPlan: Feature order, transforms, architecture, weights, threshold.
stages.interactionPlan: Introduce a feature-order or scaling mismatch and trace its impact; restore the correct pipeline.
stages.reference:
Once performance is acceptable, the final model is saved. The saved package includes the architecture, learned weights and biases, and often the preprocessing rules needed to reproduce training-time inputs.

new user input → same preprocessing used during training → saved model → prediction → application response

Deployment puts the model into a website, mobile app, server API, edge device, or business system. A model sitting in a notebook is an experiment, not a working service.

Monitor accuracy, error types, input-data changes, speed, complaints, fairness, and security. When the world changes and performance falls, the model is experiencing drift.

stages.title: Different network families organize information differently
stages.question: Why do different architectures exist?
stages.miniPlan: Tabular, image, and sequence structure.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a representation and show the relevant inductive assumption; avoid forcing every family into one tiny network diagram.
stages.reference:
Feedforward network

Information moves from input to hidden layers to output. This is the structure used throughout this lesson.

Convolutional network (CNN)

Common for images. Early layers notice edges; later layers combine them into shapes and object parts.

Recurrent network (RNN)

Designed for sequences and previous context, such as text, audio, and time series.

Transformer

Uses attention to connect relevant parts of data, allowing many relationships to be considered at once.

This layered transformation is called representation learning. Raw inputs become increasingly useful internal patterns: pixels → edges → shapes → objects, or word pieces → phrases → context.

Interpretability: weights are visible, but a representation is usually distributed across many parameters. Inspecting one large weight rarely yields a faithful human rule; use case-level explanations, sensitivity analyses, and validation evidence together.

Neural networks are powerful because they can learn complex representations. They are used for images, speech, text, translation, recommendations, medical scans, fraud detection, forecasting, game playing, and large language models. They are not magic: they still depend on good data, sensible design, testing, monitoring, and human judgment.

stages.title: Try the tiny student-pass network
stages.question: Can I predict this tiny network's answer?
stages.miniPlan: A fully numeric input-to-output calculation.
stages.interactionPlan: Expose one controlled input/weight at a time; add a reset to the authored example and a computed receipt.
stages.reference: The live network has two inputs, three hidden units, and one sigmoid output. For hidden unit j, zⱼ = wⱼ₁x₁ + wⱼ₂x₂ + bⱼ and aⱼ = g(zⱼ). The output logit is u = Σvⱼaⱼ + b and the probability is σ(u). A binary label is produced only after choosing a threshold. For binary cross-entropy, the derivative with respect to u is p − y. The learning demonstration averages gradients over training rows; the inspectable input sliders do not change the training dataset.

stages.title: One full training cycle
stages.question: Can I explain a complete training cycle?
stages.miniPlan: One row or batch across all four learning operations.
stages.interactionPlan: Step, rewind, and replay once; end playback at completion and test that gradients precede weight updates.
stages.reference:
• You choose the architecture, activations, optimizer, and learning rate.
  • Data enters and a forward pass produces predictions.
  • Loss converts prediction error into an objective.
  • Backpropagation computes gradients only.
  • The optimizer updates every weight and bias.
  • Updated parameters change the next forward pass.
  • Validation identifies the checkpoint that generalizes best.
  • Testing, deployment, monitoring, and error analysis keep the model accountable after training.

data → forward pass → loss → backprop gradients → optimizer step → updated weights → repeat ↻

What: a parameterized function. Why: to learn patterns too complex to specify cleanly. How: repeated local updates reduce loss. Why not something simpler? use a simpler model whenever it generalizes well enough and is easier to maintain or explain.

Final check

Which dataset should stay untouched until training and tuning are complete?

The test set is the final untouched exam. Training teaches; validation tunes.

stages.title: What problem is One-R solving?
stages.question: What does one feature mean?
stages.miniPlan: Features versus target in one umbrella row.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a column and keep the target clearly separate.
stages.reference:
Classification predicts a category, such as Yes or No. A feature is an input column. The target is the category we want to predict.

Our teaching sample records 14 days. Each row contains outlook, humidity, wind, temperature, and whether someone carried an umbrella.

“If I may inspect only one column, which column should I choose, and what should I predict for each of its values?”

rows 4 candidate features Yes target No target

stages.title: First, make the lazy prediction.
stages.question: Why start with a majority baseline?
stages.miniPlan: 8 Yes / 6 No → 8 of 14 correct.
stages.interactionPlan: Predict the baseline before revealing it; add an imbalanced case where accuracy is misleading.
stages.reference:
Before building a model, count the target classes. There are 8 Yes rows and 6 No rows, so the majority classifier predicts Yes for every case.

majority accuracy = largest class count ÷ all rows

This baseline is intentionally dull. That is its job. A new classifier that cannot beat it has not earned its electricity.

Class imbalance warning.

If 95% of rows are No, always predicting No scores 95% accuracy while learning nothing about Yes. Accuracy needs company.

If a dataset has 70 Yes rows and 30 No rows, what does the majority classifier predict?

Yes for every row, producing 70% training accuracy.

stages.title: Make a rule from one categorical feature.
stages.question: How is a rule built for each value?
stages.miniPlan: Value-level class counts and majority.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a category and trace its chosen prediction and errors.
stages.reference:
Choose a candidate feature, such as Outlook. Handle each distinct value separately and predict its local majority class.

Collect all rows where Outlook is Sunny. 2Count Yes and No among those rows. 3Use the local majority as the prediction for Sunny. 4Repeat for Cloudy and Rainy. Example rulebook IF Outlook = Sunny THEN Umbrella = No IF Outlook = Cloudy THEN Umbrella = Yes IF Outlook = Rainy THEN Umbrella = Yes error for a feature value = rows that disagree with that value’s majority class

stages.title: Test every feature. Keep the lowest-error rule.
stages.question: How is the winning feature selected?
stages.miniPlan: Competing feature rulebooks and training errors.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect each feature without changing rows; reveal the declared tie policy.
stages.reference:
One-R repeats the same construction for every candidate feature. Each feature gets a rulebook and a total error count.

FeatureTraining errorsError rateResult
Outlook3 / 1421.4%Selected
Humidity4 / 1428.6%Runner-up
Wind5 / 1435.7%Rejected
Temperature*5 / 1435.7%After buckets

selected feature = arg min(feature training errors)

Ties are allowed.

Declare a policy in advance: prefer fewer values, use a fixed feature order, or choose the winner under cross-validation. Do not improvise after seeing the result.

*Temperature uses the fixed teaching intervals introduced next. Exact bucketing procedures vary by implementation.

stages.title: Turn numeric values into intervals.
stages.question: Why bucket numeric values?
stages.miniPlan: Exact-value lookup versus training-derived intervals.
stages.interactionPlan: Move a query through fixed intervals; explain that exact-value rules can memorize the sample.
stages.reference:
A rule for every exact temperature would memorise the training sample and fail on a new value such as 23.6°C. One-R therefore discretises numeric values into intervals.

Sort rows by the numeric feature. 2Group neighbouring values into sufficiently reliable buckets. 3Assign each bucket its majority class. 4Merge or adjust unstable neighbours according to the chosen implementation. One possible training-only discretisation Temperature ≤ 22.5 → Yes 22.5 < Temperature ≤ 27.5 → Yes Temperature > 27.5 → No

Leakage alert.

Fit cut-points using training data only. Choosing intervals after inspecting test labels is answer-shopping in a lab coat.

stages.title: Missing values and unseen categories are part of the model.
stages.question: What happens with missing or unseen values?
stages.miniPlan: Missing, unseen category, tie, out-of-range cases.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose an edge case and trace the declared fallback; do not infer a rule from test labels.
stages.reference:
Real inputs are rarely as cooperative as textbook tables. Decide what happens when the selected feature is missing, a category never appeared during training, classes tie, or a number falls outside the observed range.

?Missing input NewUnseen category 4–4Local tie Reasonable fallback

Use the overall training-set majority class or estimated class prior. Another option is to learn “Missing” as its own category when enough training rows contain missing values.

The fitted rule uses Outlook, but a future row has Outlook = “Hazy”. What happens?

Use the declared fallback. Do not invent a rule from the test row.

stages.title: Prediction is deliberately cheap.
stages.question: Why is prediction inexpensive?
stages.miniPlan: Read feature → find category → return rule.
stages.interactionPlan: Change irrelevant input fields and show the prediction stays unchanged for the fitted one-feature model.
stages.reference:
Read the selected feature, find its stored value or interval, return the class, and use the fallback if nothing matches.

Prediction:

Outlook = Cloudy → Umbrella = Yes. Humidity and wind are ignored because Outlook won training selection.

The model is saying Outlook is the strongest standalone predictor in this sample. It is not saying the other features have no relationship with umbrella use.

stages.title: One feature cannot express an interaction.
stages.question: What can a single feature miss?
stages.miniPlan: A two-feature interaction table.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal a pattern that requires both features and compare One-R with a richer rule.
stages.reference:

stages.title: Evaluate each fold. Decide what to do next.
stages.question: Which metric matches the decision?
stages.miniPlan: Actual denominators and concrete FP/FN costs.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare fold outcomes and workload; avoid tying entire industries universally to precision or recall.
stages.reference:
Cross-validation gives multiple views of performance. Use the right metric for your goal, check stability across folds, and decide whether to proceed, tune, or collect more data.

Choose the right metric

Pick the metric that matches the problem and the cost of mistakes.

Overall accuracy

Focus when classes are balanced and both types of errors matter similarly.

Best for: General performance check, balanced datasets.

Precision

Focus when false positives are costly (predicting Yes when it’s actually No).

Best for: Spam detection, fraud alerts, medical testing.

Recall

Focus when false negatives are costly (missing actual Yes cases).

Best for: Disease screening, churn prevention, safety monitoring.

Measure stability across folds

Compute the chosen metric for each fold. Then summarize the stability.

Report individual fold scores and, when useful, repeat cross-validation with different splits.

fold_scores = scores
mean = scores.mean()
sd = scores.std(ddof=1)
range_ = (scores.min(), scores.max())

Fold scores share overlapping training data; their spread is not a confidence interval for generalisation performance.

Report all three (recommended)

Always look at these together for the full picture.

  • Mean (μ): average performance across folds
  • Sample SD: spread of performance
  • Score distribution: individual fold or repeated-CV scores

Also check the min–max range across folds.

Interpret stability in context

There are no universal percentage bands or automatic proceed/stop rules. Consider dataset size, class balance, the metric, domain, and the impact of errors.

SD and rangeSpreadJudge variation against the metric and consequences of errors.

Read together:

Mean, SD, range, and the score distribution describe these splits. Consistency alone does not establish useful performance or justify deployment.

stages.question: What can we learn without a target?
stages.miniPlan: Rows, six features, and the absence of a y column.
stages.interactionPlan: Select one student across the source table and 2D slice; label the slice versus the full fit.
stages.reference: PCA uses numerical inputs without a target label to estimate directions of variation. The live example contains eight observations and two features so every coordinate can be inspected. For centered matrix X, sample covariance is XᵀX/(n − 1). Its eigenvectors define orthogonal loading directions and its eigenvalues give variances of the corresponding component scores. Higher-dimensional PCA follows the same idea; a two-dimensional drawing cannot show every feature or component of such a model.

stages.title: The "Too Much Information" Problem
stages.question: Why compress several measurements?
stages.miniPlan: Original point and projections on two candidate axes.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare reconstruction loss after discarding a direction; avoid equating sample variance with all information.
stages.reference:
Why can't we just look at the variables one by one?

Because dimensionality explodes fast. With 6 variables you already have 15 pairwise plots, and with 10 variables you jump to 45. No single view tells the whole story.

If we only look at Speed (squashing the data to the horizontal axis), we lose all information about strength. The points overlap and hide the true shape of our students.

If we only look at Strength (vertical axis), we lose speed. Neither axis alone captures the main "soul" of the dataset, because athletic students tend to be both fast and strong.

When variables are correlated (moving together), keeping them separate is redundant. We need a way to combine them.

stages.title: Finding the First Principal Component
stages.question: Why maximize projected variance?
stages.miniPlan: Candidate direction, projected spread, reconstruction error.
stages.interactionPlan: Rotate a candidate axis continuously and mark the fitted PC1 optimum; use a centered dataset.
stages.reference:
PCA looks for a brand new direction—a line sliced straight through the cloud of data.

It rotates this line until the data points, when projected onto the line, spread out as much as possible.

The direction that creates the largest spread is called Principal Component 1 (PC1). By maximizing the spread, this line stays closest to the entire data cloud, giving us the clearest single summary.

stages.title: The Secret Sauce: Loadings
stages.question: What are loadings?
stages.miniPlan: One score as a weighted sum of standardized features.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a loading, highlight the source column, and trace its contribution for one student.
stages.reference:
How does PCA actually draw this line? It acts like a "dimmer knob", mixing the original variables together using weights.

These weights are called Loadings. They tell us how much each original variable contributes to the new component.

PC1 Score = Σ(wⱼ × standardized featureⱼ)

For this generated dataset, the PC1 loadings are computed directly from the same PCA fit used for the scores and scree plot:

PC1 blends the columns that move together into one broader summary axis.

stages.title: When Scaling Is Appropriate
stages.question: Why might scaling change the answer?
stages.miniPlan: Raw units, mean, SD, centered value, z-score.
stages.interactionPlan: Switch raw-centered and standardized fits on identical rows; retain units and model-choice explanation.
stages.reference:
There is a massive trap in PCA. Because it hunts for maximum variance, it can be bullied by units.

Even in this generated dataset, Strength naturally varies much more than Speed in raw units. Without scaling, PCA leans toward the higher-variance column; after Standardization, both columns get a fair vote.

Step 1: Mean (μ) = Average of column

Step 3: Variance (σ²) = Average of (X - μ)²

Step 4: Std Dev (σ) = √Variance

Step 5: Scaled (Z) = (X - μ) / σ

Result: After scaling, every variable has a mean of 0 and a standard deviation of 1. Units disappear, and no single variable dominates just because it has bigger raw numbers.

Scaling is a modelling choice, not a universal rule. It is normally appropriate for variables in unlike units—such as height in centimetres and income in dollars—or when raw scale should not determine the components. If measurements share the same units and their variance differences are scientifically meaningful, scaling may be undesirable. Fit the scaler on training data only.

stages.title: Capturing the Leftovers: PC2
stages.question: How is PC2 selected?
stages.miniPlan: Remaining variation after PC1 with an orthogonality constraint.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal the second eigen-direction; distinguish PCA score decorrelation from arbitrary perpendicular axes.
stages.reference:
PC1 captured the main trend (overall athleticism). But there is still some "thickness" left over in the cloud.

To capture this, PCA finds a Second Principal Component (PC2). It follows the exact same logic, but with one non-negotiable rule:

It must be exactly 90 degrees (perpendicular) to PC1.

Because it is perpendicular, PC2 is completely uncorrelated with PC1. It captures the contrasts—for example, students who are stronger than expected for their speed.

stages.title: The Transformation (Scores)
stages.question: What are scores?
stages.miniPlan: One original row versus its new coordinates.
stages.interactionPlan: Animate coordinates into the new basis with identity preserved; show reconstruction when all components are kept.
stages.reference:
Here is where the magic happens. We don't just draw lines on the old graph. We rotate the entire coordinate system.

PCA finds the directions that capture the greatest sample variance. These directions are not automatically the most scientifically important or most predictive.

The same observations are represented in a new coordinate system. When all principal components are retained, the centred data can be reconstructed up to numerical precision. When components are discarded, some sample variance and potentially useful information are lost. A few rows from the original matrix become PC scores side by side:

Student Speed Strength Endurance Agility Balance Jump PC1 PC2

stages.title: Proportion of Variance Explained
stages.question: What fraction of variance is retained?
stages.miniPlan: Eigenvalue / total eigenvalue and cumulative PVE.
stages.interactionPlan: Select component count on a scree plot; distinguish variance retained from predictive information preserved.
stages.reference:
How do we know if our components are actually useful? We look at the Proportion of Variance Explained (PVE) using a Scree Plot.

Think of the total sample variance as a pizza. PC1 takes the biggest slice and PC2 takes the next. The cumulative line approaches 100% of sample variance—not 100% of general information, scientific importance, or predictive signal.

Look for the "Elbow" in the plot. In datasets with 100 columns, you might find that just 2 or 3 components explain 95% of the variance. That's the "Magic Shrink Ray" at work.

PCA is unsupervised and ignores the target. A low-variance component may still contain important predictive or scientific information. Discarding low-variance components reduces noise only when noise mainly occupies those directions; this is not guaranteed.

stages.title: Interactive Playground
stages.question: Can I discover the best projection?
stages.miniPlan: Candidate-angle score compared with fitted PCA.
stages.interactionPlan: Give a predict/try/reveal exercise; do not call every user-selected axis a principal component.
stages.reference:
Watch how the spread (variance) changes based on the angle. Your goal is to find the angle that maximizes the variance.

PC2 is locked to stay 90° from PC1, so it always shows the next-biggest leftover spread instead of being chosen freely.

The angle with the highest variance is exactly where the math places Principal Component 1.

stages.title: The Best Summary
stages.question: What should I report and avoid claiming?
stages.miniPlan: Scaling, component count, loadings, PVE, and limitations.
stages.interactionPlan: Explain a chosen representation; include a low-variance predictive-signal counterexample in deeper reading.
stages.reference:
PCA represents centred observations along directions of greatest sample variance. Those directions need not be the most scientifically meaningful or predictive.

PCA may reduce noise when discarded directions mainly contain noise, but this is not guaranteed. Low-variance components can still contain meaningful structure or predictive signal.

Remember:

  • Decide whether scaling is appropriate based on the variables’ units and whether raw variance differences should influence the components.
  • Loadings are the weights.
  • Scores are the new coordinates.
  • Stop when the "pizza slices" of variance get too small.

stages.miniPlan: Three local regions of a curved dataset.
stages.interactionPlan: Highlight systematic residual patterns using the same points; begin with a question rather than declaring linear methods inadequate.

What we do

Plot the raw input against the response.

Why we do it

To visually check the shape. A straight line will naturally fail to capture a curved dataset.

What this means

If the data forms a hill, a valley, or an S-curve, simple math won't be enough.

Let's see what happens if we force a straight line anyway.

➔ Look at the black dots on the chart. Notice how they structurally form a curved shape rather than a straight path.

What we do

Fit a basic, flat or sloped straight line.

Why we do it

To set a baseline and prove that standard linear regression fails on curves.

What this means

The line completely ignores the true shape of our data. This failure is called underfitting.

We need to give the math the flexibility to bend.

What we do

Create new columns by squaring and cubing the input data.

Why we do it

Adding powers of the input gives the underlying formula the ability to curve.

What this means

First, we shrink the input numbers so squaring them doesn't create huge, unstable values. Then we build our Design Matrix.

Now the model has more ingredients to build with.

The algorithm calculates the best weights for each column in our matrix.

Why we do it

To find the exact mathematical combination that fits the dots.

What this means

The weights act like knobs that tell the curve how strongly to bend and in what direction.

Let's check how close our curve actually gets to the data.

stages.interactionPlan: Link a residual plot point with its original observation; preserve the training/validation distinction.

What we do

Measure the vertical distance between the true dots and our curve.

Why we do it

To see exactly where the model is still wrong.

What this means

Small random misses are normal, but a clear pattern in the misses means the model is still failing.

Let's see what happens if we add too many curves.

stages.question: Why can a flexible curve do worse on new data?

stages.interactionPlan: Scrub degree on a fixed split; highlight boundary oscillation and label any schematic curve.
stages.reference:
What we do

Push the model to extreme complexity and test it on hidden data.

Why we do it

To catch overfitting before we use the model in the real world.

What this means

Training error can look amazing while validation error gets much worse, which is the warning sign of overfitting.

We need to find the balance between too simple and too complex.

➔ Look at the validation curve. Training error drops, but validation error rises. The gold dots are validation observations used to choose degree; the final test set remains untouched.

stages.interactionPlan: Compare candidate degrees using fixed folds or a fixed holdout; noise regeneration must be explicit.

What we do

Compare candidate complexities using validation or cross-validation error.

Why we do it

The best shape changes depending on the data.

What this means

stages.title: Lock in the Model
stages.question: What gets locked before final evaluation?
stages.miniPlan: Basis, transforms, degree, coefficients, and threshold if relevant.
stages.interactionPlan: Commit the chosen setup, reveal final test once, and explain extrapolation/monitoring limits instead of claiming proof.
