Validation provides evidence about those choices; it does not prove future reliability. Evaluate the locked procedure on independent observations representative of its use. Extrapolation, distribution shift, and limited sample size remain concerns. Revising the model after a final-test result requires fresh evidence or an explicit exploratory interpretation.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: Why does a sample answer vary?
stages.miniPlan: Population, sample, statistic, and parameter in four labeled positions.
stages.interactionPlan: Draw one explicit sample and show its mean; retain the population as the stable reference.
stages.reference: Observed statistics vary from sample to sample. Probability provides a language for that uncertainty and sampling distributions describe how an estimator behaves under repeated study designs.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: How are probability, density, and frequency different?
stages.miniPlan: Discrete mass versus continuous interval area.
stages.interactionPlan: Select an interval and accumulate area; do not interpret continuous curve height as point probability.
stages.reference: Conditional probability P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B), for P(B) > 0, means the chance of A given B. Independence means P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B): knowing one event occurred does not change the chance of the other. Expectation E[X] is the probability-weighted average of a random variable; variance Var(X) = E[(X − E[X])²] measures its spread, when these quantities exist. A population distribution describes individual values. A sampling distribution describes a statistic—such as a mean—across repeated samples. Its standard deviation is the standard error.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How is a standard error calculated?
stages.miniPlan: SD, n, square root of n, and SE with units.
stages.interactionPlan: Work one numerical example; contrast individual-score spread with mean-estimate spread.
stages.reference: If individual scores have standard deviation 12, the mean of n=36 independent observations has standard error about 12/√36=2. Doubling n does not halve uncertainty; roughly quadrupling n does.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: What is the sampling distribution?
stages.miniPlan: One sample produces one dot in a distribution of means.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal the population → sample → mean chain before showing hundreds of means; explain CLT conditions in deeper reading.
stages.reference:
Discrete probability masses add directly, whereas continuous density integrates to probability over an interval. Density height is not itself point probability and may exceed one. A statistic is a random variable before data are observed, and its sampling distribution depends on the population, statistic and design. The central limit theorem supports many normal approximations but does not make every small or heavy-tailed sample normal. Standard deviation describes individual variation; standard error describes estimator variation. Clustering, unequal weights and finite-population sampling change the familiar independent-sample formula and the effective amount of information.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.question: What changes with sample size?

Assumptions

When the method fails

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I tell SD from SE?
stages.miniPlan: One short classification task plus a missing calculation.
stages.interactionPlan: Mix answer positions and explain every distractor; retain static answers and a new numerical transfer example.
stages.reference:
A sampling distribution describes…

Answer and explanation

A statistic across repeated samples. Its random object is the statistic produced by the sampling procedure.

Why does standard error often shrink with n?

Answer and explanation

Independent observations add information and averaging reduces noise. For a mean under independence, SE scales approximately as 1/√n.

Is a continuous density height a probability?

Answer and explanation

No; probability is area over an interval. A point has zero probability in a continuous model; interval area is probability.

If observations are clustered, naive SE is often…

Answer and explanation

Too small. Within-cluster similarity means less independent information than the row count suggests.

To halve a mean’s SE, n must be approximately…

Answer and explanation

Four times as large. Because SE is proportional to 1/√n, halving it requires quadrupling n.

stages.title: The Raw Data Cloud
stages.question: What differs between these class clouds?
stages.miniPlan: Class size, center, spread, and tilt.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect classes with stable row IDs and color/shape labels.
stages.reference:
Imagine sorting fruit into Apples and Pears based on two measurements: Sweetness ($X_1$) and Roundness ($X_2$).

In generative modeling, we look at where each class cluster sits and how the points are distributed across the features.

The Whole Idea of QDA

Quadratic Discriminant Analysis (QDA) is a supervised classification method. It models each class as its own independent multi-dimensional probability cloud.

Simple intuition: QDA asks: "Which of these distinct class clouds does this new coordinate fit into best?"

Unlike LDA (which forces every class to share the exact same shape), QDA allows each class to have its own unique spread, stretch, and tilt. This mathematical flexibility is what creates curved boundaries.

QDA Pipeline:

Labeled data → Split Train/Test → Fit class-specific shapes → Score new test coordinates → Make prediction → Evaluate performance

Tiny QDA Dictionary

Feature: An input variable/measurement (e.g., Sweetness, Roundness).

Label / Class: The category we want to predict (e.g., Apple, Pear).

Mean ($\mu$): The center coordinate of a class's data cloud.

Covariance Matrix ($\Sigma$): The learned shape, spread, and tilt of a class cloud.

Prior Probability ($\pi$): The baseline proportion of each class in the dataset.

Mahalanobis Distance: A shape-aware distance metric scaled by a class cloud's variance.

Posterior Probability: The calculated probability that a point belongs to a class after measuring its features.

Discriminant Score ($\delta$): The classification value calculated by QDA; highest score wins.

Regularization: Adding a small constant diagonal shift to stabilize covariance estimation.

Prior Probability Controls Apples ($N_A$): 80 Pears ($N_B$): 80

stages.title: Fitting QDA: What the Model Learns
stages.question: Which parameters does QDA estimate?
stages.miniPlan: Prior, mean, covariance; matrix entries with units.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a matrix cell to highlight ellipse spread/tilt; explain determinant volume and inverse scaling separately.
stages.reference:
To fit QDA, we estimate three key statistical parameters directly from our training set for each class $k$:

Covariance Matrix Anatomy

For our two features, the 2x2 Covariance Matrix is represented as:

$\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix} \text{Variance}(X_1) & \text{Covariance}(X_1, X_2) \\ \text{Covariance}(X_1, X_2) & \text{Variance}(X_2) \end{pmatrix}$

Diagonal entries: Represent the independent spread of Sweetness and Roundness.
Off-diagonal entries: Represent the relationship. A positive value means sweeter fruit is generally rounder, creating a diagonal tilt!

Determinants & Inverses

The Determinant ($|\Sigma_k|$): Is a covariance-volume scaling factor. Its square root, $\sqrt{|\Sigma_k|}$, corresponds more closely to geometric area or volume.

The Inverse ($\Sigma_k^{-1}$): Acts as a scaling standardizer. It mathematically divides distances by the variance in that specific direction so wide directions aren't artificially penalized.

Concept Check: What do the diagonal values in a covariance matrix represent?

Euclidean distance only measures straight-line distance. It assumes classes are perfect, un-tilted circles.

QDA uses Mahalanobis Distance, which measures distance in units of class-specific standard deviations, aligning with the class's natural stretch and tilt.

The posteriors are calculated assuming the features are strictly normally (Gaussian) distributed. If your real-world data is heavily skewed or multimodal, the model's confidence scores will be poorly calibrated!

stages.question: Why do unequal covariances yield a quadratic boundary?
stages.miniPlan: Shared versus nonshared quadratic terms.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle linear/quadratic boundaries with direct labels; distinguish geometric shape from a confidence claim.
stages.reference:
The decision boundary is defined mathematically as the curve where the score for Apples exactly equals the score for Pears:

$\delta_{\text{Apple}}(x) = \delta_{\text{Pear}}(x)$

Because the covariance matrices $\hat{\Sigma}_{\text{Apple}} \neq \hat{\Sigma}_{\text{Pear}}$, the quadratic terms in the equation do not cancel. The boundary naturally curves to encapsulate the unique shape characteristics of each class.

Use the controls below to directly overlay and compare LDA and QDA decision boundaries:

Concept Check: Why does the QDA decision boundary curve while LDA's is a straight line?

stages.title: Evaluating QDA on Unseen Data
stages.question: How should performance be evaluated while exploring?
stages.miniPlan: One confusion-cell calculation.
stages.interactionPlan: Display validation metrics while tuning; reserve test for locked settings and remove advice to repeatedly inspect changing test scores.
stages.reference:
Accuracy, Precision, Recall, and F1 Score are computed using standard equations. Observe how changing sample sizes or shapes on other stages immediately alters these validation scores!

Concept Check: Defining Apple as the positive class, what is a False Positive?

stages.title: Reading QDA Output
stages.question: What do prior and covariance outputs mean?
stages.miniPlan: Output item → source data → interpretation.
stages.interactionPlan: Focus/tap the log/table entries; state whether priors came from training frequencies or were supplied.
stages.reference: Concept Check: What does a prior probability of 0.70 for Apple mean?

stages.title: Regularization & Shape Playground
stages.question: What does regularization stabilize?
stages.miniPlan: Identity ridge versus pooled-covariance shrinkage.
stages.interactionPlan: Give separate controls or separate demonstrations; only the pooled path should be labeled as moving toward LDA.
stages.reference: A class covariance can be unstable or singular when there are few observations relative to features. Adding a small positive multiple of the identity improves invertibility but does not make unequal class covariances equal. Shrinking every class covariance toward the same pooled covariance creates a path toward LDA. The lab uses pooled shrinkage and a small numerical diagonal floor; the two interventions have different roles. Select the amount with validation, not the final test.

stages.title: Assumptions, Complexity & Synthesis
stages.question: When is the extra flexibility worth its cost?
stages.miniPlan: Parameter count by K and p with required sample support.
stages.interactionPlan: Change K/p and inspect covariance stability; conclude with a validation-based choice, not a shape-only rule.
stages.reference:
Every algorithm is a balance of flexibility and parameters. QDA estimates a separate covariance matrix for each class, which comes at a significant parameter cost.

Parameter Complexity Calculator

Adjust the class count ($K$) and feature count ($p$) to compare parameter counts:

Classes ($K$): 2 Features ($p$): 2 LDA Parameters:

7 10

When QDA Thrives:

  • Classes have completely different shapes and orientations.
  • The dataset is large enough to estimate parameters reliably.
  • Boundaries are naturally curved.

When QDA Struggles:

  • Extremely small datasets (leads to overfitting and singular matrices).
  • Datasets with many features (parameter explosion).
  • Outliers present that distort covariance matrix estimation.

Alternatives to QDA:

  • LDA: If dataset is small or class spreads are similar.
  • Logistic Regression: If you prefer to model class boundaries without making Gaussian distribution assumptions.
  • KNN or SVM: If decision boundaries are highly complex or non-Gaussian.

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: Why combine several trees?
stages.miniPlan: One unstable tree versus an average/vote.
stages.interactionPlan: Perturb one training sample and compare variability of single-tree and ensemble predictions.
stages.reference: A single tree is interpretable but unstable. Random forests average many deliberately varied trees so individual split noise cancels while shared predictive structure remains.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What makes trees different?
stages.miniPlan: Bootstrap rows and random candidate features.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal one tree's sample and a node's feature subset; distinguish row sampling from feature sampling.
stages.reference: Each tree sees a bootstrap sample and a random subset of candidate features at each split. Averaging mainly reduces variance when trees make partly independent errors.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How is a forest prediction produced?
stages.miniPlan: Three trees' votes or numeric predictions.
stages.interactionPlan: Accumulate one selected row's tree outputs; compute the aggregate directly.
stages.reference: One tree classifies 82% of validation cases, but across resamples it ranges from 74% to 87%. A 300-tree forest reaches 86% with a much narrower range. The gain comes from averaging; 300 trees are not 300 independent datasets.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: Why does correlation between trees matter?
stages.miniPlan: Independent versus highly similar prediction errors.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare averaging behavior under clearly labeled scenarios; keep bias and variance separate.
stages.reference:
Bootstrap samples vary observations and random feature subsets vary candidate splits. Diversity matters because averaging highly correlated trees removes less variance. Out-of-bag predictions provide a development estimate, but extensive optimisation against that estimate still needs outer evaluation. More trees reduce Monte Carlo noise; they do not cure leakage, biased sampling or drift. Permutation importance measures predictive reliance under disruption, not causality. Correlated predictors can substitute for one another, and partial dependence can average over unrealistic combinations. Leaf size and weighting also affect the smoothness and calibration of predicted probabilities.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: What is an out-of-bag prediction?
stages.miniPlan: In-bag membership across trees for one observation.
stages.interactionPlan: Compute votes only from trees that omitted the row; replace the current stylized OOB error curve if it remains labeled measured error.
stages.reference: Adjust tree count and features considered per split. Watch out-of-bag error stabilise and tree correlation change.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What problems do more trees not solve?
stages.miniPlan: Leakage, biased sampling, drift, and unreliable importance.
stages.interactionPlan: Show an ensemble agreeing on a wrong shortcut; explain permutation importance with correlated predictors.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

Training data must represent deployment, observations must respect split structure, and features must be available at prediction time.

When the method fails

Forests extrapolate poorly in regression, probabilities may need calibration, correlated predictors distort importance, and large forests cost memory and latency.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: How should a forest be tuned and validated?
stages.miniPlan: Leaf size, feature subset, class weights, OOB/CV, final test.
stages.interactionPlan: Tune on development estimates and compare to a baseline; do not treat OOB as an unlimited unbiased tuning resource.
stages.reference:
1. Build a simple tree baseline
  2. Place preprocessing inside resampling
  3. Tune feature sampling and leaf constraints
  4. Grow enough trees for stable error
  5. Check calibration and subgroup performance
  6. Evaluate the locked forest once

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What should be reported?
stages.miniPlan: Evaluation design, parameters, class metrics, calibration, and importance limits.
stages.interactionPlan: Build a forest summary with explicit predictive rather than causal interpretation.
stages.reference:
What to report: Report tree count, feature sampling, depth/leaf constraints, seed, resampling, OOB use, final metrics with uncertainty, calibration and importance method.

Common misuse: Treating impurity importance as a causal ranking of variables.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I trace a held-out vote?
stages.miniPlan: A row present in some bootstrap samples and absent in others.
stages.interactionPlan: Select the valid OOB voters and compute the result; give feedback explaining excluded trees.
stages.reference:
Answer and explanation

Variance. Averaging unstable learners reduces variance when errors are not perfectly correlated.

Answer and explanation

Decorrelating trees. Less-correlated errors average away more effectively.

OOB error can be misused when…

Answer and explanation

Extensive tuning repeatedly optimises it without outer evaluation. Repeated optimisation makes the estimate part of model selection.

Answer and explanation

Predictive reliance under a perturbation, not causality. Association, correlation and feature dependence shape importance.

A forest regression prediction outside the training range is…

Answer and explanation

stages.title: The problem
stages.question: Why can a high R-squared coexist with a bad model?
stages.miniPlan: Similar summary score, different residual patterns.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare two labeled examples on equal axes and ask which model claim is unsupported.
stages.reference: A fitted equation always returns numbers; diagnostics ask whether the functional form, error behaviour, and individual observations make those numbers defensible.

stages.title: Intuition and objective
stages.question: What is a residual checking?
stages.miniPlan: Actual − fitted value, with one row.
stages.interactionPlan: Link raw plot, fitted value, and residual plot by observation ID.
stages.reference: Residuals should fluctuate without systematic shape around zero. Curvature signals missing functional form, a funnel signals changing variance, a Q–Q departure challenges normal-error inference, and an isolated high-leverage point can rotate the fitted line.

stages.title: Worked example
stages.question: How does an influential point differ from an outlier?
stages.miniPlan: Residual size, leverage, and coefficient change.
stages.interactionPlan: Remove/restore a selected point in a controlled comparison; do not prescribe automatic deletion.
stages.reference: A salary model has residual spread of ±5k for junior staff and ±40k for senior staff. The fan pattern violates constant variance. Coefficients may still describe a mean pattern, but ordinary standard errors and a single-width prediction band are unreliable; robust errors or a variance model may be needed.

stages.title: Reasoning with the method
stages.question: Which diagnostic answers which question?
stages.miniPlan: Residual/fitted, Q–Q, scale-location, leverage, and VIF.
stages.interactionPlan: Focus one diagnostic at a time with a question and response; distinguish predictor normality from residual inference assumptions.
stages.reference:
Residual-versus-fitted plots examine mean form and variance structure. Q–Q plots compare ordered residuals with a reference distribution and matter for inference that relies on that reference; predictors and outcomes need not themselves be normal. Leverage describes unusual predictor combinations. Influence describes how fitted results change, so Cook’s distance is a screening tool rather than a deletion command. VIF shows how strongly a predictor overlaps the others and can explain wide coefficient intervals without proving bias. Diagnostics should prompt a scientific response: correct errors, represent nonlinearity, model variance or dependence, and report justified sensitivity analyses.

A defensible analysis connects the mathematical target to the real decision. Identify what is estimated, which observations contribute independent information, what choices are learned from data, and which uncertainty remains after fitting. Then ask how the conclusion would change under another reasonable sample, a plausible alternative specification, or a shift in the deployment population. This reasoning must happen before the final test set is opened. The test result evaluates the locked procedure; it does not choose that procedure. Sensitivity analysis is most useful when it is planned around credible failure modes rather than used to search for a preferred answer.

stages.title: Interactive laboratory
stages.question: What does a curve or funnel suggest?
stages.miniPlan: Healthy/curved/fanning residual thumbnails.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a pattern with a stable dataset; link a possible remedy to a refit, labeled illustrative if no fit occurs.
stages.reference: Switch between healthy, curved, funnel-shaped, and influential residual patterns. The plot and recommended response update together.

stages.title: Assumptions and failure modes
stages.question: What cannot a residual plot establish?
stages.miniPlan: Independence from design, causal validity, and limited sample power.
stages.interactionPlan: Show a time/group violation even when the scatter looks harmless.
stages.reference:
Assumptions

Correct functional form, independent errors, stable conditional variance, and residual normality when classical small-sample inference needs it.

When the method fails

Outliers, high leverage, extrapolation, omitted nonlinearities, dependence and multicollinearity can destabilise estimates or uncertainty.

stages.title: Practical workflow
stages.question: How should a diagnostic change the analysis?
stages.miniPlan: Symptom → investigate → justified model change → validate.
stages.interactionPlan: Choose a response and compare outcomes; retain the original dataset and model for sensitivity analysis.
stages.reference:
1. Plot outcome and predictors
  2. Fit the pre-specified model
  3. Inspect residual–fitted and Q–Q plots
  4. Check leverage, Cook’s distance and VIF
  5. Run justified sensitivity analyses
  6. Validate predictions on unseen data

stages.title: Interpretation and reporting
stages.question: What should the report say?
stages.miniPlan: Finding, changed assumption/model, sensitivity, and resulting uncertainty.
stages.interactionPlan: Assemble a short diagnostic note; distinguish a confidence interval from a prediction interval.
stages.reference:
What to report: Report coefficients with confidence intervals, residual standard error, diagnostic findings, influential-case sensitivity, validation error, and prediction intervals.

Common misuse: Deleting observations solely because their removal produces significance.

stages.title: Knowledge checks
stages.question: Can I match symptom and response?
stages.miniPlan: A novel plot and a choice of scientifically justified actions.
stages.interactionPlan: Require a reason before reveal; include a keep-and-investigate answer rather than always delete or transform.
stages.reference:
A widening residual funnel indicates…

Answer and explanation

Heteroscedasticity. Residual variance changes with the fitted value.

Leverage differs from influence because…

Answer and explanation

Leverage describes unusual predictor position; influence describes effect on the fit. Influence combines position and discrepancy to measure how much the fit changes.

For one future observation use…

Answer and explanation

A prediction interval. Prediction intervals include mean-estimation uncertainty and individual noise.

A curved residual pattern suggests…

Answer and explanation

Missing functional form. The mean relationship has not been represented adequately.

Answer and explanation

None of correctness, causality, or transportability. R² alone cannot validate the model.

stages.title: The Raw Target
stages.question: What are we predicting?
stages.miniPlan: One home's features and numeric price.
stages.interactionPlan: Link the row to the plotted house; keep outcome units on axes and prediction labels.
stages.reference:
A regression tree is a model that helps us predict a number. Not a category like "cat or dog", but a continuous value like an exam score, temperature, or a house price.

Let's look at a small dataset of houses. We want to predict the Price (in thousands) based entirely on the Size of the house (in square meters).

stages.title: From Dataset to Model
stages.question: Which rows can influence training?
stages.miniPlan: Train/validation/test role cards with immutable IDs.
stages.interactionPlan: Reveal membership without allowing test outcomes to guide splits.
stages.reference:
Before teaching an algorithm, we need a disciplined plan. A standard Machine Learning workflow protects us from creating models that look perfect on paper but fail in the real world.

The ML Pipeline: Target y The number we want to predict (e.g., Price). Features X The inputs we use (e.g., Size). Data Split Divide points into

Training Validation

sets. Tune & Predict Limit tree growth to generalize and make unseen predictions.

The data has been split. We use the 16

training houses validation houses

hidden to test general performance.

stages.title: The Clumsy Guess
stages.question: Why start with the mean?
stages.miniPlan: Three target values, their mean, and squared errors.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare candidate constant predictions and locate the minimum RSS at the mean.
stages.reference:
At the very start, the tree puts all houses in one big group (the Root Node). Before asking any questions, it asks: "If I had to guess one price for all houses, what should I use?"

The standard answer is the average. If we take all 16 training house prices and average them, we get exactly $483.1k.

Root Prediction = Average(y) = 483.1

stages.title: The First Split
stages.question: How can one question improve the prediction?
stages.miniPlan: Left and right child counts and means.
stages.interactionPlan: Slide a split and show piecewise-constant predictions; keep equality routing explicit.
stages.reference:
Now the tree asks a question to divide the data: "Can I split the houses into 2 groups so the prices inside each group become more similar?"

It checks a "cut point". Based on the math, the best first rule is: Is Size ≤ 100?

Yes No

Now, instead of one average for everything, we have two averages. A lower average ($363.3k) for smaller houses, and a higher average ($637.1k) for bigger houses.

stages.title: The Error Engine (RSS)
stages.question: How is a split scored?
stages.miniPlan: Parent RSS minus left RSS minus right RSS.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a candidate threshold and trace both children's contributions to total improvement.
stages.reference:
How did it know to split exactly at 100? The algorithm is "Greedy". It tests candidate split points between sorted training values and chooses the one that leaves the least amount of mess.

It measures "mess" using the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS). It squares all the red error lines and adds them up. Lower training RSS means a closer training fit, not necessarily better prediction.

Before vs After Split ... Root RSS ... Split RSS ... Reduction Best first split found. This threshold gives the lowest RSS among the tested candidate splits.

stages.title: Real Trees Check Many Questions
stages.question: Why test many candidate questions?
stages.miniPlan: Feature/threshold/RSS ranking table.
stages.interactionPlan: Step through adjacent-value midpoint candidates; keep ties deterministic and explain greedy search.
stages.reference:
In real machine learning, a regression tree is not limited to checking just one feature. It considers multiple input variables simultaneously, checking every possible partition point across size, age, rooms, and locations.

The tree runs a "Greedy Search": it picks the single feature and threshold that yields the largest drop in RSS.

Feature Candidate Rule Post RSS Reduction
Size Size ≤ 100 m² 61,743 +295,201
Rooms Rooms ≤ 3 74,300 +282,644
MRT Dist Distance ≤ 2 km 82,000 +274,944
Age Age ≤ 15 years 90,500 +266,444

Note: For teaching clarity, the extra feature splits here are illustrative. In a real dataset, the tree would calculate these RSS values from actual feature columns.

Winning Split:

Size wins because partitioning by Size ≤ 100 m² leaves the least error (lowest post-split RSS) among all candidate features.

stages.title: Recursive Splitting
stages.question: What makes the process recursive?
stages.miniPlan: The same split recipe reused in one child.
stages.interactionPlan: Expand one node at a time and update its spatial region; keep other nodes stable.
stages.reference:
After finding the best first split, the tree does the exact same thing inside each new group. It splits, then splits inside the split. Like cutting a cake into pieces, then cutting those pieces again.

This is called Recursive Binary Splitting. With every split, the prediction line stops looking flat and starts looking like a set of stairs.

stages.title: The Anatomy of a Tree
stages.question: How do I read a tree?
stages.miniPlan: Root, question, branch, leaf, prediction.
stages.interactionPlan: Trace one selected house through both tree and feature space, with keyboard step controls.
stages.reference:
Even though we call it a tree, data scientists draw them upside down.

  • Root Node: The top, where all data starts.
  • Internal Node: A fork in the road where a decision is checked (e.g., Size ≤ 100).
  • Terminal Node (Leaf): The final box that gives the prediction number.
Interactive:

stages.title: The Overfitting Trap
stages.question: Why can a deeper tree overfit?
stages.miniPlan: Leaf sizes and train/validation error comparison.
stages.interactionPlan: Increase depth on a fixed dataset; show tiny leaves without revealing final test metrics.
stages.reference:
What happens if we never tell the tree to stop? It will keep splitting until every single data point is alone in its own leaf, creating a zero-error fit on training data.

This creates a massive risk of Overfitting—the model memorizes the random noise in our training set and fails to generalize to unseen houses.

Tree Depth Bias Variance Description
Too Shallow High Low Underfits (Misses pattern)
Balanced Medium Medium Best fit (Generalizes)
Too Deep Low High Overfits (Memorizes noise)

stages.title: Stopping Rules
stages.question: Which stopping rules constrain growth?
stages.miniPlan: Maximum depth versus minimum leaf size.
stages.interactionPlan: Change one rule at a time and explain which proposed split becomes invalid.
stages.reference:
To prevent overfitting, we enforce Stopping Rules (also known as pre-pruning). We restrict depth and control minimum partition requirements before splits can occur.

  • Do not choose the model based solely on the lowest training error.
  • Use validation error to estimate performance on unseen, real-world data.
  • Prefer lower validation error. Minimize this value to find the sweet spot.
  • If two settings perform similarly, always pick the simpler tree (Occam's razor).
  • Use both rules together: max_depth limits levels, while min_samples_leaf prevents tiny leaves that isolate individual outliers.

Notice that making the tree deeper eventually makes training error drop to 0, but the validation error starts increasing. That turning point is the sweet spot.

stages.title: Pruning: Let It Grow, Then Cut It Back
stages.question: How does pruning differ from stopping early?
stages.miniPlan: Full subtree versus pruned leaf and its penalty.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub a pruning path; keep validation-based selection separate from training cost complexity.
stages.reference:
Sometimes stopping early (pre-pruning) can be too short-sighted. It might stop before discovering splits that become useful in combination with other splits.

The alternative is Post-Pruning: We allow the tree to grow deep first, and then collapse weak, low-utility sub-branches back into parent leaf nodes using a complexity penalty called ccp_alpha.

stages.title: Trees vs. Lines
stages.question: When does a tree differ from a line?
stages.miniPlan: Smooth additive trend versus stepwise prediction.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare both fits on identical observations and splits; avoid implying one always wins.
stages.reference:
Linear regression fits a smooth, straight line. It assumes a constant rate of change. Regression trees carve the world into intervals and assign a flat average to each.

If the data has sudden thresholds or "if/then" behaviors, trees capture it naturally. If it's a smooth trend, lines win.

stages.title: Reality Check: Limitations
stages.question: What are the characteristic failure cases?
stages.miniPlan: Extrapolation, instability, staircase, and axis-aligned split thumbnails.
stages.interactionPlan: Switch a labeled failure scenario; use a controlled data perturbation to show instability.
stages.reference:
While extremely powerful and explainable, single regression trees have key engineering limitations that you must look out for in practice.

Trees predict flat averages. If a house size is larger than any seen in training (e.g., 220 m²), the tree cannot continue a trend upward; it flatlines at the average of the largest leaf.

Jagged Step Predictions Staircase

Real-world factors often rise smoothly. Trees build staircases with sudden step jumps, struggling to cleanly represent smooth curves without huge depths.

High Instability (Variance) High Variance

A tiny shift in data (e.g., swapping one point's price) can completely re-arrange the root split boundary, producing a highly unstable prediction layout.

Axis-Aligned Splits Orthogonal

Basic trees split one feature at a time at right angles, making it difficult to capture diagonal correlations (like price dropping when size decreases and age increases simultaneously).

Easy to Overfit High Complexity

Without strict stopping rules or pruning, deep trees will easily grow until they isolate every single point, memorizing individual training points instead of discovering generalizable patterns.

stages.title: Synthesis
stages.question: Can I reconstruct the algorithm?
stages.miniPlan: Arrange root → candidates → best split → recurse → validate → leaf.
stages.interactionPlan: Complete the sequence and explain why an ensemble may help; do not promise every ensemble removes bias.
stages.reference:
Let's review the final sequence to build and use a regression tree:

. Put all training data in the

Root Node

. 2. Test possible splits (greedy thresholds) across all available features. 3. Pick the feature/split that results in the

lowest RSS

. 4. Repeat the process recursively inside each new branch. 5. Use validation error to choose stopping rules or pruning, instead of trusting training error alone. 6. Each final leaf predicts the

average target value

While a single regression tree can be unstable on its own, this recursive logic is the fundamental building block for advanced modern algorithms like Random Forests and Gradient Boosting.

Ensemble Learning:

Ensembles improve single trees by combining hundreds of them, smoothing out jagged steps and yielding highly stable predictions.

stages.title: Points, labels, and a decision boundary
stages.question: What does a decision boundary decide?
stages.miniPlan: Signed score and class label for one point.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a point and inspect its score; reserve probability language for calibrated output.
stages.reference:
Each point is one labelled training row with two features. Colour marks the class. A classifier needs a rule that places a future point on one side or the other.

In two dimensions the boundary is a line. In three dimensions it is a plane. Beyond that, it becomes a hyperplane, a dramatic name for the same separating idea.

The plot uses two features because humans remain tragically dependent on visible space. The model itself can work with many features.

stages.title: Why not choose any separating line?
stages.question: Why is one separator preferable to another?
stages.miniPlan: Two correct separators with different nearest-point clearance.
stages.interactionPlan: Slide a candidate line and highlight the limiting points.
stages.reference:
When the classes are separable, several lines can classify every training point correctly. Training accuracy alone cannot tell us which line is safer.

Narrow clearance

Fits the training rows, but a small measurement change can flip a prediction.

Wide clearance

Leaves more room before the nearest point crosses the boundary.

A linear SVM adds a preference: choose the separator with the greatest distance to the closest points from either class.

Quick check: what extra criterion does SVM use?It chooses the separating line with the largest margin, subject to the model’s allowance for violations.

stages.title: The margin is protected space
stages.question: What is the margin?
stages.miniPlan: Decision plane versus ±1 support planes and geometric width.
stages.interactionPlan: Link the weight norm to margin width; keep functional and geometric margins distinct.
stages.reference:
The margin is the gap between two parallel support planes touching the closest training points on each side.

Margin boundaries: wᵀx + b = +1 and −1

Geometric margin width = 2 / ‖w‖

Maximising the margin is equivalent to keeping the weight vector small while still satisfying the classification constraints.

A wide margin can make the separator less sensitive. It cannot rescue biased data, leakage, poor labels, or a mismatched kernel. Geometry is useful, not divine intervention.

stages.title: Support vectors are the points that matter most
stages.question: Why do support vectors matter?
stages.miniPlan: A safely distant point versus a constraining point.
stages.interactionPlan: Move each in a fixed-data example and compare refits; qualify ties and soft-margin cases.
stages.reference:
Support vectors lie on or inside the margin. They directly constrain the fitted boundary.

Only rows with αᵢ > 0 are support vectors.

Move a distant, safely classified point a little and the boundary may not change. Move a support vector and the solution can shift immediately.

Important distinction:

“support vector” means the row constrains this fitted margin. It does not mean the row is causally or commercially important in every possible sense.

stages.title: Hard margins break when reality overlaps
stages.question: Why allow violations?
stages.miniPlan: Slack 0, between 0 and 1, and above 1 examples.
stages.interactionPlan: Introduce an overlapping point and show the constrained fit; handle the boundary case ξ=1 precisely.
stages.reference:
A hard-margin SVM demands perfect separation with every row outside the margin. Real classes overlap, labels contain errors, and outliers appear because datasets enjoy sabotage.

A soft-margin SVM introduces slack variables ξᵢ so violations are allowed but penalised.

yᵢ(wᵀxᵢ + b) ≥ 1 − ξᵢ, with ξᵢ ≥ 0

SlackMeaning
ξ = 0Correct and on or beyond the margin
0 < ξ ≤ 1Correct side, but inside the margin
ξ > 1Misclassified

stages.title: C decides how expensive violations are
stages.question: What does C penalize?
stages.miniPlan: Wider margin with violations versus expensive violations.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub C on a logarithmic scale; compare actual training objective terms and validation behavior.
stages.reference:
Small C

Violations are cheaper. The model accepts more errors to preserve a wider, smoother margin.

Large C

Violations are expensive. The model fits training rows more aggressively, often with a narrower margin.

C is an inverse regularisation parameter: larger C means less regularisation.

A huge C does not mean “more accurate”. It means “punish training violations more”, which can also mean “memorise the noise with confidence”.

stages.title: Scale features before comparing distances
stages.question: Why fit scaling inside a fold?
stages.miniPlan: Training mean/SD applied to a new row.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare raw and scaled geometry with the same data; preserve feature-unit explanations.
stages.reference:
SVM geometry uses dot products and distances. A feature ranging from 0 to 100,000 can dominate another ranging from 0 to 1, even when the smaller-scale feature is actually informative.

standardised value = (value − training mean) ÷ training standard deviation

Fit the scaler inside each training fold, then apply that fitted transformation to validation, test, and production rows.

Two distinct failures:

scaling before the split leaks information; scaling the test set separately changes the coordinate system. Both are wrong in impressively different ways.

stages.title: Hinge loss ignores easy correct points
stages.question: Why do easy correct points have zero hinge loss?
stages.miniPlan: y·f(x) and max(0,1−margin).
stages.interactionPlan: Move a query along the hinge-loss curve and link its margin position.
stages.reference:
hinge loss = max(0, 1 − y × f(x))

Signed margin y f(x)LossInterpretation
≥ 10Correct and safely beyond the margin
0 to 1positiveCorrect but inside the margin
≤ 0≥ 1Misclassified

Once a point is correctly beyond the margin, its hinge loss is zero. Distant easy points stop pulling the boundary.

Quick check: y f(x) = 1.7. What is the loss?max(0, 1 − 1.7) = 0.

stages.title: The decision score is not automatically a probability
stages.question: Why is a score not a probability?
stages.miniPlan: Score / signed distance / calibrated probability distinctions.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect a score and an explicitly fitted calibration example; never relabel sigmoid output as calibrated without evidence.
stages.reference:
The decision function reports which side of the boundary a row occupies and how strongly it lies in that direction.

larger positive f(x) → stronger Class +1 decision

larger negative f(x) → stronger Class −1 decision

For a linear SVM, the score relates to signed distance after accounting for ‖w‖. For a kernel SVM, treat it as a boundary score rather than literal distance in the original plot.

f(x) = 2 does not mean 200%, nor twice the probability of f(x) = 1. Probability estimates require a separate calibration model fitted with held-out predictions.

stages.title: A straight boundary cannot solve every pattern
stages.question: How can a nonlinear feature help?
stages.miniPlan: x₁, x₂, and squared radius for one point.
stages.interactionPlan: Map a ring example to radius space and show the resulting simple threshold.
stages.reference:
Imagine one class forming an inner cluster and another forming an outer ring. No straight line can separate them in the original two-feature space.

A transformed feature such as squared radius can reveal the structure:

In transformed space, a simple threshold on r² can separate inner from outer points. A curved boundary in the original plot can still correspond to a linear rule elsewhere.

stages.title: The kernel trick avoids explicit feature explosion
stages.question: What does a kernel compute?
stages.miniPlan: Similarity of two selected points at two gamma values.
stages.interactionPlan: Inspect an RBF influence profile; link C/gamma changes to the real fitted boundary with stale-fit cancellation.
stages.reference:
A kernel computes similarities that behave like inner products in a richer feature space, without explicitly constructing every transformed coordinate.

RBF: K(x,z) = exp(−γ ‖x − z‖²)

Small gamma

Each point has broad influence. The decision surface changes slowly.

Large gamma

Influence becomes local. The boundary can wrap tightly around training points.

Large gamma plus large C can create an intricate boundary that remembers noise instead of learning structure.

stages.title: Tune the whole pipeline inside cross-validation
stages.question: How do we choose C and gamma?
stages.miniPlan: Pipeline inside each inner fold, outer evaluation separate.
stages.interactionPlan: Explore a bounded validation grid; use train-fitted scaling and keep final test sealed.
stages.reference:
Kernel, C, gamma, class weights, and preprocessing are hyperparameters. Choose them using validation folds inside the development data.

Pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC())

GridSearchCV(C, gamma, kernel, scoring) Create an untouched final test set when the dataset is large enough. Fit scaling and feature processing inside each training fold. Score candidate settings using a metric aligned with the task. Refit on all development data, then evaluate once on the test set. Search C and gamma on logarithmic scales. If the winner sits at the edge, extend the range rather than declaring the boundary divinely optimal.

stages.title: Measure the errors the problem actually cares about
stages.question: What matters beyond accuracy?
stages.miniPlan: Error costs, minority recall, calibration, and multiclass strategy.
stages.interactionPlan: Select a concrete goal and inspect matching validation metrics; explain OVR/OVO separately from the binary illustration.
stages.reference:
Accuracy alone can hide minority-class failures. Use confusion matrices, per-class recall, and precision–recall analysis when the positive class is rare.

Class imbalance

Consider class weights when minority-class mistakes deserve a larger penalty.

Operational thresholds

Tune the decision threshold on validation data when the default boundary is unsuitable.

Calibration

Map held-out SVM scores to probabilities using sigmoid, isotonic, or another calibration method.

Multiclass

Combine binary models using one-vs-rest or one-vs-one decisions.

One-vs-one classifiers: K(K−1)/2

One-vs-rest classifiers: K A calibrated 0.8 has a frequency meaning: among cases assigned about 0.8, roughly 80% should belong to that class. Raw margin scores make no such promise.

stages.title: Change the knobs and watch the boundary answer back
stages.question: Can I diagnose the fitted boundary?
stages.miniPlan: Support count, chosen settings, validation result, and a query receipt.
stages.interactionPlan: Add a labeled training point explicitly, refit, and compare; preserve a baseline and provide an equivalent form input.
stages.reference:
scale within a pipeline start linear when appropriate cross-validate C and kernel inspect support-vector count measure class-specific errors calibrate only when needed

Strengths

Effective in high dimensions, flexible kernels, margin regularisation, sparse dependence on support vectors.

Limits

Kernel training can scale poorly, tuning matters greatly, probabilities are not native, nonlinear models are hard to interpret globally.

Final concept check: extremely large RBF gamma?Each point’s influence becomes very local, enabling an irregular boundary and increasing overfitting risk.

stages.reference:
Before any complex math, a time series begins as a sequence of observations. Imagine a company asking: "What will product demand look like over the next two years?"

In standard data analysis, you can shuffle rows without losing meaning. In time series, order matters. Because today affects tomorrow, shuffling the dates destroys the story.

stages.title: The Time Plot
stages.question: What should I notice before modeling?
stages.miniPlan: Trend, recurring pattern, and unusual point thumbnails.
stages.interactionPlan: Tap or focus a date to pin its value; highlight time windows without requiring a hover.

The very first step in analysis is visual. A Time Plot connects our raw observations chronologically.

By mapping time on the x-axis and our measured value on the y-axis, human intuition can instantly spot behaviors that spreadsheets hide. Does the sequence climb steadily? Does it repeat in a wave? Are there violent spikes?

stages.title: The Assumption of Stationarity
stages.question: What stays stable in a stationary process?
stages.miniPlan: Mean, variance, and lag covariance definitions.
stages.interactionPlan: Compare drifting mean and changing variance separately; use a reading window without implying it proves stationarity.
stages.reference:
Many advanced statistical models require a series to be stationary before forecasting. For weak stationarity, the mean and finite variance are constant, and autocovariance depends only on lag, not calendar time.

  • Constant Mean: The average does not drift up or down.
  • Constant Variance: The spread (volatility) stays consistent.
  • Lag-dependent Autocovariance: Covariance between observations depends on how far apart they are, not when they occur.

Watch the rolling moving average on the plot. If it climbs or falls significantly, the mean is not constant. This series violates the assumptions of basic autoregressive modeling and requires transformation.

stages.title: Fixing It: Differencing
stages.question: What does differencing actually subtract?
stages.miniPlan: This month − previous month, with original units.
stages.interactionPlan: Select two adjacent values and trace the resulting difference; show that differencing does not guarantee stationarity.
stages.reference:
To stabilize the mean of a trending series, we apply differencing. Instead of looking at raw values, we analyze the change between consecutive months.

t t t-1

Differencing can remove or reduce certain trends and help achieve stationarity. Check the transformed series: one difference does not guarantee stationarity.

stages.title: Looking to the Past (Lags & ACF)
stages.question: What is a lag?
stages.miniPlan: The same series shifted by one and twelve periods.
stages.interactionPlan: Scrub lag while linking paired points and the ACF bar; explain approximate bounds and multiple-lag interpretation.
stages.reference: Lag k compares observations k time units apart. The displayed sample autocorrelation uses a common normalization: sum of (yₜ − mean)(yₜ₋ₖ − mean), divided by the sum of squared centered values across the full series. Its interpretation depends on trend, seasonality, sample size, and the fitted model. Approximate significance bands are not displayed here; a sequence of sample correlations should not be interpreted as independent causal tests. The lag view shows the actual paired values used for the selected gap.

stages.title: Forecasting the Future
stages.question: How do we evaluate forecasts honestly?
stages.miniPlan: Expanding-window train/validation strip.
stages.interactionPlan: Step the forecast origin forward; compare a real naive baseline, and label the current forecast fan as heuristic until calibrated intervals replace it.
stages.reference:
Validation must move forward in time. Never randomly shuffle observations. Use a chronological holdout, expanding-window evaluation, or rolling-window evaluation, and state whether forecasts are one-step or multi-step. Compare against naïve, seasonal-naïve, drift and moving-average baselines before treating a complex forecast as useful.

Since this is an interactive environment, we project the future using a structural simulation forecast built from our known trend and seasonal generators, rather than estimating an ARIMA model from scratch.

A forecast is an estimate, not a prophecy. The shaded area represents the 95% prediction interval.

Note: The expanding fan shown here is a simplified heuristic to illustrate how uncertainty accumulates over time, rather than a mathematically derived forecast variance.

stages.title: Diagnostics: Evaluating Residuals
stages.question: What patterns should residuals not retain?
stages.miniPlan: Residual definition with one date's calculation.
stages.interactionPlan: Toggle a missing seasonal component and show residual ACF; distinguish random-looking residuals from proven model validity.
stages.reference:
How do we know if a real-world forecasting model is adequate? We subtract the model's historical predictions from the actual raw data to check the residuals.

t t t
  • Centered around zero: No overall drift up or down.
  • Constant spread: Variance shouldn't wildly fan out.
  • No waves or patterns: All seasonality and trend should be captured by the model.
  • Occasional outliers: Random spikes are normal, but they shouldn't cluster.

Toggle the switch to see what happens when a model fails to capture the underlying seasonality. A robust model leaves residuals that closely resemble pure random noise.

stages.title: Limitations & Caveats
stages.question: When might yesterday stop predicting tomorrow?
stages.miniPlan: Stable period versus structural break.
stages.interactionPlan: Add a level shift and compare rolling versus expanding fitting windows; explain the conditional nature of forecasts.
stages.reference:
Time series models fundamentally rely on the assumption that the future will structurally resemble the past. It is crucial not to overclaim the certainty of any forecast.

  • Black Swan Events: Standard models cannot predict unprecedented external shocks (pandemics, sudden market crashes).
  • Structural Breaks: If a company pivots its business model at month 100, data from month 1 is no longer highly relevant.
  • Infinite Horizons: Prediction intervals eventually grow so wide that long-term forecasts become practically useless.
